title: Penn State men's basketball defeats Mississippi State behind 2nd half performance
author: Myles Hannak | Sports Editor
description:
It just means more.

Penn State faced its first SEC opponent since its 2023 NCAA Tournament clash, which ended in a win over Texas A&M. This time around, the Nittany Lions continued the trend with a win over Mississippi State, 68-63, in the third-place game of the Battle 4 Atlantis Championship Bracket.

The blue and white started with even tempo as the Bulldogs, behind a starting lineup that inserted wing Brant Byers instead of Thomas Allard — who’d struggled in Penn State’s last clash against No. 24 Memphis, going 0-of-6 from the field.

Despite an even pace between the two sides, Mike Rhoades’ squad couldn’t stop a Mississippi State unit lugged along by senior guard Tajuan Simpkins, who had 10 points on 3-of-4 shooting through ten minutes — the score was 18-15 in the Bulldogs’ favor.

Penn State continued to hang in the game with Mississippi State despite the Bulldogs’ consistent scoring, yet it was a complete team approach for the blue and white. Rather than usual 7-footer Ivan Jurić as the conduit of the offense, big man Tim Oboh saw minutes instead.

The Zagreb, Croatia, native remained a key part of the offense, however, as Jurić had nine points and seven rebounds, both team highs, as well as two long-range makes. Both teams shot under 40% from the field at the break in an offensively sparse game; Mississippi State led 36-29.

That deficit doubled for Rhoades’ unit after five minutes to start the second half, as Penn State went 1-for-7 on field goal attempts out of the break. With 14:23 left, Jurić snagged a rebound to mark his eighth consecutive double-double, setting program history and offering a lift in a game that had slipped out of reach.

"It feels great just seeing the work pay off, and (I) just would want to give credit to my coaches that work with me throughout the summer," Jurić said. "I'm just super excited just for my work to be paying off against great opponents."

The blue and white went on a quick run at the midpoint of the second frame to cut the deficit to 10, highlighted by an and-one from guard Dasonte Bowen. That soon turned into a 10-0 Penn State run, which cut it to a five-point game, as the Bulldogs couldn’t score to end their drought.

Bowen eventually tied it on a floater, as the blue and white’s defense continued to hold firm — setting up a 54-54 game with a little under seven minutes.

Behind Bowen and Jurić, the Nittany Lions found the basket. Allard and Byers became effective spot-up shooting threats in the second half to giving the blue and white a downtown edge.

"When we all lock in and really put it together, I think we're capable of being anybody we play," Bowen said. "I think we showed that tonight, and I think our veteranship really showed. Not crumbling when we were down by 16, and being able to just stick together and chop it down play by play."

Penn State took a lead late in the second half for its first advantage since early in the opening minutes, and began to slow the pace to confidently attempt a second-half steal for the result.

The blue and white ultimately stole the game with its second-half performance, despite a late Bulldogs push where they had a threatening look. Penn State’s second-half defensive performance pushed it forward, as it held the Bulldogs to 28.1% from the field in the final frame and went 1-for-10 from downtown.

For the Nittany Lions, Jurić had 15 points and 17 rebounds with two long-range makes and a team-high four assists. Bowen scored 18 for a Penn State high, while Byers and Allard both benefitted from the rotation switch.

"I just thought offensively we got the ball hopping a little bit, hit some threes," Rhoades said. "Brant and Thomas on the same night made some threes — That was huge, and I thought we got downhill a little bit."

Allard scored 11, while Byers had 13 points and three blocks. Fifth-year forward Josh Reed struggled to score, going 1-of-7 from the field.

The Nittany Lions shot 38.9% as a team and 42.3% from three, while they also committed nine more turnovers than Mississippi State.

As a result, the blue and white split the games in its inaugural Battle 4 Atlantis appearance and improved to 1-2 against Quad 3 opponents this year. Penn State now sits at 6-2.

Injury report

Guard Roberts Blums remains sidelined due to a broken finger, only appearing in the blue and white’s season opener on Nov. 2.

Up next

Penn State returns to Happy Valley for its first game of December on Tuesday against UAlbany. It’s the blue and white’s Fight for Literacy game with tipoff at 7 p.m.

title: Penn State women’s basketball overwhelmed by No. 25 Baylor in Paradise Jam
author: Gianna Dowling | Sports Editor
description:
The Lady Lions set sail to the U.S. Virgin Islands for their Thanksgiving week affairs.

Penn State kicked off its time at the Paradise Jam against No. 25 Baylor, its first ranked opponent of the season.

The Bears proved to be too much for coach Tanisha Wright’s squad to handle, as the blue and white fell 82-56.

Penn State won the tipoff and quickly got on the board behind an Enjulina Gonzalez short-range jumper. After forcing a Baylor turnover, the Lady Lions had a chance to go up two possessions less than two minutes in, but Savannah White missed two free throws.

However, the graduate student made up for the missed points on her next try, finding an open spot to score inside the paint.

A perfect trip to the charity stripe for Reese Ross gave the Bears their first points of the game. From there, it was a back-and-forth battle until the five-minute media timeout, with Baylor holding a 13-11 edge.

Sophomore guard Ava Black’s steal and score out of the break tied it again, but nine unanswered Baylor points broke the game open.

Bears’ coach Nicki Collen’s call to put on a daunting press out of the break proved to be the difference maker as her squad held a 22-13 lead at the end of the opening frame. Penn State, meanwhile, couldn’t hold its early-quarter momentum, going scoreless in the final three and a half minutes.

The Lady Lions used their best efforts to crawl back in the opening portions of the second frame, with early points from Gonzalez and forward Cristen Carter. However, every time the blue and white tried to call, Baylor answered.

Baylor’s leading scorer Taliah Scott scored five straight points, putting her squad up 32-17 with seven minutes left in the frame. Black got two from the free throw line for Penn State, marking the last points over the next two minutes before the break.

Ross broke away for a quick steal and score immediately following the timeout, as the turnovers continued to be costly for the Lady Lions.

The blue and white briefly stepped up on the defensive end, denying any Baylor opportunities. This was backed by a 5-0 run, putting Penn State within 10.

However, the Bears remained unfazed. Following a Devyn Quigley three, Baylor forward Kayla Nelms splashed one of her own, which started an 8-2 run to end the half.

The run was topped by a Scott 3-pointer that put the Bears up 42-26 at the half, its largest lead of the game. The guard led all scorers with 13 points. Gonzalez led the Penn State offense with eight points.

Both teams got off to a quick start in the second half, with eight combined points in the first minute. The scoring went quiet for the next two minutes, but Baylor picked up the energy with four straight points.

A Quigley 3-pointer before the five-minute pause put the score at 50-34.

Coming out of the timeout, the Lady Lions had a golden opportunity to build momentum. The Bears were cold for the first time in a long time, going scoreless for two and a half minutes and missing their last seven field goals.

Four straight Gonzalez points cut the Baylor lead to 12, but a Kyle Abraham fast break ended the drought.

After being down by as much as 19 in the third quarter, the Lady Lions got within as few as 10 points. With 40 seconds left in the quarter, Carter nearly got the blue and white back within single digits, but missed a jumper in the paint. An Abraham layup with two seconds on the clock put Baylor up 58-46 at the end of the frame.

Quigley and Gonzalez spearheaded the strong Penn State third frame, combining for 14 points. The Lady Lions' offense cleaned up, recording just three turnovers after committing seven in the previous quarter.

Penn State didn’t keep the tide changed for too long, as Baylor returned to its dominant form at the start of the fourth quarter. The Bears outscored the blue and white 13-7 in the first four minutes.

It wasn’t until the 5:45 mark that a player not named Enjulina Gonzalez scored for Wright’s squad.

An and-1 for Lorena Awou ahead of the media timeout matched the Bears’ largest lead of the night as they led 73-54.

Following the break, a 3-pointer from Ines Goryanova gave Baylor its first 20-plus point lead of the night. Shortly after, another Penn State turnover turned into a fast break for Skylar Jones, and the writing on the wall began to appear for the Lady Lions.

Penn State never caught fire from its third quarter momentum, and Wright’s squad went scoreless for the final five minutes of the fourth frame.

The bright side of the blue and white’s loss was Gonzalez’s 21 points, leading all scorers and marking a season best.

Up next

Penn State awaits the result of Seton Hall vs. USF, then faces the loser tomorrow at 5:30 p.m. ET.

title: Former Penn State OC Joe Moorhead parting ways with Akron as HC
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Akron and former Penn State offensive coordinator Joe Moorhead have parted ways.

Moorhead spent five years as the head coach of Akron from 2022 to 2026, with his time coming to an end after the Zips' loss to Buffalo on Friday concluded a 2-10 season.

"After careful consideration and thoughtful discussions with my family, I informed University of Akron officials of my decision to pursue other opportunities at the conclusion of this season," Moorhead said in a post on X.

Moorhead's time as head coach came to an end with an underwhelming record in five seasons, finishing with a 15-45 record at Akron's helm.

Prior to his time at Akron, he spent two seasons as the offensive coordinator with Oregon. He was the head coach at Mississippi State in 2018 and 2019, where he went 14-12.

Moorhead was Penn State's offensive coordinator during some of its best seasons. He was the Nittany Lions' offensive coordinator in 2016 and 2017, leading them to a Big Ten title, a Rose Bowl appearance and two top-10 finishes.

title: Staff predictions | Can Penn State finish out the regular season with a win over Maryland?
author: The Daily Collegian football staff
description:
The final regular season game of Penn State’s first year under Matt Campbell is here.

Campbell and the Nittany Lions will travel to Maryland to close out their 2026 regular season at 3:30 p.m. Saturday, with both teams coming off losses to Rutgers and USC, respectively.

Who will end their season on a high note? Here’s what we think.

Andrew Deal: Penn State 24, Maryland 13

Penn State has a chance to end the regular season on a high note and likely give itself higher odds at a better bowl game. Meanwhile, Maryland won’t be playing for bowl game contention, sitting at 4-7.

The Terrapins have a chance to end the Nittany Lions regular season with two bad losses, and that’s going to give them more motivation to come out of the gates hot.

However, whenever everything gets settled down, Penn State will show it's the better team when everything is said and done. Maryland doesn’t have the players to slow down a receiver like Chase Sowell, who’s going to have to be even bigger in Saturday’s game with wide receiver Brett Eskildsen listed as doubtful.

Between Rocco Becht and Sowell’s connection, the big presence of tight end Benjamin Brahmer and the running game having success — especially if running back Quinton Martin Jr. is the lone healthy back, who can run with motivation to prove himself — Maryland’s defense will have its hands full.

The only thing that can keep the Terrapins in the game is the pass rush. Linebacker Zion Elee leads the team in sacks, and Penn State’s offensive line has shown the inability to protect Becht from time to time.

Maryland will keep things close early, but the Nittany Lions will pull away as they show a bit more consistency throughout all 60 minutes of the game to finish the regular season 7-5.

Andrew Mercer: Maryland 21, Penn State 20

Losing to Rutgers has Penn State at rock bottom, and the Nittany Lions’ lengthy availability report will spell doom in the regular season finale.

That said, this is going to be a dogfight. Maryland’s only potential meaningful loss will be wide receiver Chris Durr. Jr., who's doubtful as of Thursday, but Penn State may have to rely on Sowell and Brahmer to generate offense if running backs Carson Hansen and Cam Wallace aren’t able to play.

Make no mistake, Sowell and Brahmer are fantastic targets, but we all know how it’s gone when the Nittany Lions have to rely solely on the pass game. It’s just not a winning formula.

Look at the Michigan game for instance. Sowell balled out, and it wasn’t enough for the win because the run game wasn’t moving and Becht’s turnovers were costly. Contrast that with the Washington game, where both the pass and run blended seamlessly, and the winning formula was clear as day.

The Nittany Lions need the team that played the Huskies in the first half. They need all of their weapons for a balanced attack. They need Hansen, who’d been steadily gaining momentum before his injury against Minnesota.

Penn State may not have that team. I have the Terrapins winning this Week 13 battle by a point.

Lexie Linderman: Penn State 28, Maryland 24

If I’ve learned anything about the Nittany Lions this year, it’s that they cannot win in the Big Ten if they’re not running the ball effectively.

That was evident in Penn State’s three straight wins coming out of the bye week when the rushing game was humming. When it faltered last week against Rutgers, the ripple effects were evident.

The Nittany Lions might be without their top two rushers on the year, with Hansen and Wallace both questionable as of Thursday night. James Peoples has already been ruled out after injuring his left leg on just his second carry against Rutgers.

So Penn State could be in deep trouble if both Hansen and Wallace are out, as that would leave Martin as the only healthy running back available that’s seen playing time in Big Ten play.

But if there’s any time for the Nittany Lions to let the pass game carry them to a win, it’s in what’s potentially the last game of Sowell’s collegiate career.

Sowell goes for 175 yards and two touchdowns against a Maryland pass defense that’s allowing 216.4 passing yards per game this year, willing Penn State to one last regular season victory in 2026.

Noah Aberegg: Penn State 27, Maryland 17

Before Penn State was upset by Rutgers last week, I would’ve projected this game as a blowout for the Nittany Lions. But considering anything is possible, I think it could be a close contest in the season finale.

Penn State has the much stronger team on paper, led by the best passing defense in the Big Ten. Maryland quarterback Malik Washington has thrown for 2,309 yards this year and 11 touchdowns, but has also thrown 10 interceptions, something the Nittany Lions could look to exploit.

Durr leads the Terrapins receiving core with 848 yards and five touchdowns on the year, presenting top cornerbacks Audavion Collins and Daryus Dixson with a challenge. That is if Durr is able to play, as he’s currently doubtful.

On offense, the Nittany Lions will have the opportunity to line up against one of the weaker defenses in the conference. The Terrapins have given up the fifth-most yards in the Big Ten, including the fourth-most rushing yards.

The status of Penn State’s rushing attack is unknown with all the injuries the running back room is dealing with. But even if the run game can’t get going, the Becht and Sowell connection has been strong and could pick up significant yardage in their final regular season game.

Regardless of the method for offensive yardage, Penn State should come out with a victory heading into bowl season.

title: Players to watch | QB Malik Washington, 2nd-string WR rank as Maryland’s top players in Week 13
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
The final regular season game is here, as Penn State will face Maryland at SECU Stadium on Saturday afternoon.

Quarterback Malik Washington’s dual-threat capabilities, a second-string receiver and a standout linebacker highlight the Terrapins’ top available players in Week 13.

Here’s who to look out for on the home side.

Malik Washington, quarterback

Malik Washington returned from injury in the Terrapins’ 35-21 loss to USC last week, throwing for 251 yards and two interceptions, although he rushed for a score.

Washington is a sophomore and a second-year starter after having set the records for passing yards and completions as a freshman, completing 273 passes for 2,963 yards and 17 touchdowns in 12 games last season.

This year, Washington has thrown for 2,309 passing yards and 11 touchdowns, averaging 230.9 passing yards per game, which ranks fifth in the Big Ten. However, he’s also prone to interceptions, as he’s thrown 10 this season — tied for first in the conference.

He’s a dual-threat quarterback, which is an archetype Penn State has struggled with at various points of the season. Washington is capable of slinging the ball around and exploiting sluggish secondaries, but isn’t afraid to take matters into his own hands on broken plays.

Washington ranks third on the team with 172 rushing yards and second with five rushing touchdowns. The Terrapins may utilize his legs, as the Nittany Lions have the best pass defense in the Big Ten.

Na’eem Abdul-Rahim Gladding, wide receiver

With No. 1 wide receiver Chris Durr Jr. doubtful for Saturday as of Thursday night, Na’eem Abdul-Rahim Gladding is the next man up to be Washington’s top target.

Gladding spent two years at Old Dominion before transferring to Maryland this offseason. He was the Monarchs’ top receiver with 667 yards and six touchdowns and was named an All-Sun Belt honorable mention.

As a Terrapin, Gladding ranks second on the team with 441 receiving yards and three touchdown catches, averaging 44.1 yards per game.

His best performance came in Week 3 against UConn, when he’d led the team with 130 yards and a touchdown. Although his numbers dropped in subsequent games, Gladding tallied 78 yards and his most recent touchdown against Purdue on Nov. 7.

DeJuan Williams, running back

Running back DeJuan Williams leads Maryland with 592 rushing yards and seven touchdowns despite missing three games due to injury, but availability won’t be a concern for Williams this week, as he’s not on the injury report.

The redshirt sophomore has been on a roll recently, too. Before he tallied 83 rushing yards and two touchdowns against USC last week, he had 99 yards and a touchdown against Purdue and 72 yards against Wisconsin.

Williams is averaging 74 yards per game heading into Maryland’s final matchup.

He also owns a receiving touchdown scored against Rutgers on Oct. 17, showcasing his adaptability.

Jamare Glasker, defensive back

Maryland’s best all-around defender is defensive back Jamare Glasker. He owns a team-leading nine pass breakups, six tackles for loss, two interceptions and a sack. Glasker also tied his career-best 37 tackles on the year going into Saturday, originally set in his redshirt sophomore season at Wake Forest.

Fans can expect him to match up against wide receiver Chase Sowell in man coverage, as Brett Eskildsen is doubtful for the game. Penn State’s ability to score may come down to this particular matchup.

Daniel Wingate, linebacker

Fortunately for Maryland fans, linebacker Daniel Wingate is listed as probable for Saturday’s game.

Wingate leads the Terrapins with 70 tackles, but he also has 3.5 tackles for loss, two forced fumbles, two fumble recoveries, a pass breakup and an interception.

With running backs Carson Hansen and Cam Wallace questionable for Saturday, Wingate is positioned for a big day in stopping Penn State’s run game.

title: Jamison Patton a ‘game changer’ at safety for Penn State
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
After starting eight games this year, Jamison Patton has been a rising talent for Penn State at the safety position and will be so for another year, as Patton said Tuesday that he’s planning on coming back for a fifth year in 2027.

“I do plan and intend on coming back,” Patton said. “I love the guys and the culture that (Matt) Campbell’s brought over and created, and I do plan on coming back for that.”

Coming into this season for the Nittany Lions, Patton’s role in the secondary was unknown. But between issues with Jeremiah Cooper’s recovery from a torn ACL and poor pass coverage from Marcus Neal Jr., Patton was elevated to a starting role and has made the most of it.

“I think that’s something that I’ve gotten better at just through the years is getting more reps,” Patton said. “I feel like as a young guy, I was rotating in. I had some guys ahead of me that were playing great ball, so just taking notes from them and just growing and learning little bits and pieces from them.”

It hasn’t just been Patton’s additional reps on the field that’s made him a rising star, though. It’s what he’s done in those moments that’s given him the opportunities he’s in today.

Against Michigan, Patton stuffed running back Jordan Marshall, marking the biggest play he’d made as a Nittany Lion to that point. A week later, he picked off Purdue quarterback Ryan Browne as the Boilermakers were driving down the field. The Nittany Lions, in turn, kicked a field goal to extend their lead.

“(He’s) very smart, (a) vocal leader,” cornerback Daryus Dixson said Wednesday. “He’s a game changer.”

Besides adjusting to a new school and new teammates, Patton also had to adjust to a new scheme. He was previously playing in a 3-3-5 formation at Iowa State, but under D’Anton Lynn, he’s had to adjust to playing in a 4-2-5 lineup.

“It’s a new system, so that took a little time to get used to and understand how I fit within the scheme and how to make plays within the scheme,” Patton said. “I think (safeties coach Deon Broomfield) has done a great job. It’s nice to have him in my pocket, just to translate from what we did at Iowa State and how it compares to here.”

In the new formation, Patton has had the opportunity to play in different positions and line up in different spots. Instead of playing in a three-safety shell, he’s had reps playing near the line of scrimmage this season.

“You’re pretty much a linebacker, which I personally enjoy,” Patton said. “It’s fun being up there, and I could definitely see myself growing in that area. The more I get in there, the more comfortable I get.”

Patton has played more during the 2026 season than the senior safety had before in his career, starting just three games last year at Iowa State. He’s grown into a player Penn State needs on the field, as the defense struggled after he left the field against Rutgers.

Campbell said Tuesday that Patton was dealing with an illness last week, but he’ll be ready to go for Saturday’s matchup against Maryland.

“Thought we were going to be able to get more of him,” Campbell said. “Just wasn't able to do it. I think for the betterment of the team, almost to the point where he couldn't stand up anymore. You couldn't play him anymore.”

With just two games left in the season — one conference matchup and a bowl — Patton said he’s still motivated to finish the year out strong. But looking forward, he wants to grow in certain areas for his final year in 2027.

That could be easier for Patton, who won’t have to relearn a new defensive scheme, barring an unforeseen departure from Lynn this offseason, and he’s looking to take advantage of the bonus season of college football he’s getting.

“Just clean up the fundamentals and technique of whether it’s playing man coverage or tackling or anything in general,” Patton said. “Just the knowledge, just over preparing, and now that I have so much experience, just anticipating things, communicating, getting guys on the right page and making sure all 11 people are on the same page, flying to the ball.”

title: Penn State vs. Maryland preview | Weather, betting odds for Saturday’s matchup
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Penn State and Maryland are both coming off losses after winning the previous week, but played very different teams ahead of their matchup against each other.

The Nittany Lions had one of its worst losses in program history to a struggling Rutgers team, while the Terrapins stayed competitive early with a ranked USC squad.

The teams will face each other at 3:30 p.m. Saturday at SECU Stadium in College Park, Maryland, with Penn State having won 44 of the 48 matchups in the teams’ history.

Here’s a look at how the teams line up against each other and more information ahead of Saturday’s game.

Forecast

The weather will be on the normal side of a late November day in Maryland, according to AccuWeather.

With a high of 51 degrees around game time and partly cloudy skies, it’s likely to feel a bit warmer with the sun shining. As the sun starts to go down, temperatures will fall to around 35 degrees in the second half.

There’s a 20% chance of precipitation with upward of 23 mph wind gusts, with 9 mph of normal wind heading in the west to northwest direction.

Betting, how to watch

Penn State enters as a 7.5-point favorite, according to FanDuel. Despite the loss last week to Rutgers, the sportsbook still has the Nittany Lions winning by over a touchdown.

The over/under is set at 49.5, which means it thinks the Nittany Lions will win 29-21.

The matchup will be on Fox Sports 1 at 3:30 p.m., with tickets going for as low as $23 at SECU Stadium.

About Maryland

The Terrapins have been through a lot this year. Former head coach Mike Locksley was fired, and interim head coach Aazaar Abdul-Rahim has turned things around a bit for a previously struggling squad.

Maryland enters the game with a 4-7 record, which included back-to-back wins against Purdue and Wisconsin. Against USC, the Terrapins had their young quarterback, Malik Washington, return after missing their matchup against the Badgers.

Washington threw the ball 38 times, completing 24 passes for 251 yards. However, he was intercepted twice in the 35-21 loss.

He’s led Maryland to a middle of the pack passing attack in the Big Ten that averages 235.5 yards per game in the air. On the flip side, the run game has struggled, sitting 14th in the Big Ten.

Running back Dejuan Williams leads the way with 592 rushing yards, with the Terrapins rushing for 124.9 yards per game. They’ll likely have to utilize the run game more if it wants to have success against a Penn State defense that’s very strong against the pass.

On the defensive side of the ball, Maryland sits near the bottom in both passing and rushing in the conference. With only two wins in the conference, the Terrapins have struggled to contain Big Ten offenses, leading to losses.

About Penn State

Penn State is attempting to rebound from a bad loss against Rutgers, but it faces another team that fell to the Scarlet Knights and is another one of the worst teams in the conference.

The Nittany Lions are led by Rocco Becht who has the passing offense at 10th in the conference with 232.5 passing yards per game. He’s consistently connected with star wide receiver Chase Sowell, who’s become one of the top receivers in the Big Ten.

The rushing attack is dealing with multiple injuries, as Carson Hansen, Cam Wallace and James Peoples have injury designations. Peoples is already listed as out, while Wallace and Hansen remain questionable.

If Wallace or Hansen can’t go, it could open up the opportunity for running back Quinton Martin Jr., who has 172 yards and a touchdown this season.

The defensive side of the ball is headlined by the cornerbacks and Tony Rojas, who’s having one of the best seasons in program history with 87 total tackles, 15.5 tackles for loss, 6.5 sacks and two interceptions.

Cornerbacks Audavion Collins and Daryus Dixson have created one of the top duos in the country. The two will be tasked with slowing down Maryland receiver Chris Durr Jr., but have shown the ability to keep opposing teams’ top receivers quiet.

title: Best moments of Hannah Prince’s inaugural season with Penn State field hockey
author: Riley Warner | For the Collegian
description:
The 2026-2027 season has brought many coaching changes across Penn State's teams.

One of these changes was the hiring of Hannah Prince as Penn State's new head field hockey coach, and if the season’s results say anything, it’s that Prince is likely here to stay.

The blue and white had a tumultuous season in recent months, with key moments like beating No. 1 Northwestern on Oct. 30 in a 2-0 shutout and an eight-game win streak from Sep. 28 to Oct. 23.

The team’s success can be attributed in part to Prince. In her inaugural season, the former Saint Joseph’s head coach has whipped the program around and led Penn State to end the regular season at third in the Big Ten.

With the Nittany Lions’ season now over, here are the highlights of Prince’s time in charge so far.

The Prince era

The state in which the 2026 Nittany Lions ended the season does not resemble theirs from the year prior, nor does it reflect how the team started the season. The blue and white went from a record of 7-10 in 2025 to one of 12-6 in 2026.

With this record, coach Prince was also able to improve Penn State’s Big Ten standing from No. 8 in 2025 to third, as well as becoming nationally ranked at No. 13.

The Nittany Lions weren’t able to get to that point overnight, though.

Penn State’s opening match against then-No. 5 Virginia was a loss, and losing to top-ranked teams became a theme early in the season with consecutive losses to then-No. 4 Princeton, then-No. 5 Maryland and then-No. 19 Monmouth from Sep. 13-20th. Prince and the Nittany Lions were able to learn from these losses and improve, as after they went on to win eight consecutive games.

With the Nittany Lions coming in at No. 8 in the Big Ten for total season shots and falling in the middle of the pack in most other categories, this is a team that still needs work. However, given the way the blue and white was already able to flip its stats from last season to this one, with Prince at the helm, there’s no question that Penn State won’t continue to climb those rankings in the coming seasons.

Penn State has completely changed offensively from 2025 to now. Last year, the Nittany Lions were outplayed, with opponents scoring more goals and taking more shots in every game Penn State played.

This season, however, the opposite happened. Penn State had 38 goals this season while their opponents had a total of 22; they had 211 shots while their opponents were held to only 170; 116 shots on goal compared to 98 by opponents; 11.722 shots per game with 9.444 for opponents.

The players themselves

As the saying goes, a good coach is only as good as their players, and Prince had a team full of them this season. Most of the players on this Nittany Lions squad were returners, and Prince relied on the team’s established relationships and chemistry to turn the blue and white into a winning squad.

Both during the season and after, the Nittany Lions roster earned recognition from not only the Big Ten but also the National Field Hockey Coaches Association.

The blue and white earned four Big Ten weekly awards, with graduate student Camryn Standish and junior goalie Aby Deverka both winning Defense Player of the Week (Deverka doing so twice) and junior Ella Gaitan winning Offensive Player of the Week.

Additionally, Deverka was named NFHCA National Defensive Player of the Week twice this season, becoming the first Nittany Lion to earn this distinction at the national level and the first player in Penn State history to do so twice in the same season.

The accolades didn’t stop with the season; the blue and white earned seven post-season Big Ten honors. Backs Lily Holmes and Kira Takahashi-Trader were both named Big Ten All-Freshman after playing key roles in Penn State’s defensive attack throughout the season. Senior Emmy McCulley won the Big Ten Sportsmanship award. Sienna Dunn and Gaitan were both All-Big First Team selections, and Lara Pyle and Olivia Marthins were both All-Big Second Team selections.

The fans

The team’s success under Prince gave Penn State supporters a reason to show up, and fans did. Fans tended to come to see the Nittany Lions in droves, with a total of 5,544 fans coming to the Penn State Field Hockey Complex this season and an average of 550 fans per game.

Penn State fans are not new to showing up for the blue and white; as far back in 2011, Penn State ranked second nationally in total attendance. Now, Penn State fans have continued this trend, ranking No. 3 in cumulative attendance.

Coach Prince and the Nittany Lions gave these fans something to believe in and a reason to keep coming back, and with their success in the 2026 season, that’s unlikely to change for a while.

title: Column | 5 Nittany Lions starred in Penn State women’s soccer season
author: Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian
description:
Friday was a historic night for No. 24 Penn State, but not a positive one.

The Nittany Lions suffered an overtime 1-0 loss to Villanova in the first round of the NCAA Women’s College Cup, marking it the first time since 1997 that the blue and white didn’t advance to the second round.

Despite the loss, Penn State played a strong season it should be proud of. Finishing 9-5-5 overall and 7-2-3 in the Big Ten, the Nittany Lions made an impact on both ends of the field, with eight of their nine wins coming by shutout.

The blue and white had depth in their roster this season, allowing them to perform the way they did. Even with Penn State being the sturdy squad they are, it still had standout athletes who made their presence known this year.

Here are some of the Nittany Lions’ top performers from the 2026 season.

Aubrey Kulpa

Kulpa spearheaded the blue and white’s successful season. The junior forward led her squad in points with 21 via eight goals and five assists, earning her a spot on the First Team All-Big Ten team.

Tallying 55 shots on the year, the Cromwell, Connecticut, native was a brutal offensive force that opposing teams struggled to tame. Kulpa started in all 19 matches for Penn State, showing how much coach EricaDambach and the team relied on her production.

As a junior, the Park Avenue Army has another season to watch the blue and white star. Kulpa has continuously produced for Penn State, recording 17 points in her freshman season and 22 in her sophomore year.

Kulpa will continue to showcase her skills in the 2027 season and prove herself yet again as a standout performer for the Nittany Lions.

Paige Kalal

Kalal is right behind Kulpa with 20 points via seven goals and six assists. The forward transferred in from Minnesota to play her senior season with the blue and white.

Starting in all 19 games, the Brooklyn Park, Minnesota, native notched 35 shots in 1402 minutes and earned a Second Team All-Big Team honor.

Kalal’s most impressive performance this season came in the Notre Dame game on Aug. 16. She recorded five shots and one goal, showing Penn State early that she didn’t come to Happy Valley to mess around.

Kalal plans to continue her soccer career and take her dominant attacking style to the professional level.

Kayleigh Herr

On defense, Herr has been the backbone of the Nittany Lion lineup all season. The redshirt senior defender logged 1680 minutes this season, starting in all 19 matches.

Herr’s performance this season earned her a spot on the All-Big Ten Second Team. Being the blue and white’s most-played athlete, it is no shock Herr made her way to this list.

The Cary, North Carolina, native began her collegiate career in her home state with the Tar Heels before moving to Happy Valley for her third year. She came in as a redshirt sophomore and instantly made an impact on the Penn State back line as a consistent starter.

One of Herr’s top performances was during the Nittany Lions’ matchup against Purdue earlier this month. Despite falling to the Boilermakers 1-0 in overtime, Herr put on an amazing defensive performance, blocking shots from Big Ten Forward of the Year, Jaiden Anderson.

Herr’s presence on Jeffrey Field will be missed as she also looks to continue her career at the professional level.

Mackenzie Gress

Staying on the defensive, Gress has been a constant in the net for the blue and white. She was named Big Ten Goalkeeper of the Week on Sept. 1 and continued her dominance in net for the rest of her season.

The redshirt senior goalkeeper started in all 19 matches for Penn State, recording 1643 minutes on the season.

The Lyndhurst, New Jersey, native posted a 0.795 save percentage on 62 saves. Gress was a wall in the net all season long, recording five solo shutouts and three combined.

Gress’s best performance this year came against Virginia Tech on Sept. 3. The keeper faced 11 shots, saving 10 to help the Nittany Lions to tie the match 1-1.

Paige Pasinski

Last on this list is Pasinski, a freshman midfielder who instantly made an impact on the blue and white roster. Pasinski was named to the Big Ten All-Freshman Team, the first time Penn State had a player picked since 2022.

The Phoenix native tallied six points via two goals and two assists. Playing in 18 matches and starting in 15, Pasinski was an influential first-year performer for the Nittany Lions.

Pasinski recorded three of her season highs during the Maryland matchup on Sept. 18, logging five shots, four shots on goal and one goal against the Terps, showing Dambach just how influential she can be in her first year for the blue and white.

Alongside Pasinski as an additional attacking outlet, she is versatile on the pitch, contributing in multiple areas of the field, making her a valuable piece to the Nittany Lions rotation this year and for seasons to come.

title: Ivan Jurić leads Penn State men’s basketball again, ties school record
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Death, taxes and Ivan Jurić double-doubles.

The sophomore forward racked up 19 points and 11 rebounds in a team-high 36 minutes in Penn State’s 83-70 loss to No. 24 Memphis on Wednesday night.

“He's our best player, so we need him to play against a team like Memphis at a really, really high level at both ends of the court,” Mike Rhoades said after the game.

Jurić’s performance tied John Amaechi’s school record for consecutive double-doubles with seven. He’ll have a chance to break the record on Friday against Mississippi State in his second Battle 4 Atlantis game.

The Memphis contingent praised Jurić after the matchup. Penny Hardaway, the former NBA star who is now the coach of his alma mater, drew on his professional experience while evaluating the seven-footer.

“Playing in the NBA and understanding how bigs of his magnitude get their positioning, when I watched the film on him, man, he's a problem,” the four-time all-star said. “He can't be guarded one-on-one; he needs a double team. You need a double team to guard him, and he was definitely everything I thought he would be, and more. He was bigger in person, girth-wise.”

If Jurić was the star for Penn State, Memphis guard Jayden Reid was the star of the game. The senior scored a career-high 32 points and added nine assists, bringing his season average up to 23 points per game.

Reid transferred to the birthplace of rock n’ roll from Northwestern last offseason, so he has now faced Jurić three times in his career. Even though “Jurić is gonna get his double-double,” Reid felt that the undersized Memphis forwards did a solid job defending the tallest player on the floor.

“I already knew since last year he was a good player. Even coming into this game, I knew how big and skilled he was,” Reid said. “But they did a good job just battling him. A good player is going to get theirs, have a good game. So, just making him work for it, he got 11 rebounds, which is a little bit too much, but he just had to work for it. He felt all of our bigs.”

The Tigers were Penn State’s first ranked opponent, but they did not bring the biggest front line the Nittany Lions have seen this year.

Memphis started Maxim Logue, a 6-foot-9 junior, and the tallest player Hardaway brought off the bench was the 6-foot-10 fifth-year, Corneilous Williams, so Rhoades still wanted to see more from his star, especially on defense.

“His defense wasn't very good today,” Rhoades said after praising Jurić’s offensive performance. “That really hurt us, but he's still a young player, so he's got work to do. That's what's great about Ivan: he's willing to hold himself accountable, and that's why I think you've all seen him get better and better all the time, so he's improving.”

The blue and white get their next chance to improve on Friday against Mississippi State after the Bulldogs lost to Wake Forest late Wednesday night.

title: How Penn State men’s basketball struggled defensively in Battle 4 Atlantis loss to Memphis
author: Will Horstman | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State fell to 5-2 on the season with an 83-70 loss to No. 24 Memphis on Wednesday, but it was worse than what the scoreboard says.

The Tigers led 79-55 with just over seven minutes left in the game before taking their foot off the gas. The Nittany Lions’ defense was gashed inside Imperial Arena on Paradise Island, Bahamas.

“They played their style and enforced their style on us,” Mike Rhoades said. “They just made it really hard for us right from the start … They took it to us in a lot of different ways.”

Memphis’ offense centered around guard Jayden Reid, who scored a career-high 32 points on 12-for-15 shooting from the field. He added nine assists as he led an offense that shot 51.6% from the field and 44.8% from 3-point range.

The Tigers shot effectively because they kept using ball screens to throw Penn State’s defense off. The Nittany Lions kept over-rotating, which often allowed Reid to find an open look or an open teammate.

“We just allowed him to space us way too much, and he got the ball hot,” Rhoades said. “A couple times he turned the corner and got into his pull-up that he can get off even against bigger guys contesting him.”

Penn State had the size advantage over Memphis. The Nittany Lions average 6-foot-7, while the Tigers average 6-foot-4. Reid is listed at 5-foot-10, which is shorter than anyone on Penn State’s roster.

But Reid and Memphis were quicker than Penn State players, who were often out of position to defend a shot. The Tigers had 23 assists on 33 made baskets.

Penn State was only down 30-28 with 5:28 to play in the first half, but the Tigers were missing wide-open looks. Memphis finally started hitting its open looks consistently when it went on a 19-9 run to close out the first half with a 49-37 lead. The Tigers made three 3-pointers during that run.

“I thought we got beat off the dribble a lot,” Rhoades said. “That just puts us in rotation. I said it from the start: We have to be able to, on the perimeter, guard the ball, and when you give J-Reid a lot of space, he can go boogie. You're putting us in rotation. You're putting two on the ball to stop him at the rim, and then you're having long closeouts.”

Penn State’s defense currently ranks 142nd in the country by KenPom’s efficiency ratings. The Nittany Lions are allowing 71.1 points per game through a 5-2 start to the season.

The defensive issues continue from last season, when Penn State allowed 79.3 points per game and went 12-20, including 3-17 in Big Ten play. This year’s roster is much more talented than last season, but the defensive struggles could keep it from improving much record-wise if it doesn’t improve.

Big Ten play starts with tests against No. 21 Nebraska and No. 4 Illinois. The Fighting Illini just set the Big Ten single-game scoring record with a 133-83 win over Winthrop earlier this week.

Penn State’s defense could be really ugly in Big Ten play, and it needs major improvement.

title: Penn State men’s basketball loses to No. 24 Memphis in program’s debut Battle 4 Atlantis appearance
author: Myles Hannak | Sports Editor
description:
It was Penn State’s first Battle 4 Atlantis appearance in Penn State history, and one to forget.

The Nittany Lions faced their first ranked opponent of the year, No. 24 Memphis, in the first round of the 15th annual Battle 4 Atlantis tournament and fell in a one-sided matchup, 83-70.

The result drops the blue and white to 5-2 and 0-2 in Quad 3 games on the season after Penn State’s loss to Pittsburgh earlier this year.

Both sides came out of the gates with streaky shooting, which allowed the blue and white to take a quick lead with all but one starter contributing early scores. Despite an early sprint, the Tigers chased down the Nittany Lions to a 13-9 advantage, with Memphis 5-foot-10 senior guard Jayden Reid logging nine of those early points.

At the midpoint of the first half, Penn State held a narrow two-point lead in an offensively stalled game. Starting guard Dasonte Bowen led scoring for the blue and white with six points, as the graduate student was the only Penn State player to make more than one bucket at that point.

Over the following minutes, the Tigers’ defense prevailed to pick up slack where their rebounding couldn’t, allowing Memphis to flip the scale toward its own narrow lead. Mike Rhoades didn’t really utilize much of his bench up to that point.

Only guard Jay Rodgers and wing Brant Byers, who returned after two flu absences for this game, were used as primary substitute options. Byers had a pair of big blocks for the blue and white in the half, which was integral for a Penn State unit that had one other swat in the first half aside from those two.

Those trends continued despite brief appearances from 7-footer Tim Oboh and wing François Wibaut off the bench, as a turnover from starting forward Roko Prkačin allowed Memphis to score on the other end to take the largest lead of the night, 37-28.

That was how things went going into the break, with Reid continuing to torch the blue and white defense up until halftime behind his long-range shot. The Westbury, New York, native had 20 points with four downtown makes — Penn State as a team had only made two 3-pointers in the first half.

Starting 7-footer Ivan Jurić led the Nittany Lions with 10 points and seven rebounds at the break, but Penn State shot a measly 41% from the field and committed nine turnovers to the Tigers’ five.

Coach Penny Hardaway’s Memphis squad started the second half at the same tempo to extend their lead. Out of the break, the Tigers outscored the blue and white 15-10 over the first 6:30, as time for readjustment didn’t stop Memphis’s offense.

That’s what followed for the blue and white: the Tigers shook off whatever they threw at them. Starting wing Josh Reed began to get more offensive looks for Penn State, but the scores weren’t coming efficiently enough to stop the onslaught.

It just continued to snowball as time ticked on, as Memphis’ win felt certain still with double-digit minutes on the clock, which became certain as time ticked on.

Penn State shot 24% from distance and 36% from the field in the Bahamas, as it only had an edge in shooting from the charity stripe.

In the defeat, Jurić had 19 points and 11 rebounds, meaning he’s had a double-double every game so far with his seventh straight, which also ties a program record set by forward John Amaechi (1992-95). Byers, Prkacin and Reed also all reached double-digit scoring.

Memphis’ Reid led total scoring with 32 points on 12-of-15 shooting with six downtown makes, all career highs.

Injury report

With Byers’ return, the blue and white are still missing one player – guard Roberts Blums, who remains sidelined with a broken finger. The Riga, Latvia, native has been out since the season opener against Canisius and has missed six straight games.

Up next

The blue and white are set to face the loser of the Wake Forest and Mississippi State matchup later Wednesday night. The third-place game is set for Friday.

title: Preview | Penn State men's hockey set to face Princeton amid losing stetch
author: Chase Fisher | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State returns home and re-enters the nonconference slate for a standalone game against Princeton on Friday, with puck drop scheduled for 5 p.m.

The Nittany Lions (2-11-1) are in the midst of a seven-game losing streak, its second-longest in program history. Their record is also the worst in school history through 14 contests after being swept by Wisconsin on the road last weekend. Penn State enters Friday 2-4 in non-conference play.

Princeton (4-4) travels to State College after a sweep against Air Force. Unlike the Nittany Lions, the Tigers are 4-0 in non-conference games.

Friday marks the fifth all-time meeting between Penn State and Princeton. The Nittany Lions hold a 2-1-1 edge against coach Guy Gadowsky’s former team, which he coached from 2004-11. Penn State is 15-14-2 all-time against the ECAC, and 0-1 this season after a 6-3 home loss to Quinnipiac.

Here’s what else to know about this weekend’s matchup.

Scouting Penn State

Penn State is near the bottom of the Big Ten in most major statistics. The Nittany Lions are sixth in goals per game (2.57) and save percentage (.886) and seventh in goals-allowed average (4) and shots percentage (.08)

Where Penn State stands out is on special teams. It ranks fifth in the conference and 11th nationally in power-play percentage (.279), while third in the Big Ten in penalty-killing percentage (.745).

The Nittany Lions are paced by winger Justin Poirier, who has posted 17 points through 14 games. His nine goals are tied for 17th in the country and third in the conference. Poirier has scored in four straight games and has an 11-game point streak, which is tied for the longest in program history, set in 2018 by forward Evan Barratt.

Defenseman Jackson Smith is the only other skater on Penn State with double-digit points. His 15 tallies are tied for the Big Ten lead among defensemen.

Goaltender Josh Fleming leads Penn State between the pipes. He’s started in eight of its 14 games, posting a 1-6-1 record, a 3.13 goals-against average, and a .901 save percentage. That’s a stark difference from last season, when he totaled a 10-7-2 record, a 2.61 goals-against average and a .924 save percentage.

Scouting Princeton

Princeton matches the Nittany Lions offensively, scoring 2.8 goals per game.

But defensively, it separates itself from Penn State. The Tigers allow just 2.62 goals per game, which ranks 22nd nationally. In four non-conference games, they are allowing 1.25 goals per game.

Princeton’s backbone is its special teams. It owns the fourth-best penalty-kill percentage in the country (.917), third-highest among programs with at least 15 attempts against. And its power play rates 12th nationally, converting at 26.9%.

The Tigers are led by defenseman Kai Greaves, who has 12 points in eight games. Forward Jake Manfre leads the team in goals, with four goals and a 0.5 goals-per-game average.

Goaltender Arthur Smith has started seven of the program’s eight games this season, boasting a 3-4 record, a 2.54 goals-against average and a .909 save percentage.

title: Preview | Penn State women’s basketball set to compete in Paradise Jam
author: Gianna Dowling | Sports Editor
description:
It’s been a slow start to the Tanisha Wright era, with the Lady Lions standing at 1-5 as the new coach’s first month of play with the blue and white nears its end.

Penn State earned its first win of the season last Thursday against Bowling Green, but couldn’t carry momentum into its next contest, falling to Saint Joseph’s on Sunday.

Devyn Quigley leads the Lady Lions in scoring with 14.2 points per game, but lately the blue and white’s top performer has been Enjulina Gonzalez. The Miami native has a combined 37 points in the last two contests, after totaling 23 in the first four games.

The blue and white will test its luck in international waters, traveling to the U.S. Virgin Islands for two games as part of the Paradise Jam. The Lady Lions are set for a Black Friday matchup with No. 25 Baylor and will face either Seton Hall or USF on Saturday.

Baylor

Penn State kicks off its feast week, facing Baylor at 5:30 p.m. ET Friday. The Bears have had a stellar start to the season, posting a 6-1 record, with their lone loss a nine-point deficit to No. 4 USC.

Baylor brings a balanced offensive attack, with seven players averaging double-digit figures. 2026 All-Big 12 First Team selection Taliah Scott leads the effort, averaging 15.7 points per game.

Scott was stellar against the Trojans, scoring a season-high 24 points in 37 minutes. Next is 6-foot-5 Kate Koval, who averages 13.6 points and 8.7 rebounds per game, along with 13 blocks in the young season. Koval will be a tough match for Penn State’s 6-foot-4 Petra Božan, who’s been underwhelming in the paint this season, averaging just 3.3 rebounds per game and only recording two total blocks.

Guard/forward combo Savannah White has been Penn State’s best performer near the rim, owning team-highs with 6.5 rebounds per game and 11 total blocks this season.

Gonzalez, Quigley and Co. have a tough task ahead, facing a Baylor team that has overwhelmed opponents this season. The Bears own a 39.7-point scoring margin, which ranks 11th in the nation.

Seton Hall/USF

Depending on how the Lady Lions fare against Baylor, they’ll face either Seton Hall or USF on Saturday. If Wright’s squad pulls off the upset in its first try against a ranked opponent this season, then it’ll play in the championship game on Saturday at 8 p.m. ET. A loss on Friday will put Penn State on the schedule for a 5:30 p.m. EST tipoff.

Seton Hall is 3-4 on the season, with three of its losses coming against Power Five opponents. In the Pirates’ most recent outing, they earned an overwhelming 79-44 victory over in-state foe Rider.

Similar to Penn State, veteran head coach Anthony Bozzella’s squad has two outlying scorers. Senior guard Savannah Catalon, a 2025-26 unanimous All-Big East First-Team selection, leads the offense with 16.1 points per game. Catalon’s highlight of the early season was a 29-point outing in a loss to Fairfield on Nov. 12, which helped her surpass 1,000 career points.

The Mansfield, Texas, native is an all-around threat, also leading the Pirates with 24 assists and 16 steals on the season, and has turned the ball over just six times.

Catalon has help from fellow guard Ja’Kahla Craft, who averages 11.4 points per game and is coming off a 23-point performance against the Broncos. The 5-foot-9 Craft is also Seton Hall’s leading rebounder, averaging 6.3 boards per game.

Switching over to Tampa Bay, USF is off to a strong 5-2 start in its first year under Kristy Curry. The new head coach was a surprise for the Bulls, after spending the last 27 years coaching at the Power Four level. Curry’s most recent stop was in Tuscaloosa, where she spent 13 years leading Alabama and made the NCAA Tournament in five of the last six seasons.

Curry also spent time at Texas Tech and Purdue, where she coached against Wright and led the Boilermakers to the National Championship game in 2001.

USF brings an equal offensive production, with six players averaging at least eight points per game. Fatou Diakite leads the effort with 11.9, but Stefanie Ingram isn’t to far behind, averaging 11.6 points a contest. Both are the driving force for the Bulls’ offense.

The 6-foot-3 Diakite leads the team with seven rebounds per game, with Ingram racking up the most assists at 29. However, Ingram has turned the ball over 25 times in seven games.

Seton Hall and USF will tipoff at 8 p.m. EST Friday, following the conclusion of Penn State versus Baylor.

title: ‘I know where I stand’ | Penn State TE Andrew Rappleyea weighs his options for next season
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Tight end Benjamin Brahmer, linebacker Kooper Ebel, safety Jamison Patton and kicker Ryan Barker all said they intend on returning to Penn State next season.

Tight end Andrew Rappleyea was more cryptic with his answer to the same question.

The redshirt junior said he’s still weighing his options, solely focused on playing Maryland on Saturday afternoon in the final game of the regular season. However, Rappleyea said Wednesday he’s been thinking about his decision a lot, and has been trending toward one side for a while — a side he declined to reveal.

“Obviously, I’m thinking about it,” Rappleyea said. “I'd be lying to you if I were to tell you that I haven't been thinking about it. I just think that you have to talk to your people on both sides, and you weigh your decisions, your options from there, where you stand, things like that. So, I have a good idea of what I'm gonna do, but it's just not time for that.”

According to Rappleyea, nobody in the locker room has stepped forward to publicly announce their plans for next season, despite the aforementioned players telling the media their intentions to stay. Regardless of their decisions, however, Rappleyea said beating the Terrapins should be the top priority.

“You’re just some niche dude,” Rappleyea said. “There hasn't been anyone to publicly say what they're doing, but for some guys who are done and not coming back, and for the guys who are deciding to come back, it's still the last game for the season. I want to win that thing, man.”

Rappleyea said the people on the outside he’s spoken to are his “family and representation.” Specifically, his older brother, Allan Rappleyea Jr., who played left tackle at Wake Forest from 2017 to 2021 and has been an instrumental part of guiding him through this experience.

When former Nittany Lion tight end Luke Reynolds followed James Franklin and Ty Howle to Virginia Tech, Rappleyea had his sights set on being one of the biggest contributors on offense in the first season under Matt Campbell. That hasn’t quite happened for him, as the tight ends have taken a backseat to the wide receivers and running backs. He alluded to his underwhelming season as a factor of his decision-making process for next season.

Rappleyea has 303 receiving yards and three touchdowns, narrowly ranking second among tight ends behind Brahmer. Meanwhile, Reynolds has 633 yards and six touchdowns and is a John Mackey Award finalist.

While he believes he’s played good football, there was more Rappleyea wanted to accomplish this season, and he couldn’t help but share his disappointment. But he still has optimism about his ability to play within Penn State’s system, claiming he does fulfill his role on the team “better than anybody in the country.”

“Reminding myself that comparison is the thief of joy is something I've always kept close to my heart,” Rappleyea said. “I ain't Luke Reynolds. I only got 60 for whatever he's got, and he's having a great year. I'm happy it worked out for him, but it's different football over here.”

Rappleyea may still be waiting to finalize his decision until after Saturday’s game or the upcoming bowl, but he fully understands the position he’s in as someone with one remaining year of eligibility.

“I know where I stand, so obviously it's been not ideal how things have gone,” Rappleyea said. “There's been plenty I've left out there.”

title: Series history | Penn State holds dominant lead in lengthy history against Maryland
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Similarly to Penn State’s last matchup against Rutgers, the Nittany Lions hold a commanding advantage over Maryland in their series history.

In 48 matchups, Penn State holds a 44-3-1 record, riding a four-game winning streak against the Terrapins.

Here’s how the series has gone down.

20th century dominance

Penn State and Maryland first met in 1917 in State College, and the result was a sign of how the series would go. The Nittany Lions won 57-0 in dominant fashion. It was a high-scoring affair, especially given the time period.

Penn State went on to shut out the Terrapins in four of the first five matchups, rounding it out with a 45-0 victory in the first game between the teams in College Park, Maryland, in 1943.

The Nittany Lions carried the dominance into the Joe Paterno era. The teams played every year from 1960 to 1975, with Penn State winning every game but one during that stretch. The highlight of the time period was a 63-27 win in Beaver Stadium in 1971.

Penn State and Maryland played for the final time in the 20th century in 1993, which was a matchup in College Park that showcased the type of program the Nittany Lions had at the time.

The Terrapins’ quarterback, Scott Milanovich welcomed the Nittany Lions for what could’ve been a shootout despite Maryland’s winless mark that season. However, it was Penn State’s rushing attack that took over.

In a 70-7 victory, the Nittany Lions ran for 526 yards including 159 from Ki-Jana Carter, who reached the end zone three times on 13 carries. The defense also limited Milanovich to 158 yards while picking him off three times.

Penn State’s four non-wins

The Nittany Lions haven’t won four times in the over 100 years of games played. That includes three losses, and yes, one tie.

The first loss came in a road defeat in 1961, with Maryland coming out on top, 21-17. It was the most points the Terrapins had scored against Penn State at the time.

It took 28 years for Penn State to once again leave a matchup against the Terrapins without a win. With the Nittany Lions up 13-10, Maryland quarterback Neil O’Donnell had an open touchdown pass, but his poorly thrown ball was batted down, forcing the Terrapins to settle for a field goal. The game ended in a 13-13 tie in 1989.

Maryland’s next win came in the first Big Ten matchup between the teams. In 2014, the Nittany Lions led 16-7 heading into the fourth quarter, but two field goals and a rushing touchdown gave the Terrapins a lead. The 20-19 win sent Maryland out on a high note after starting the game with some flares, choosing not to shake hands with Penn State’s captains during the coin toss.

The final Maryland win came in 2020, where the Terrapins earned their biggest victory behind quarterback Taulia Tagovailoa and wide receiver Rakim Jarrett.

Tagovailoa tallied 282 yards and three touchdowns, connecting with Jarrett five times for 144 yards and two touchdowns. The 35-19 win was Maryland’s most points scored in a game against the Nittany Lions.

James Franklin, Mike Locksley provide sparks

James Franklin and Mike Locksley stood across from each other on the sidelines six times. Franklin dominated the matchup, going 5-1 while at Penn State against Locksley, who was hired by Maryland in December 2018.

In 2024, the two made headlines for their conversation after the game. Penn State took the game 44-7, and held a 38-7 lead with time winding down. However, it was a late touchdown pass from backup quarterback Beau Pribula to depth wide receiver Tyseer Denmark that had Locksley upset.

As the two departed from each other at midfield, Franklin shouted, “if that’s what you think then fine.” It was clear that Locksley wasn’t happy with the touchdown as time was expiring.

After leaving the field, Locksley gave his thoughts on the late score.

“Bulls— is what it was. I respect the game, I’ve got a ton of respect for James, his program. I think it was bulls—,” Locksley said.

It was the final time Franklin and Locksley coached against each other at their respective colleges, although they met this year in Virginia Tech’s matchup at Maryland. Penn State and the Terrapins didn’t play in 2025, and Franklin was fired during the season. But the final matchup between the two coaches provided an added spark to a “rivalry” dominated by the Nittany Lions.

title: Penn State women’s hockey notebook | Jeff Kampersal talks power play, staying discipline
author: Brady Welsh | For the Collegian
description:
Coach Jeff Kampersal met with the media Wednesday to discuss his team’s upcoming D1 in DC series against Boston College and No. 2 Minnesota, taking place in Arlington, Virginia, this weekend. Friday is the first time Kampersal will be behind the bench since Nov. 13, as he missed the Delaware series due to an eye procedure.

Matilde Fantin update

Forward Matilde Fantin has made progress battling a lingering injury from last season that has sidelined her for the entire 2026-27 campaign so far. She posted a video of herself last week on Instagram getting back on the ice for the first time in over 200 days.

Back in September, this weekend was originally given as an optimistic time for her return to game action. However, Kampersal is now hoping that Fantin will make her long-awaited season debut “at some point in January,” with her personal well-being taking priority.

Powerplay concerns

A powerplay that has been a bright spot for most of the season was the complete opposite in last week’s series against Delaware. The Blue Hens took 11 total penalties in the two games against Penn State, however, the Nittany Lions only scored once on the advantage. This included the third period of Game 2, where the Nittany Lions largely dominated, but failed to convert on any of the five power plays they were awarded.

Associate head coach Makenna Newkirk, who runs the power play and served as head coach in Kampersal’s absence, told the media postgame Friday that she was trying out some new power play lines as the game went on. At one point in the third, Penn State had its entire fourth line out on the ice for a power play, awarding freshman players such as Kayla McCarthy some time to make their net-front presence felt.

“We’re not like ‘hey, we’re set on these 10 players, and there's no chance for anybody else to get on the power play,’” Kamperal said. “I think in those games where the lead is comfortable, where we can get players opportunities to play on power play and look to try to discover something that we might not be recognizing in practice that gives those players opportunities to succeed and to overtake somebody’s power play spot if they're performing.”

There is no greater test to find out what is and isn’t working on the man-advantage than Friday against Boston College. The Eagles have the second-best penalty kill percentage in the nation (94.7%) and are tied with Quinnipiac for the fewest power play goals allowed in the NCAA with two.

Against an aggressive penalty kill like Boston College, Penn State could be looking to utilize a more “down low” approach rather than getting the puck to the point.

Staying disciplined

The Blue Hens weren’t the only team that had trouble staying out of the penalty box as the Nittany Lions took 10 total penalties of their own last week. While Penn State may have been able to get away with most lapses in judgment against a four-win Delaware team, Kampersal knows it will need to stay disciplined against the Eagles and especially the Golden Gophers, who are scoring at a 34.2% clip on the power play this season, ranking third in the nation.

“We can't take penalties,” Kampersal said. “BC’s Ava Thomas is an elite player, lead powerplay player. Minnesota has a handful of those players that are elite, and so if we spend time in the box, we're in trouble.”

Kampersal also recognized that officiating and how the game is called could be a large factor as well. Co-captain Grace Outwater was penalized for body checking in the second period of Thursday’s game, even when the NCAA has been more lenient on it in women’s hockey this year. Kampersal described Outwater as a “power-forward” who will play physical and referred to the first series of the year against Ohio State as an example of the referees letting body checking go for both teams.

“I think we have to sort of body manage if that makes sense,” Kampersal said. “If we're bigger and stronger than a team, like we can.”

Penn State will play both Boston College and Minnesota back-to-back days on Friday and Saturday, with puck drop scheduled for 5 p.m. for both games.

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell says Carson Hansen, Cam Wallace are questionable
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Matt Campbell met with the media Wednesday in the Lasch Building ahead of Saturday’s showdown at Maryland.

Campbell discussed the health of his running backs, the return of kicker Ryan Barker and the Nittany Lions’ development this season and into the future.

Here’s a look at what Campbell had to say.

Running back health

Campbell said Tuesday that he’ll know more about running back Carson Hansen’s status later this week, that Cam Wallace was dinged up and that James Peoples would be out for Saturday. He returned to the podium Wednesday with positive updates about the group.

“I will say both (Hansen and Wallace), I do think are trending, at least in a positive direction,” Campbell said. “I do think both guys will probably be more leaning toward game-time decisions, but I think they’re more positive.”

He then clarified that both are currently questionable.

Of the four running backs who've consistently seen the field this year, Quinton Martin Jr. is the only fully healthy one as of Wednesday. Depending on the status of Hansen and Wallace, Martin may take a bulk of the reps against the Terrapins.

“Obviously Q is ready to go, and I think has been prepping for his time,” Campbell said. “He’ll get a great opportunity as well.”

Campbell also said he’s looked to other parts of Penn State’s roster as potential depth running backs for Saturday in the case multiple players are sidelined, saying “I think it’s all hands on deck if we need them.”

Ryan Barker’s return

Barker announced Tuesday his plan to return to Penn State, contingent on “just a few conversations with my coaches.” Campbell spoke about his return and the importance Barker has on the Penn State program.

“I think he’s a young man that’s proven to be such a valuable piece to Penn State football,” Campbell said. “I think Ryan would tell you he’s got a chance to be a great senior in the program, a great senior leader, and obviously we’re really excited about what he stands for.”

When Barker was available to the media on Tuesday, he said his performance this season has been subpar, discussing in detail his miss in Week 2 against Temple. He’s also missed three other kicks this year, including two against Purdue.

However, Campbell hasn’t seen Barker’s performance as a negative.

“He’s got really high expectations for himself, what he's got the ability to be, and it puts a lot of pressure on himself to be the best,” Campbell said. “I really appreciate that about him because I think there's a high-end standard for who he wants to be and really what he's shown to be for Penn State football, not only this year but in its past as well.”

Building a program

After Campbell said Tuesday his team lacked mental toughness, he was asked again about moving forward through that as a team. With his first year in Happy Valley almost over, he knows how he wants to grow into the future.

“The thing that you can only demand is the ability to get better every day and get better and strain to have growth and improvement,” Campbell said. “I would say that’s the thing that I’ve been really proud of with this group.”

Despite the loss to Rutgers on Saturday, the Nittany Lions have “stayed the course” through the stretch of four straight loses to open Big Ten play. They bounced back and won three straight, showcasing perseverance through adversity.

“They refuse to flinch and waver and try to build the right foundation to where we want to go and who we want to become,” Campbell said. “The great thing about being here at Penn State is there’s great expectations, and there should be.”

title: Preview | Penn State men’s basketball set for Battle 4 Atlantis debut, 1st ranked matchup
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State has landed in the Bahamas with Reggie Grodin’s sunscreen and a 5-1 record in tow.

The Nittany Lions are set to compete in a four-team Battle 4 Atlantis bracket with No. 24 Memphis, Wake Forest and Mississippi State.

Mike Rhoades’s squad is coming off a Jekyll-and-Hyde-style home win over IU Indy on Wednesday night. The blue and white trailed by 11 points in the first half, but came back with a 16-0 run in the second to pull off a stressful 81-74 win.

"As long as Reggie Grodin gets some sunscreen, we're going," Rhoades said after the IU Indy game. "We're moving up in weight class, which is great. We need to, because when the Big Ten (schedule) rolls around, you can't hide, you can't duck and I'm excited to see how our guys compete and how we get after them."

Sophomore forward Ivan Jurić led the Nittany Lions with 21 points and a career-high 16 rebounds. The performance marked Jurić’s sixth consecutive double-double, which leads the country.

The Zagreb, Croatia, native’s 13.2 rebounds per game also ranks second nationally, trailing only former Nittany Lions center Demetrius Lilley.

When Jurić and Co. step on the court Wednesday, they’ll stare down their first ranked opponent of the season. Memphis is making its AP Poll season debut this week at No. 24.

"Having older guys, they should know by now what it's all about, the discipline they need to have individually and as a team to to find a way to beat good teams," Rhoades said postgame after IU Indy. "So we're going down there to become a better basketball team, no matter what. But let's go find a way."

The Tigers earned their ranking with early victories over then-No. 18 Iowa State, VCU and then-No. 10 Louisville. Memphis renewed its historic rivalry with Louisville on Nov. 15, and blew Pat Kelsey’s expensive roster out of the water, 98-78.

Entering this season, Penny Hardaway was the face of the hot seat in college basketball. The Memphis legend and former NBA star was billed as the man to revive the proud program, but his first eight years haven’t gone to plan.

Since Hardaway was hired in 2018, Memphis has seen more top-ranked recruiting classes, two, and NCAA scandals, three, than March Madness victories. The Tigers won their lone NCAA Tournament game under Hardaway in 2022.

As Memphis athletic director Ed Scott said on “The Gary Parrish Show” before the season, this is Hardaway’s last chance to turn it around. Barring unforeseen circumstances, the Tigers need to win the American Conference championship and make the NCAA Tournament for their most famous alum to remain the head coach.

So far this season, Memphis has been up to the task. The Tigers are 4-1, with their only stumble coming on the road against No. 14 Vanderbilt.

Jayden Reid has emerged as the blue and gray’s best player, averaging 21.2 points, five assists and 2.4 steals per game. The Northwestern transfer racked up 14 points and nine assists in the Wildcats’ victory over Penn State in last season’s Big Ten Tournament.

Tylik “Bully” Weeks is adding 15.6 points per game for the Tigers. Weeks, a 2025-26 Sun Belt first-teamer at Southern Miss, scored 24 points in Memphis’ upset victory over Louisville.

The third player capturing hearts in the Bluff City is Luke Almodovar. The senior averages 17 points per game on 52.6% shooting from three-point range.

Those three Tigers account for 62.6% of the team’s 86 points per game, so Penn State’s chances will largely hinge to its wing defenders’ ability to keep the trio in check.

After facing Memphis, the Nittany Lions will take Thanksgiving Day off before facing either Mississippi State or Wake Forest on Friday.

In year five under Chris Jans, Mississippi State is 5-1. The Bulldogs’ biggest win is an 86-83 road win over UCF, but they lost their only other Power 4 contest to Xavier, 83-61.

Senior guard Josh Hubbard leads Mississippi State. The career Bulldog has started 88 consecutive games and appeared in every possible contest. This season, Hubbard is averaging 16.3 points and leading the team in assists with 23.

Wake Forest’s resume parallels its three bracket-mates in a few ways. Like Penn State and Mississippi State, the Demon Deacons are 5-1, and, like Memphis, their lone loss came against Vanderbilt inside Memorial Gymnasium.

Wake Forest has a strong lead guard at the head of the snake, but unlike the Bulldogs, it’s from a transfer. Sophomore Kevair Kennedy leads the team in scoring and assists and is second in rebounds.

Kennedy, a Merrimack transfer, made history last year as the first player in conference history to win MAAC Rookie of the Year and Player of the Year in the same season.

Before Penn State faces off against Kennedy or Hubbard, it needs to get through its battle with Memphis. The Nittany Lions will make their Battle 4 Atlantis debut Wednesday at 5 p.m. ET on ESPNU.

"I told them this is a business trip. You will enjoy the sun and the water, but it's a business trip," Rhoades said after the IU Indy game. "You have an opportunity to play college basketball at a place like the Bahamas against really good teams, great coaching on national television."
