title: Penn State women’s basketball drops tight battle with Saint Joseph’s
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State played its most complete game of the season on Sunday at Rec Hall. The Lady Lions led until the 1:46 mark of the third quarter, then battled with Saint Joseph’s until the final whistle.

Ultimately, 15 points from Enjulina Gonzalez and winning the turnover battle were not enough to ground the Hawks, and the Lady Lions lost, 71-66.

Early turnovers by each side kept things scoreless until the 8:15 mark of the first quarter, when Gonzalez took the lid off the basket with a pull-up jumper.

The graduate student was the driving force behind Thursday’s comeback victory over Bowling Green. In the second half alone, she shot 8-for-11 from the field for 20 points.

Petra Božan continued right where she left off on Thursday with two early three-pointers. In her last three games, Božan is shooting 73% from beyond the arc.

Saint Joseph’s, the unanimous preseason favorite in the Atlantic 10, stayed in it with three triples of its own, and the Hawks trailed 14-11 at the first media timeout.

Ava Black and Cristen Carter came off the bench at the break, and Black immediately made an impact. She scored from the mid-range on her first possession, then chased down an offensive rebound that led to a Skylar Durley jumper.

Carter got on the board moments later to continue the 6-0 Penn State run and extend the 20-13 lead.

Saint Joseph’s broke its nearly three-minute scoring drought with a buzzer-beating layup to end the first quarter, and Penn State led 20-15 after the opening frame.

Penn State held its five-point advantage early in the second, but Carter picked up two quick fouls and exited the game.

The Hawks scored four straight points to cut the lead to one, but Gonzalez stepped confidently into a three and drained it to make the score 27-23 with 4:57 left in the half.

A minute later, Durley laid in her third bucket of the game on a backdoor cut on the offensive end, then gave up the same score to Gabby Casey on the other side of the floor.

Saint Joseph’s drew within one with a fast-break layup by former Lady Lion Jill Jekot, but Gonzalez made a free throw to reach double figures and maintain the halftime advantage. Penn State led 35-33 at the break, its first halftime lead all season.

The teams traded baskets early in the second half, but Penn State still never surrendered its lead. The Lady Lions led 44-40 with 4:26 left in the quarter after four quick Carter points.

In the midst of a 4:41 scoring drought, Penn State lost the lead for the first time all game with 1:46 on the clock. It was Casey, a preseason all-A10 first-teamer, who knocked down the jumper to take the lead, but Penn State snatched it right back with a Quigley 3-pointer.

Jekot closed the penultimate frame with a 3-pointer to give the Hawks a 49-48 lead. The Cumberland Valley product led all scorers with 11 at the break.

Sharp passing opened up a Gonzalez 3-pointer and a Carter layup, but Aleah Snead scored twice on the opposite end and assisted a Jekot three to extend the Hawks’ lead to 57-53.

Turnovers slowed down the pace of the final four minutes, and Saint Joseph’s maintained its slim advantage. Every time Durley or Gonzalez made a play, the Hawks came right back with Snead or Jekot.

Down five with under a minute left, the Lady Lions were forced to foul, and Saint Joseph’s was reliable from the charity stripe. The crimson and gray made four of its six free throws in the closing stages, and Penn State couldn’t crawl back.

Up next

The Lady Lions travel to the U.S. Virgin Islands for the Paradise Jam, where they’ll face Baylor at 5:30 p.m. ET on Friday.

title: Stock up, stock down | RB Cam Wallace falls off, pass rush nearly wins the day in loss to Rutgers
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s matchup with Rutgers, which the world thought would be a walk in the park, flipped on its head under the Saturday night lights.

The Nittany Lions fell to the Scarlet Knights, 25-24, on a walk-off two-point conversion. They were debilitated by injuries, regression in the run game and an inability to finish strong.

Here’s whose stock rose and whose stock fell after Penn State’s disastrous Week 12 loss to Rutgers.

Stock down: Cam Wallace

Running back Carson Hansen was ruled out pregame due to an injury sustained in the first half against Minnesota last week, so Cam Wallace was named the starter. He’d been a great No. 2 running back in the past three games with multiple big runs, so he was poised for his first true takeover performance.

While he had a 56-yard rushing touchdown in the first quarter, he couldn’t do much else. Penn State’s run game completely fell apart, as Wallace was only able to finish with 95 yards on 16 carries. Similar to his performance against Washington, a single breakaway rush carried Wallace’s stats.

The Nittany Lions needed consistency, something Hansen was bringing to the table as the powerful running back who was proficient in short yardage situations. Wallace wasn’t good in the short game, and it showed in Penn State’s regression on offense.

But he’s all Penn State has at this point of the season. The No. 2 running back on Saturday was James Peoples, but he got hurt in the second quarter and didn’t return to the game after being carted off. That brings Quinton Martin Jr. back into a meaningful role, but he equally struggled on the ground.

Penn State needs Wallace to perform in these final two games. But he hasn’t shown that he’s No. 1 running back material at this stage in his career.

Stock up: Chase Sowell

It was surprising to see Chase Sowell without a catch against the Golden Gophers after tallying 125 yards the week prior against Washington. However, he returned to form against the Scarlet Knights, tallying 123 receiving yards and a touchdown on six catches.

His touchdown catch was a beauty, too. Rocco Becht threw a ball in the end zone along the sideline, and Sowell readjusted to bring it into his chest.

Injuries continued to pile on in the wide receiver room, as Brett Eskildsen went to the locker room after he jumped for a deep ball, crashing to the ground hard. Without Eskildsen and Koby Howard, Sowell’s leading a lineup of younger talent, including Zay Robinson and Amarion Jackson.

Becht will have to continue to utilize Sowell as he did against Rutgers, because he can catch just about anything thrown his way, and there aren’t many proven options left.

Stock down: Josiah Zayas

One of Penn State’s flashiest players got caught flat-footed more than a few times in pass coverage Saturday. He finished with four tackles, two pass breakups and 0.5 tackles for loss. But with how many times he was targeted, those numbers could’ve been much higher.

On Rutgers’ game-winning drive, the Scarlet Knights continued to exploit Zayas’ poor gap control, and quarterback AJ Surace strung together a series of short but substantial gains to gradually charge down the field.

Not only that, but his undisciplined play got him in trouble with the officials, and it nearly cost Penn State a score if it weren’t for a strong pass rush. He defended an end zone pass attempt and celebrated by aggressively putting on his seatbelt.

But the referees deemed he was taunting the opposing player as he stared down the intended receiver, giving Rutgers an automatic first down at Penn State’s 9-yard line.

The safety room lost Zion Tracy and Jamison Patton to injuries, so the Nittany Lions needed Zayas to step up big, and he didn’t.

Stock up: Pass rush, Tony Rojas

Penn State’s pass rush has improved steadily across the year, but it still wasn’t enough to seal the deal in Week 12.

Nine tackles for loss, seven quarterback hurries and four sacks made for an extremely productive night from the Nittany Lions, and it was again led by Tony Rojas, who played like an All-American with 2.5 tackles for loss, three quarterback hurries and 1.5 sacks in addition to a team-high 15 tackles.

When it seemed Rojas’ stock couldn’t go any higher, he joined an elite group of Brandon Short, LaVar Arrington and Dan Connor as the only players in program history to have at least five sacks and 15 tackles for loss in a season. Rojas is the first player to do so since Connor in 2007.

But although it’s an improvement from past weeks, the final drive painted a different picture. Surace had all the time in the world to sling the rock to win the game, and then defensive end Alexander McPherson blew his coverage on the Scarlet Knights two-point conversion when he could’ve shut the play down along the flat.

Stock down: Outlook on Matt Campbell’s first season at Penn State

People were already disappointed in the Nittany Lions during the four-game losing skid to kick off conference play. Many felt the team should’ve easily gotten to nine or 10 wins, capitalizing on a weaker Big Ten schedule for a strong start to Matt Campbell’s tenure in Happy Valley.

That didn’t happen, so when Penn State had the opportunity to win out and finish 8-4, the result didn’t look so bad after all.

Now that’s impossible, as the best possible regular season result is 7-5 with a win over Maryland at SECU Stadium on Saturday.

Losing to Rutgers caused mass outrage over social media, and it has people calling for Campbell’s job after only 11 games. They’re voicing disapproval at James Franklin’s firing, and the cries for Vice President for Intercollegiate Athletics Pat Kraft’s departure have grown from loud to deafening.

For this particular loss to occur in Campbell’s first season at Penn State is a travesty. Rutgers hadn’t scored a touchdown at Beaver Stadium since 1994, was on an 18-game series losing streak and was the worst team in the Big Ten. There was no worse game for Campbell to lose than this one.

title: ‘I hurt for him’ | Penn State LB Tony Rojas emotional after Senior Day
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
Tony Rojas has seen it all at Penn State. A freshman year with losses to Michigan to Ohio State. A College Football Playoff run the very next year. A torn ACL. His coach getting fired just two games after that. A brand new coaching staff.

But his love for this program has never wavered. Rojas said in February that Penn State is home to him, which is why he never left even with options to.

“(Penn State) means the world to me,” Rojas said. “Obviously, been here through the thick and thin. Just seeing all the goods and the bads, lows, whatever it is. I'm grateful for that. Just being with my brothers, even through a tough loss. But just having that brotherhood, able to lean on each other, hug each other, whatever it is. Just being able to have those connections and relationships.”

Rojas was emotional after what could’ve been his final game in Beaver Stadium on Saturday in Penn State’s 25-24 loss to Rutgers. He said postgame it was his last appearance in Happy Valley, but a program spokesperson clarified Rojas is still weighing his options.

“Just all emotions coming at that moment,” Rojas said. “Last game here, just missing everything, really, just trying to soak it in, and obviously it hurt not coming out with the W at the end of it.”

Whether the curtain has or hasn’t closed on Rojas’ Penn State career, he’s become a legend in this era of Nittany Lions football, and his performance against Rutgers only solidified that.

Rojas had a team-high 15 total tackles, 2.5 tackles for loss, 1.5 sacks, three quarterback hurries and two pass breakups. With a sparse crowd, he was one of the only seniors who garnered a loud cheer from the crowd when he walked during Penn State’s Senior Day ceremony.

“Tony Rojas loves Penn State,” linebacker Kooper Ebel said. “He was obviously very emotional after the game, and it hurts a lot. I hurt for him.”

In this era of Penn State football, Rojas is a legendary member of “Linebacker U.” He hit 15.5 tackles for loss and 6.5 sacks on the year with his showing on Saturday, joining LaVar Arrington, Dan Connor and Brandon Short as the only Nittany Lions’ linebackers to have those numbers in a single season.

But when asked about that accomplishment, Rojas said he’d rather win and have zero tackles than sit among that company. Regardless, he still felt it was an honor.

“Just having the knowledge of being up there with those guys, especially coach Connor, who I watched a lot of film on, is super special,” Rojas said.

Not many players can tear an ACL, come back the next year and have the season Rojas is having right now. Take safety Jeremiah Cooper for example, who’s had to sit at times because of lingering soreness from his ACL tear. Or even tight end Gabe Burkle, who said this week he had “a really hard offseason” while recovering from his knee surgery.

Rojas has always been capable of playing the way he is now, it just hasn’t always showed up. He played in all 13 games as a true freshman in 2023, flashing that potential, but then he played all of 2024 with a lingering injury and only saw the field in four contests last year before his season-ending injury.

This is the first year Rojas has truly had the chance to show the world what he can do. And it’s safe to say he’s doing that.

“I think I've grown every single year in the little details, the little things on the field,” Rojas said. “I think obviously I'm playing my best ball right now, and I think you know I just can't be complacent. I know I have things to fix.”

Rojas has also grown as a leader this season as one of the veteran presences in the linebacker room and on the defense, being named a captain twice this year. And he’s also one of the few players on Penn State’s roster this season that has been with the Nittany Lions for four-plus seasons.

“I bleed blue and white, and I’ll die for these colors,” Rojas wrote in a Senior Day post by Penn State football.

Next weekend against Maryland might be the last time Rojas suits up in the blue and white, barring whether he decides to play in the bowl game. If it is the final dance for Rojas, it’s surely been one incredible career.

“(Playing with Rojas has been) unbelievable,” Ebel said. “I can't say enough great things about Tony. He's a great leader. He's a great football player, obviously, but I would say above all things, he's a great human. He cares a lot. Yeah, really hurt for that guy.”

title: ‘It hurts a lot’ | Emotions heavy after Penn State’s upset loss to Rutgers on Senior Day
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
When Rocco Becht took the field for the Senior Day festivities ahead of Penn State’s game against Rutgers, he embraced Matt Campbell and said all five years of his collegiate career flashed before his eyes.

He’d been waiting for this day since his freshman year — the flowers, the support from his family and the honor of making it through a college football career.

But when night fell upon Beaver Stadium, the Scarlet Knights ruined what was supposed to be a ride into the sunset for the seniors, defeating Penn State, 25-24, on a walk-off two-point conversion.

“I didn't have us prepared to play our best football game on Senior Day, the end of the season, and that really hurts me,” Campbell said postgame. “It puts a lot of responsibility on my shoulders.”

According to wide receiver Chase Sowell, you could hear a pin drop in the Nittany Lions’ locker room in the immediate moments after the loss. Sowell said nobody screamed or complained despite the emotions. Their hearts were heavy.

But there was a clear message once the senior leadership spoke up — Penn State was on to the next game because, although it was the seniors’ last time playing at Beaver Stadium, the job is still unfinished.

“Not happy,” Sowell said regarding the locker room atmosphere. “Silent, quiet, but that's expected after a game like that. Our message was ‘How are we gonna respond?’ We still got one more game, and we owe it to this place and owe it to these fans to finish it out the right way. We owe it to the seniors to finish it out the right way.”

Sowell said although he’s only been at Penn State for a season, he understands the pain his longer-tenured teammates are going through. However, he’s said there’s more important things to worry about going forward, such as appreciating the team culture, the memories and keeping a smile on your face.

He also said it’s “not the worst day” of his life despite losing on Senior Day. Sowell noted how there’s bright things to come in the future, and having a positive outlook on the situation is just as important.

“A lot of guys have sacrificed a lot for this place, they care so much that it just hurts,” Sowell said. “It hurts a lot. Having the courage to speak up even when things aren't going good, and still having the courage to be the positive guy and still have a smile on your face going into this last week and still come to work and do the same thing was the biggest thing that we told our guys.”

Becht knew his team was playing for him, not only as a senior, but as the starting quarterback. But he also knew the game was bigger than himself as a newer face in Happy Valley.

He shed light on the implications of bringing home a victory on Senior Day, a day meant to honor the graduating class who have poured years of their lives into Penn State.

“It definitely sucks,” Becht said postgame. “I'm just super passionate about all these other seniors on this team. I've been here for a year, but the guys that have stayed here and were here for four or five years, I was playing for them today. I know guys were playing for me, but shoot, they don't got to play for me. Play for those guys.”

The result was crushing even for the underclassmen. Defensive end Alexander McPherson said the team’s been focused on improving as a collective, but winning on Senior Day was supposed to be a feat dedicated to the older players.

McPherson said he feels bad specifically because he’s a younger player who watched him and his teammates fall short on a one-of-a-kind day meant to celebrate this year’s group of seniors.

“We all feel the same way, it's all about the team,” McPherson said. “But at the end of the day, it is Senior Day. We wanted to get a win, and that didn't happen for the seniors, and I feel bad myself because I'm not a senior, and I feel like I personally didn't do enough to get a win. And I'm sure all the underclassmen feel the same way.”

title: Penn State shows once again it's an inconsistent team in loss to Rutgers
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Beaver Stadium was silent as running back DK Gilley had nothing but green grass in front of him for the two-point conversion to win the game for Rutgers, 25-24, as time expired.

It also showed that Penn State is still dealing with inconsistencies throughout the team, as it couldn’t close out the game after holding leads of 16-0 and 24-10.

“As you go back into it, you just felt like you can never, getting up 16-0, you control the game, and then after that, you could never play complementary football,” Matt Campbell said postgame. “The offense goes down, scores in the third quarter. You feel like you're in a great spot, and then you give up two long drives. You just felt like you never had the ability to put the final blow in.”

The Nittany Lions seemed as though they were turning a corner on the season, entering Saturday’s game with a three-game winning streak after four straight losses. However, they reverted back to how they played during that losing stretch to allow Rutgers to stay in the game and eventually come out with the victory.

While Penn State hasn’t been consistent from game-to-game, it has also struggled to find consistency throughout all 60 minutes of one singular contest. Campbell said “there’s a mentality to play 60 minutes to a standard,” but also recognized, “that is not where we’re at yet.”

“There's been 30 minutes, there's been 42 minutes, there's been 48 minutes, but playing 60 minutes to a standard of excellence,” Campbell said. “That has escaped us. And again, why we haven't gotten there, how we haven't gotten there, those things are on the head football coach.”

The players also noticed the inconsistencies out of the half, especially given the 56-24 difference in third quarters during Big Ten play. It also trails in the fourth quarter, with a 56-38 deficit to close out games.

“Just coming out slow, coming out complacent on both sides of the ball,” wide receiver Chase Sowell said. “I think there has to be a greater sense of urgency to kind of go put that dagger in the game, and honestly, you should have even put a dagger in the game before the second half.”

At times, Penn State looks like a completely different team in the second half the past couple of weeks compared to the first. In the last two wins, it led 28-0 and 28-6 entering the half, and then the production slowed down, similar to Saturday’s comeback defeat.

“I feel like for the most part our defense has been good,” defensive end Ikenna Ezeogu said. “But, other than that, I feel like we just got to just lock into our little details. This stuff been happening all season.”

The struggles for consistency were across the board. On Rutgers running back Antwan Raymond’s second touchdown, he broke two tackles to fight to the end zone. Prior to Saturday’s game, the tackling had made improvements during the win streak.

The offense was stuffed on multiple occasions with a chance to keep drives going, and instead it gave the ball back to Rutgers with momentum flipping. Without running back Carson Hansen, who’s proven to be a reliable short-yardage running back, the Nittany Lions’ threat to gain a yard decreased.

“It is a mentality and mentality to finish the game, but I would say the same thing on the offense, right?” Campbell said. “We get the ball on the 1-yard line. I don't know. We got two, third-and- -1s, a fourth-and-1 and a fourth-and-1 down on the goal line, and we don't finish. And to me, our ability to do hard things is still escaping this team from becoming its best.”

On special teams, punter Nathan Tiyce, who’s averaging 41.2 yards per punt and has a long of 60 yards on the season, sent a 31-yard punt to give Rutgers more optimal field position to go down and score in the final seconds. That was right after Tiyce placed a near-perfect 48-yard punt that was downed at the 6-yard line on the previous drive.

The failure to put together the same performance from half-to-half, and game-to-game, is a reason Penn State now sits at 6-5 — the Nittany Lions could be upwards of 9-2 if they played similar halves.

“Hard is playing great defense in the third and fourth quarter,” Campbell said. “Hard is playing great offense down on the 1-yard line and down on a fourth-and-1 situation. Those are the hard things, and I felt like we made great strides at times, but obviously we took a step backwards tonight, and that's disappointing.”

title: ’It obviously sucked’ | Penn State’s defense collapses in final drive against Rutgers
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
With zero seconds on the clock, Rutgers’ quarterback AJ Surace took the field with DK Gilley in the backfield. The Scarlet Knights had just scored a touchdown to bring the game within one point, and they were going for the two-point conversion to win.

Some of the Penn State faithful were loud in an attempt to disrupt Rutgers, while others were in disbelief as to what had just happened. Surace took the snap and watched as Gilley ran into the flat, passing him the ball as he made his way across the goal line to upset Penn State 25-24 on Senior Day.

“We gotta win,” Kooper Ebel said postgame. “We gotta have better technique. We can't leave it to chance. There's a lot of things. We had a lot of opportunities to get off the field in that game.”

The Nittany Lions had been challenged all day by the Scarlet Knights, but it was the final drive that decided the game. For a Penn State team that had been improving with three straight wins, Saturday’s contest was a big step in the wrong direction.

“We should have put the nail in the coffin a lot earlier,” defensive end Alex McPherson said. “It didn't really come down to that. It's everything leading up to it. They should have never been in the red zone. All the whole nine.”

Penn State’s defense held the Scarlet Knights to short pickups for the first 90 seconds of the drive, but after the two-minute warning, things began to fall apart.

In the second play after the break, Surace attempted a deep ball to wide receiver Ben Black III, which fell incomplete, but a flag laid on the field. Cornerback Audavion Collins was called for pass interference, placing the ball at the 26-yard line.

“(It) obviously sucked,” Rojas said. “You can't leave it in the hands of the ref. We just got to be better with little details, whatever it is.”

For the next 90 seconds, Rutgers continued to push the ball down the field both on the ground and through the air. Surace completed a pair of passes to Black and wide receiver Dyzier Carter, while running back Antwon Raymond had a short gain.

Raymond was a key factor to the Scarlet Knights’ resurgence, as he contributed heavily to the offense. When he wasn’t handed the ball in the backfield, he would run quick routes into the flat and was often open.

“The running back was priding it out,” Ebel said. “That's where they were resorting to. That's what they had found their niche in the second half to get the ball out to the running back — frustrating.”

Ebel ultimately deflected Surace’s pass on third down to bring up fourth-and-goal from the 8-yard line with just 10 seconds to go.

After a timeout from Rutgers, Surace lined up for the snap with what many thought was the last play. But it wasn’t, as the Nittany Lions were called for pass interference for the second time in the final two minutes, putting the ball at the 2-yard line.

“I felt like we were in great position,” Ebel said. “A lot of those plays they made the play in the moment. Whether it's pass interference or they go in, they go up and high point a ball and make a play on fourth down, whatever it is. We got to win the moment. We can't leave it to chance.”

The Scarlet Knights now had six seconds to play as Surace swung the ball wide to Raymond, who was open after Rojas slipped in coverage. Collins had Raymond wrapped up and short of the goal line, but he pitched the ball back to Black as he crossed into the end zone.

“Dude just made a play, man, that just happens,” defensive end Ike Ezeogu said. “That was a heads up play he made, and we weren't in the right spot to get him down, so it happens.”

Rutgers then converted the two-point conversion as Gilley made his way into the end zone.

It appeared to many as though McPherson was late to his assignment in covering Gilley. But Rojas said “everybody did their job correct,” and that it was “the right play for them to go.”

“You just got to be better at that,” Ezeogu said. “Everybody got to be on top of their stuff when that stuff happens in critical moments.”

With the two-point play, Rutgers came away with the last-second victory, marking a déjà vu moment for Penn State, as the Wisconsin game in Week 4 had a similar ending.

“Third quarter, second half, that's always been our problem, and I thought we've been getting better at it slowly, and then today it came back,” Rojas said. “Whether it was we were too complacent, whatever it is, coming after halftime, we have to be better at that.”

title: 3 takeaways from Penn State's disastrous loss to Rutgers
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Rutgers pulled off the unthinkable Saturday night.

A late fourth quarter touchdown drive by the Scarlet Knights ended with a game-winning two-point conversion, effectively ruining Penn State’s farewell to the seniors on Senior Day. The Nittany Lions fell, 25-24, to the last-place team in the Big Ten.

Here are three takeaways from Penn State’s upset loss to Rutgers.

Slew of injuries could hurt Penn State down the stretch

Running back Carson Hansen was injured in last week’s game against Minnesota, forcing Penn State to start Cam Wallace against Rutgers.

Hansen’s addition to the injury report alongside Koby Howard, cornerback Jahmir Joseph and defensive end Caleb Bacon wasn't enough, as multiple players got injured in the first half against Rutgers alone.

Wide receiver Brett Eskildsen and running back James Peoples were each injured in the first quarter and didn’t return, while safety Jamison Patton jogged off on his own power in the second quarter, but also didn’t come back in the game.

Safety Zion Tracy didn’t play in the game because Matt Campbell said he “tweaked” something in pregame warmups.

“The safety room took a hit,” Campbell said postgame. “When Zion went out, obviously that was a big hit for us. I did think Bryson (Williams) did some good things, so we'll have to watch and see what that video looks like from his end of things. But we’ve got enough good football players to be able to play the way we need to play, and unfortunately we just didn't today.”

On his first target of the game, Eskildsen went up to receive a deep pass and crashed down hard into the turf. He was shaken upon getting up and was immediately taken to the locker room. Despite coming back to the sidelines, he didn’t play.

Peoples went down with a leg injury on his second rush of the game, which went for 15 yards, when a defender fell awkwardly on his left leg. He was carted to the locker room.

Center Brock Riker was also carted to the locker room after being helped off the field by his teammates. Vaea Ikakoula took the final snap at center in the first half, but Riker returned to the game for the final 30 minutes.

Penn State has dealt with injury issues all season but has gotten by because of strong depth. Now the depth chart is even slimmer, and the team will have to rely more on Wallace, Chase Sowell and the tight ends for production offensively. Younger receivers such as Zay Robinson and Amarion Jackson could also play a big role moving forward, as they combined for four catches and 66 yards on Saturday.

Penn State couldn’t spark run offense without Carson Hansen

If there was a game for the run game to go nuclear, it should’ve been this one, and a 56-yard rushing touchdown by Cam Wallace wasn’t enough to get the job done.

But outside Wallace’s big gain, the run game couldn't penetrate the Scarlet Knights’ defense — the worst run defense in the Big Ten.

“I think we've been as good as anybody all season in short yardage situations,” Campbell said. “I think the thing that's really frustrating is at this point of the season to regress and not be as good at it tonight.”

Carson Hansen was the heartbeat of Penn State’s offense the past three weeks, but he was injured prior to halftime against Minnesota after tallying 126 yards in that first half.

Penn State needed Wallace to step up as the No. 1 running back, but many of his runs were stuffed at the line of scrimmage and his lone touchdown run carried his stats. He finished the game with 95 rushing yards, averaging 5.9 yards per carry.

“We got to do a better job, sustaining our blocks to be able to help the running back out to hit the holes for us,” offensive lineman Anthony Donkoh said. “To get those first downs for us to not be in those third-and-long yardage or third-and-short yardage, and keep the clock running.”

Additionally, he fumbled a handoff in the third quarter, giving the Scarlet Knights an opportunity to work in Penn State territory. While it didn’t result in a score for Rutgers, those mistakes can’t happen.

Regardless, the depth chart has come down to Wallace and Quinton Martin Jr., the only other running back currently healthy that’s seen the field this season. Because Martin couldn’t generate offense either, Wallace will have to be more consistent if Penn State wants to get back to the strong ground game it showcased in the last three weeks.

“Our ability to do hard things is still escaping this team from becoming its best,” Campbell said. “Hard is playing great defense in the third and fourth quarter. Hard is playing great offense down on the 1-yard line and down on a fourth-and-1 situation.”

Pass rush holds Scarlet Knights at bay for most of the game

Rutgers had its fair share of opportunities to score. Multiple three-and-outs, a fumble recovery and moments of undisciplined play from Penn State made this game a lot closer than one would’ve imagined.

The Nittany Lions’ pass rush played hero on Saturday, and defensive end Ikenna Ezeogu’s sack in the fourth quarter was a prime example of it. After Marcus Neal Jr.’s 15-yard penalty for a late hit, Ezeogu sacked quarterback AJ Surace on third down for a loss of seven.

Surace felt the heat all game long, too, as Penn State finished with nine tackles for loss, four sacks and seven quarterback hurries.

Tony Rojas had a monster performance behind the line of scrimmage with 2.5 tackles for loss, 1.5 sacks and three quarterback hurries. Linebacker Kooper Ebel, defensive end Yvan Kemajou and defensive tackle Siale Taupaki also hurried Surace.

“Tony Rojas loves Penn State,” Ebel said. “I can't say anything other than that. Simple, plain. He was obviously very emotional after the game, and it hurts a lot. I hurt for him.”

Ebel, defensive tackles Ty Blanding and Armstrong Nnodim, defensive ends Ezeogu and Alexander McPherson and cornerbacks Audavion Collins, Josiah Zayas and Daryus Dixson all contributed to the tackles for loss.

Penn State’s pass rush has been steadily improving after an abysmal start to the season, and it was a big reason why the Nittany Lions were outpaced earlier in conference play.

After a season’s worth of growth, coupled with facing weaker opponents, Penn State has found consistency in getting home, and it nearly helped the Nittany Lions’ win the game.

“We just continue to just keep getting better with each and every week, and I know we got talented guys on that defensive line,” Ezeogu said. “So the pass rush didn't really surprise me today. It hasn't really showed up on the season, but it showed up today.”

title: Preview | Penn State women’s basketball looks to carry momentum into Saint Joseph’s matchup
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Tanisha’s time finally arrived Thursday afternoon in Rec Hall. Penn State won its first game of the Tanisha Wright era, 72-70 over Bowling Green on Education Day.

The Lady Lions trailed by as many as 18 points in the first half but came back to escape the winless club. Enjulina Gonzalez scored all 20 of her points in the second half and powered the comeback.

“It's thrilling, it's exciting, especially in the in the manner of which it happened,” Wright said about her first victory. “Being down in the second half and just watching your team continue to fight and never give up and give in.”

In her return to the starting lineup, Savannah White led the team in rebounds with nine. On the flip side, Devyn Quigley came off the bench for the first time this season and racked up 14 points before an ejection in the third quarter.

The 11 a.m. matinee was Penn State’s best-attended game of the season thanks to the 18 school field trip groups that flooded Rec Hall. 2,977 fans were in the house, clearing the previous high-water mark of 2,083 set on the road against Arizona State.

“I want to be the joy and the energy that they see, and I just I to be somebody that is looked up to,” Gonzalez said after the game. “I just want to thank the kids for coming out because they obviously brought all the energy, and we fed off of that.”

Penn State will look to build off of that energy when they return to Rec Hall on Sunday afternoon against Saint Joseph’s, the unanimous favorite to win the Atlantic 10.

The Hawks are 3-1 in the first two weeks of the season, including a 67-56 road win over Cincinnati. Penn State fell to the Bearcats, 76-53, in its trip to the Queen City.

Gabby Casey, a preseason A10 first-teamer, drives Saint Joseph’s on both ends of the court. The senior leads the team in minutes, points and steals. On the sheet, Casey averages 14.3 points per game and 3.5 steals.

She has been a mainstay for the Hawks since her freshman year. Against Drexel on Nov. 15, Casey made her 100th appearance in the crimson and gray and her 66th start.

Saint Joseph’s also returned the 2024-25 A10 Sixth Woman of the Year, Aleah Snead. The senior hasn’t shot the ball well this season, but she still leads the team in assists and is a member of the preseason conference all-defensive team.

Rhian Stokes is a junior guard who hasn’t started a game yet this year, but averages 11 points per game and gets to the charity stripe at an alarming rate. The preseason all-A10 third-teamer has already shot 22 free throws, and Penn State hasn’t been the most disciplined defensive team so far in the young season.

The Hawks will travel to Happy Valley on Sunday afternoon for a 1 p.m. tip-off at Rec Hall before the Lady Lions ship out to the U.S. Virgin Islands for the Paradise Jam.

title: ‘The game owes you nothing’ | Penn State women’s soccer wins possession, loses match
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State dominated its 100th NCAA Tournament contest at Jeffrey Field. The Nittany Lions outshot Villanova 18-4 and possessed the ball for 67% of the match.

For 98 minutes, the blue and white pounded on Hannah Dickinson’s door, but the Villanova goalkeeper never bowed to the pressure. Instead, the Wildcats converted a miraculous golden goal and upset the No. 6 seed Penn State to move on to the second round of the tournament.

“We talked this week about Muhammad Ali,” Villanova coach Samar Azem said. “You know, he was historically known for rope-a-dope, right? Sit on the ropes, let him punch, let him feel comfortable, and then all it takes is one punch and a knockout. And it's pretty cool that that's kind of how that worked out today.”

It wasn’t very cool for Penn State. Coach Erica Dambach’s squad put seven shots on goal and had countless more chances. The blue and white also earned five corner kicks while Villanova couldn’t muster one.

“It doesn't matter how much you have the ball, doesn’t matter how many shots you have,” Dambach said. “Our sport is a particularly cruel one. It doesn't matter how much you have the ball, but you see these score lines all around the world for this very reason. You've got to figure out a way to win the game and figure out a way to put the ball in the back of the net.”

One of the primary reasons why the Nittany Lions couldn’t find the back of the net was Dickinson’s performance in net. The graduate student made save after save in big moments and wound up with seven in total.

She racked up the BIG EAST conference awards this season. After recording 10 shutouts in the regular season, Dickinson earned BIG EAST Most Outstanding Defensive Player, BIG EAST Goalkeeper of the Year, and first-team all-BIG EAST honors. In the BIG EAST Tournament, the Seattle native allowed just one goal and was named to that All-Tournament team.

Dickinson continued her fearless play tonight behind an especially stout performance by her defense.

“I think my defense does a great job at making my job easy,” Dickinson said. “I think they make it predictable for me, so I can do my job in the best way possible. And I think that as a team, defensively, we played incredible.”

On the other side of the field, Mackenzie Gress closed her prolific Penn State career by letting the golden goal slip off the back of her gloves. Dambach’s message to her redshirt senior wasn’t one of blame, but almost an apology.

“I think the biggest message to Mack is, ‘that game should have been over a long time ago,’” Dambach said. “I think she's a big enough person to put her hand up and say that was a mistake. I think there were plenty of mistakes made all over the field, and I think that game's got to end in regulation. We shouldn't have even been in that place, and I told her as much.”

Gress only faced two shots on goal all game, largely because her defense cleared almost every Villanova attack before it reached the goal line.

After Dambach watched her team control the pitch in front of a record crowd for a first-round NCAA Tournament game at Jeffrey Field, the national championship-winning coach felt the realities of a single-elimination tournament.

“The game owes you nothing, and that's the reality of it. It doesn't matter who's got the ball or who's the higher seed or who's the home team. It owes you absolutely nothing,” she said. “It's not going to do you any favors. You've got to go and get it and take it, and that's a hard lesson to learn tonight.”

title: Penn State men’s hockey extends losing streak, falls to No. 2 Wisconsin
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
After being swept by then-No. 2 Michigan, Penn State has no break as it hits the road once again to face another top-ranked Big Ten opponent in No. 2 Wisconsin.

Despite one of their strongest showings of the season, the Nittany Lions fell 2-1 to the Badgers.

A fast start is crucial when playing one of the best teams in college hockey.

That didn’t seem to be the way Penn State was headed, however, after junior defenseman Nick Fascia was called for cross-checking just two minutes in, giving Wisconsin’s No. 2-ranked power play an early opportunity.

The Nittany Lions held strong against the Badgers’ man-advantage, however, and limited them to just two shots.

Carrying over its penalty-kill momentum, the blue and white continued to play neck and neck with Wisconsin in a defensive-heavy battle.

Wisconsin forward Grady Deering got tangled up with senior captain Reese Laubach and was sent to the box for slashing, giving Penn State its first power play of the night and a prime chance to open the scoring.

Instead, Wisconsin broke the ice at the Kohl Center after junior forward Gavin Morrissey tallied his second shorthanded goal of the season.

Morrissey went unseen behind the blue and white defenders, and, after an off-target pass from the Nittany Lions ended on the stick of sophomore forward Finn Brink, he found Morrissey on a breakaway, who stickhandled the puck through goaltender Josh Fleming.

Maintaining momentum after getting scored on is something Penn State has struggled with at points throughout the season.

That theme wasn’t evident on Friday, however. Although heading into the first intermission trailing 1-0, the Nittany Lions held a 7-4 shots advantage and put together a strong 20 minutes against the No. 2 team in the country.

The middle frame was much the same, with Penn State continuing to play some of its best minutes of the season, while Wisconsin slowly picked up the intensity.

One of the Badgers’ best opportunities of the period came from former Nittany Lion JJ Wiebusch.

Wiebusch entered the transfer portal this offseason after being a crucial part of the blue and white’s success over the last few seasons, and his departure left a sizeable hole in its top-six scoring unit.

Late in the second period, the junior forward sent a cross-ice pass to freshman forward Zach Wooten, and Fleming had to make a tough angle save to keep the game a one-goal difference.

Just as time was winding down in the middle period wound down, the blue and white found its equalizer thanks to leading scorer Justin Poirier.

With just 16 seconds left, the sophomore forward picked a corner. It fired a shot from the high slot that found its way past goaltender Alexis Cournoyer, sending the Nittany Lions into the final period tied at one with the Badgers.

Penn State’s lead was short-lived, however, and Wisconsin answered less than two minutes into the final 20 minutes.

Sophomore forward Bruno Idźan’s initial shot took a few bounces in front of the net before sophomore Vasily Zelenov batted it into the blue and white’s net.

While Penn State kept up the intensity, the Badgers had their best period of the night and now held the shots advantage 25-17 by the 10-minute mark.

The Big Ten leaders in shots per game were throwing everything at the Nittany Lions through the last five minutes of the third period, but Fleming made save after save to keep his team in it.

Despite one of the blue and white’s strongest performances of the season, the early third-period goal proved to be the game winner, and it fell to No. 2 Wisconsin, 2-1.

Up next

Penn State concludes its weekend in Madison, Wisconsin, on Saturday, with a 7 p.m. puck drop at the Kohl Center, scheduled for its rematch against No. 2 Wisconsin.

title: Penn State women’s soccer eliminated from NCAA Women’s College Cup by Villanova, ending season at home
author: Joey Bolger | For the Collegian
description:
The Penn State Nittany Lions returned to Happy Valley to host the Villanova Wildcats in the first round of the NCAA Women’s College Cup.

It was the first time the two programs have faced off in 20 years; Penn State won that matchup 2-0 in the 2006 NCAA tournament.

The Nittany Lions were 6-0-3 at home this season and looked to stay undefeated at Jeffrey Field; the blue-and-white also hoped to bounce back from a 2-1 overtime loss to Purdue in the Big Ten Tournament Quarterfinals.

The Wildcats entered the NCAA tournament with a full head of steam; they were on a five-game winning streak, including upset victories over Seton Hall and No. 25 Xavier on their way to becoming Big East champions.

That form ultimately propelled Villanova to end the Nittany Lions’ undefeated home record in a 1-0 overtime victory; the Wildcats advance to the next round of the NCAA Women’s College Cup while the Nittany Lions end their 2026 season.

“This game owes you nothing, and that’s the reality of it,” said coach Erica Dambach. “You’ve got to go and take it, and that’s a hard lesson to learn tonight.”

Villanova wasted no time: a throw-in from the Wildcats left Penn State goalkeeper Mackenzie Gress one-on-one with a Villanova forward, but Gress controlled the ball and saved a potential goal.

The blue-and-white started to settle in as they applied constant pressure to the Villanova defense throughout the first 13 minutes; a through ball to forward Ellie Kocher left her and Wildcat goalkeeper Hannah Dickinson alone, but Dickinson was able to beat Kocher to the ball.

Since the first two minutes of the match, Villanova has struggled in transition as the Nittany Lions' midfielders and defenders have been relentless on every Wildcat attempt to advance into Penn State territory.

The same theme continued through the last 10 minutes of the first half, as the Penn State offense kept finding looks at the goal, but the Villanova defense would not break.

This defensive matchup went into the half scoreless. The Nittany Lions controlled the ball for most of the half and did not allow the Wildcats to get a single shot, while Penn State had 2 shots on goal; Dickinson saved both.

Less than a minute into the second half, Penn State came out aggressive, sending a cross into the penalty area and finding an open look for Kocher, but Dickinson was there to save it again.

Villanova started to show why they won the Big East tournament, finally breaking through the Penn State defense as forward Dez Zapata bent the ball and landed just above the top right corner of the goal.

Dickinson continued to shut down the relentless Nittany Lion attack midway through the second half; any good look the blue-and-white had, Dickinson was already a step ahead, saving three shots on goal in one possession.

“She’s one of the smartest goalkeepers I’ve ever met,” said Villanova coach Samar Azem. “It’s like having another coach on the field.”

A Corner kick from the blue-and-white found defender Bella Ayscue with a wide-open look, but she could not time the shot, allowing the Wildcat defense to clear once again.

All half the Nittany Lions were finding look after look at the net, but they either could not capitalize on the opportunity or the Wildcat defense was right there for the block.

Still scoreless heading into the final minutes of regulation, the same trends from the first half continued in the second half. Penn State found opportunities to break the silence, and Villanova had an answer for the Nittany Lions every step of the way.

“You’ve got to figure out a way to put the ball in the back of the net,” said Dambach. “We weren’t able to do that tonight.”

Penn State held the ball at midfield in the last seconds of regulation, heading into overtime, with both teams refusing to let this be the end of their season.

Three minutes into overtime, Wildcat defender Meredith Palmer committed a foul, giving Penn State a free kick, but the referees waved it off.

A foul by defender Lilly Burger gave Villanova a free kick, and the Wildcats walked it off with a game-sealing goal from Kaydee Amorosa right over Gress. Penn State swarmed at the ball and made contact when it went over the line, but it couldn't prevent the upset.

“Our team did a phenomenal job, I’m really proud.” said Azem.

title: No. 7 Penn State women’s hockey launches precise attack on the ice, defeating Delaware 6-1
author: Henry Bustin | For the Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions dominated the Delaware Blue Hens this Friday in Pegula Arena, ending the game with a 6-1 victory. The blue and white's superb performance was a result of coordinated efforts and hard work from the offense, allowing for consistent scoring throughout the game that kept pressure on Delaware.

The first period began with an exchange of force between Penn State and Delaware, trading possession of the puck. It wasn’t until the 16th minute that the Blue Hens landed a successful goal on Penn State, which would soon end the period 1-0 Delaware. Although it was an intimidating start to the game, the Nittany Lions were confident in their ability to persevere and retaliate.

“Nothing changed with our game plan, really. Offensively, we just talked and really tried to solidify it,” associate head coach Makenna Newkirk said. “So, in between the first and the second, just going over what we’re looking for and making sure that they’re upholding that end.”

Early in the fourth minute of the second period, freshman forward Sofia Ismael landed the first goal for the Nittany Lions against Delaware. This prompted a surge of momentum that continued for the rest of the game. The hostility wasn’t only shown in the blue and white’s offensive effort but also in the defending and precise goalkeeping of Morgan Stickney.

“Just reminding our group of who we are; we stick to our structure and when we do good things happen and we’ll chip away at them,” Newkirk said. “That first goal, it was four consecutive shifts which got them in their zone and let them chip at them.”

The blue and white’s offense launched an aggressive onslaught against the Blue Hens, with intense pressure applied as Penn State kept possession of the puck for the majority of the period, notching numerous shot attempts. Finally, in the 20th minute during a power play, Sophie Morrow scored a second goal for Penn State, leaving the Nittany Lions ahead at the end of the period 2-1.

It was collaborative teamwork and communication between the offensive forwards that allowed the Nittany Lions to continue to score and work against the efforts of the Blue Hens. The blue and white demonstrated its resilience and skill as it orchestrated a precise attack on the ice that fueled success throughout the entire game following the first period.

With the blue and white drive still ongoing, Penn State didn’t drop its guard for a second. The third period kicked off with continued aggression on Delaware, and the excitement continued when freshman Lorelai Nelson scored against the Blue Hens in the second minute, on a pass assisted by Alanna Devlin. Penn State’s offensive push didn’t end there. Shortly after, Kylie Amelkovich scored once again for Penn State.

In the seventh minute, forward Nicole Hall scored a fifth goal for the blue and white. The Nittany Lions continued with pressure, not giving the Blue Hens a chance for an opening. With the fans cheering in excitement, Hall once again scored in the 11th minute, electrifying the stands. As the buzzer sounded, Penn State’s six unanswered goals guided the Nittany Lions to victory for the second day in a row against the Blue Hens.

The Nittany Lions accumulated 43 shots in the game, while Delaware only had nine, demonstrating the adversity of the blue and white’s offense.

title: Six unanswered goals, reckless Blue Hen sticks lead No. 7 Penn State women’s hockey over Delaware
author: Brady Welsh | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State defeated the Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens by a score of 6-1 to earn a weekend sweep and improve to 6-0 all-time in the head-to-head series. It was the Nittany Lions’ 10th conference win of the season.

Unlike Game 1, Delaware put the pressure on right out of the gate, getting the first two shots of the game, but just like the opener that saw 12 total penalties, the undisciplined hockey from both teams continued.

Grace Tullock took a penalty for interference early and Delaware struck first on a man-advantage that has been plaguing them all season. Katie Belk, in the slot, fired the puck past Morgan Stickney on the low glove side to give the Blue Hens an early 1-0 lead over three minutes into the game. It was their first lead over the Nittany Lions in team history and the freshman’s second score of the series.

Penn State had a powerplay later in the period as Kyla Schneider went to the box for tripping, but couldn’t convert. The Nittany Lions' discipline problem continued as Lorelai Nelson went to the box with seven minutes left for a tripping call of her own. Delaware’s powerplay lasted only 43 seconds as Shea Frost tripped Abby Stonehouse right in front of the referee to make it a four-on-four. However, neither team converted.

Penn State took nine of the 12 total first period shots that occurred since the Belk goal, but none went in as the first period ended with Delaware on top.

The Nittany Lions began the second period with a lot of pressure, playing the majority of the first five minutes in the Delaware zone, but Blue Hen goalie Mattie Robitzer continued to stand tall.

After a Delaware icing, the precise puck movement from the Nittany Lions continued and succeeded as they grabbed a freshman goal of their own. Sofia Ismael snuck the puck under the pad of Robitzer on an awkward backhand from the right post for her seventh goal of the year to tie the game at one.

Reese Reid took a hooking penalty shortly after the goal for the second Penn State power play of the night, but Delaware was once again able to kill it off. After Reid went back to the box again less than four minutes later, Delaware’s penalty kill continued to fend off a Penn State power play that had been one of its biggest strengths all season.

With five minutes left in the second, yet another penalty was called this time on Ashley Kokavec of the Nittany Lions for holding. Penn State got the majority of the chances shorthanded and effectively killed it off.

Frost’s second penalty of the game, with under a minute left in the period, was costly for the Blue Hens. Sophie Morrow got the puck at the point and sniped it past Robitzer to give the Nittany Lions a 2-1 lead late in the second period, with that being the score heading into the final frame. Penn State outshot the Blue Hens 14-3 in the period.

“One big thing for us is, it's all about urgency, and so I think just reminding our group in terms of who we are, " associate head coach Makenna Newkirk said. “We stick to our structure, and when we do, good things happen.”

The Nittany Lions continued the pressure to begin the third as Nelson had a wraparound goal less than two minutes in to make it a two-goal lead. Kylie Amelkovich followed it up with one of her own. After a four-assist performance on Thursday, Amelkovich scored on a wrist shot from the slot two minutes later, putting Penn State up 4-1.

Delaware’s penalty issues continued afterwards as a Lily Myers elbow was determined to be a five-minute major after a lengthy review. Frost then took her third penalty of the game for two minutes of the major to be played at five-on-three. Penn State didn’t waste time and capitalized on this opportunity to continue building momentum. Nicole Hall dug at a puck in the crease and got it through to put the Nittany Lions up 5-1.

Hall followed up with another goal four minutes later, burying a Megan Hosman shot that ricocheted off the boards for her second of the game and the sixth unanswered for Penn State. It was her third in the first series since the IIHF World Championships.

Wren Abboud would then tack on two more penalties for Delaware, making it nine on the night for the Blue Hens, six being stick infractions.

“So I think for us, it was just trying to get more people involved, and just time on ice, and make sure that our player loads are good. So, you know, you never want to take a power play off,” Newkirk said. “They certainly don't, but I also think it's a good learning experience for all those kids.”

Penn State outshot Delaware 21-0 in the final frame and were able to win 6-1.

“You never want to go down 1-0 to start a game, but definitely proud of this team,” Newkirk said. “They've been resilient all year, and so it's right on par for them.”

title: ‘Once a Lady Lion, always a Lady Lion’ | Tanisha Wright wins first game as Penn State women’s basketball coach in memorable fashion
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
A shocking home loss to Cleveland State. A less surprising drubbing by Cincinnati. A tight loss to Dayton. An emphatic 45-point blowout at the hands of Arizona State. Those four games added up to the worst start in program history, but all was forgotten for a few early afternoon hours on Thursday inside Rec Hall.

Tanisha Wright, a 2005 Penn State graduate, won her first game as the head coach of her alma mater on Thursday. Her team trailed by as many as 18 points, but came all the way back, winning the second half 47-29 to emerge with a 72-70 victory.

“It's thrilling, it's exciting, especially in the in the manner of which it happened,” Wright said. “Being down in the second half and just watching your team continue to fight and never give up and give in. We talked about being clothed with toughness, and I think we made a lot of tough plays today both physically and mentally.”

Almost all of her team’s tough plays came in the second half. Across the first two quarters, Penn State turned the ball over 14 times and gave up 23 fast-break points. In the final two frames, the Lady Lions scored 16 points off turnovers to Bowling Green’s three.

Wright explained that her message at halftime was simple. Even though this group hadn’t shown it on the court through four games, she knew they had a comeback in them.

“We talked about being being composed, playing with composure, and settling in,” she said. “We were turning the ball over, and I think one of the main messages that we had was (to) actually settle in and execute, keep the ball.”

The Lady Lions certainly settled in early in the second half. From 7:36 to 4:02 in the third quarter, Penn State put together a 15-3 run, including seven points from Enjulina Gonzalez.

The graduate student scored all 20 of her points in the second half and added seven total assists. Gonzalez, who is on her fourth school, discussed what getting this first victory for Wright meant to her.

“I've been waiting for this. I was waiting to just win. It means so much for a coach to just pour so much confidence into you,” Gonzalez said. “There was many games that we feel like we could have won, but she didn't give up on us, and she just kept pouring confidence into us.”

Wright has consistently praised her team, especially Gonzalez, through the turbulent start for things like defensive energy that don’t show up in the box score. The Miami, Florida, native hadn’t made a three-pointer before Thursday and was shooting just 25.7% from the field.

“Verbatim, she (Wright) said, ‘I wouldn't want to be with anybody else rather than you guys.’ And that just makes you feel confident about yourself, and knowing that obviously she's been at the pros, coached the pros, like that's what you want to hear from coach,” Gonzalez said. “Day in and day out, she's a great person of just pouring confidence into you. That's so big to me, so winning for her, it just means the world.”

Throughout the Enji explosion, her typical energy fed off of the 18 school groups in attendance for Education Day. Elementary and middle schools from across Central Pennsylvania flooded Rec Hall and provided an electric home environment.

“Kids' day is always a special day,” Wright said. “We understand that it's bigger than the game. Being able to impact such young lives from a young age is really special. Our girls really take that serious. That's why we're out in the community. That's why we do things like this, so that there's a connection to it, and so that's always been a special day as a player for me, and now as a coach.”

The youngsters brought the noise, but the older clientele provided a strong backbone of support for the debutante coach. One of the featured guests was Wright’s former teammate, Ashli Shay. Shay, the varsity girls basketball coach at Cedar Crest High School, brought her program along for the matinee.

Lady Lion alums dotted the historic arena, including the second-leading scorer in program history, Maggie Lucas. Lucas is now an assistant coach at Bowling Green, and Penn State presented her with a gift before the game.

“We're a very proud program; we're a very traditional program,” Wright said. “We always have been, and we always will be. And so, the support that the alums always give and continue to give is always going to be a part of who we are. We love to say, ‘Once a Lady Lion, always a Lady Lion.’”

title: ‘He’s a gamer’ | Backup QB Alex Manske flashes his potential after 1st career touchdown pass
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
On a first down in Minnesota territory, quarterback Alex Manske was pressured, and off his back foot he lobbed a ball right into the arms of running back James Peoples for a touchdown.

The pass was Manske’s first touchdown of his collegiate career while sitting behind Rocco Becht for two years. It was a glimpse of what could be the future of the quarterback position for Penn State, with Becht out of eligibility after this season.

“It was an unbalanced formation that I felt Alex would know what the picture would look like,” Taylor Mouser said. “Just being able to give him simple looks with simple outlets that he could go do and be successful because Alex is in there not just as much as Rocco is, but he's a guy that doesn't leave the facility.”

Penn State fans haven’t gotten a ton of looks at the young quarterback, who’s thrown a total of 16 passes this season. His minimal time against Minnesota was the first action Manske saw in Big Ten play. Still, he went 2-for-2, completing a pass to freshman wide receiver Amarion Jackson earlier in the drive.

However, the quarterback hasn’t batted an eye when he’s stood on the sidelines. He’s a player who “knows that it’s Rocco’s team” this year, according to Mouser.

“Just from a raw talent standpoint, he's as talented as you'll find, and his time is coming, and he knows that,” Mouser said.

What Manske has done this season is continuing to grow as a player in practice, while also helping out the quarterback in front of him. Becht recognized the maturity Manske has developed despite still being a redshirt freshman.

He’s helped out Becht in practice, making sure that the receivers are ready and also getting the looks they should when they go out there with the starting quarterback. Manske’s seemingly bought into the backup role to help the team find success this season.

“Even in just practice, helping me out with the guys that are doing the reps, the receivers on the sideline, the tight ends, helping them being able to see what I'm seeing,” Becht said. “He's just a second voice, and I think for me, he's been so patient.”

Mouser has also noticed Manske’s work while looking on. It’s part of the process to prepare his young quarterback for game reps, while also getting him prepared for the future when he’s in the starting role and can make the reads that both of them are seeing from the sideline.

“He stands right next to me when Rocco's in there, and we talk through different stuff with him and (quarterbacks) coach (Jake) Waters,” Mouser said. “Of yeah, like, ‘That's not where the ball should go.’ Like, ‘Where should the ball go?’ And he should have quick answers, and he does most of the time.”

The offensive coordinator has also ensured he’s in a position that if something were to happen to Becht, Manske could go in and keep the offense flowing if needed. With this, Mouser said that he “has to prepare to be the starter.”

Earlier in the season, Mouser said that Manske was a player that was forcing them to play him. That hasn’t happened, mostly because of the other struggles in the offense that needed to be corrected.

However, Manske still didn’t complain or question anything as he continued his role strictly as the backup quarterback.

“Manske's done a good job in the two years I've been with him, has never complained about being on the field whether we've been good or haven't been good,” Mouser said. “When we give that kid reps like one of the most competitive guys that we have, one of the best spirits that we have.”

Manske looks to be the quarterback waiting in the wings, potentially for the 2027 season. He’s flashed his arm talent and athleticism in minimal minutes, but recognizes this year isn’t a season for him to be getting on the field on a consistent basis.

“He's waited his time,” Becht said. “I think in the future this program is going to be in good hands because he's a gamer.”

title: Light Up Night brings holiday cheer, showcases small businesses
author: Isabella Gearhart | For the Collegian
description:
As the holidays approach, State College has transformed into a winter wonderland, featuring festive lights wrapped around trees, decorated storefronts and feelings of cheer in the air.

Light Up Night gave locals and visitors the chance to take in the jolly sights of downtown and experience holiday festivities while supporting small businesses Thursday from 5 to 8 p.m.

The evening featured live music, a reindeer pen for visitor viewing and the lighting of the large, downtown Christmas tree at 7:30 p.m. As the tree lit up in the night, the crowd erupted with excitement, sharing a moment of holiday spirit that brought the town together.

Attendees also had the opportunity to explore local vendors and shop for handmade products. For many vendors, the event is not only an opportunity to make sales but also a chance to share the stories behind their work.

Among the vendors participating in this year’s event were Rise and Design Art Studio, Layered Leaf Studio and The Tinkering Pixie Boutique, each offering a wide variety of products inspired by personal interests, artistic creativity and a love for their craft.

For Rise and Design Art Studio, pottery began as a hobby before growing into a full-time business.

“I was doing pottery on the side for a couple of years, and I got to a point where there weren't enough hours in the day, and so I had to decide,” Sabrina Shankar, 30, of Watsontown, Pennsylvania, said. “Do I just keep doing what I’m doing and work my full-time job or leave my job and do pottery full-time?”

Shankar decided to leave her job two years ago and since then has been running her own business.

Rise and Design features handmade ceramic products, including wine glasses and her most popular seller, mugs.

The holiday season also plays a crucial role in the studio’s production schedule.

“With the holidays a lot of shops like to stock, so I sell to a lot of boutiques around the country,” Shankar said. “I have to have holiday products done by October. Whatever I have for myself to sell, I start making those from October to the beginning of November.”

Shankar said that she is already working on Valentine’s Day products while preparing for the current holiday season.

The business has also developed a strong connection with the State College community by attending shows in the area and sharing its locally-inspired collection.

Light Up Night marked a different milestone for Layered Leaf Studio, a business creating watercolor greeting cards and 3D-printed earrings, among other handmade products.

“This is my very first craft festival, my first thing with my business,” Jessica Rotthoff, 45, of State College, Pennsylvania, said. “It’s the start, and I’m really excited about it.”

Rotthoff’s interest in art began after taking a nature sketching class at the Arboretum, which led her to explore watercolor painting. She later expanded her creative interests to include other forms of art.

The name of the business reflects these different artistic processes involved in her work.

“Part of why I picked Layered Leaf is because anything I’ve ever done, craft wise or art wise, is layers,” Rotthoff said.

With the holiday season approaching, her products reflect that time of year. Her current greeting cards feature Christmas themes, while previous collections have reflected fall and other seasonal celebrations.

Another vendor, The Tinkering Pixie Boutique, brought a different kind of creativity to Light Up Night through its rocks, crystals and minerals.

Mariah Kowalczyk said her interest in crystals began during childhood after discovering a rock shop in her hometown.

“They had a rock room that was filled with crystals, and the gentleman that ran that was Mr. Pomper,” Mariah Kowalczyk, 49, of State College, Pennsylvania, said. “He let us go up there and play with everything. I always grew up and wanted to have my own rock and crystal store.”

The business features a variety of rocks and minerals, including some of her most popular products, amethyst, tiger’s eye and quartz.

Although much of The Tinkering Pixie Boutique is online, participating in community events allows for an opportunity to meet customers face-to-face.

“It’s about making connections with people and people that might not be into rocks and minerals, it’s just about getting out and letting them experience a museum-type experience,” Kowalczyk said.

The holiday season also brings a creative addition to the business through handmade mineral ornaments.

“One of my favorite things to do around the holidays is make little ornaments,” Kowalczyk said. “I don’t make a lot of them because they’re so intricate and time-consuming, but I really like bringing the comforts of the holiday and taking minerals that you normally see and bringing them into an element that you can use to decorate for the holidays.”

title: Preview | Penn State men’s hockey heads to Madison for matchup with No. 2 Wisconsin
author: Sawyer Klasnick | For the Collegian
description:
For the second weekend in a row, Penn State travels to play the No. 2 team in the country. After Michigan swept the Nittany Lions last weekend at Yost Ice Arena, the Wolverines jumped up to the No. 1 spot in the rankings, replacing Penn State’s next opponent, Wisconsin.

Penn State is carrying a five-game losing streak into Madison, and its 2-9-1 record is the worst 12-game start to a season in program history. The blue and white will play Friday at 8 p.m. and Saturday at 7 p.m. at the Kohl Center.

Penn State remains winless against Big Ten opponents and won’t face another conference opponent until January after this weekend’s series.

Penn State

In his weekly media session Tuesday, Guy Gadowsky discussed the need for a cleaner approach to start the season, with penalties being a major issue in recent weeks.

“We're trying to establish a bit of a gritty, like back to what you guys have all seen in the past, pretty gritty hockey team,” Gadowsky said.

Staying out of the box was an issue for his Nittany Lions last weekend against Michigan. Penn State entered Ann Arbor with the top-ranked penalty kill in the Big Ten before surrendering eight power-play goals on 13 opportunities, including allowing a hard-to-believe seven power-play goals Saturday night. If the Nittany Lions hope to snap their losing streak in Wisconsin, avoiding penalties will be key.

One of the few bright spots for the blue and white this year has been Maine transfer Justin Poirier, who scored twice last weekend, bringing his team-leading total to seven. The forward’s point streak now sits at nine games.

Senior captain Reese Laubach also had a big weekend, scoring a goal Friday night and picking up two assists on Saturday. In his first three seasons at Penn State, Laubach was consistently one of the Nittany Lions’ best offensive players, scoring 37 goals in 107 career games. However, the San Jose native and San Jose Sharks draft pick struggled out of the gate this year and was without a goal through the first 10 contests. His recent production could be an important boost for a Penn State team looking to get back on track.

Wisconsin

Last year, Wisconsin was the Cinderella of the NCAA Tournament, upsetting Michigan State and North Dakota on its way to the title game. The Badgers were 20 minutes away from the program's seventh National Championship before squandering a 1-0 lead to Denver in the third period.

This season, Mike Hastings’ Badgers have picked up where they left off, rolling to an 8-0-1 start, the second-best start in the storied program's history. Wisconsin finally suffered its first loss last Saturday, falling to Ohio State 2-1.

Much of Wisconsin’s success has come from its elite special teams play. The Badgers lead the Big Ten in both penalty-kill percentage and power-play percentage, with their power play clicking at an absurd 40.5%.

There isn’t a better defensive team in the country than Wisconsin, allowing just 10 goals in its 10 games played thus far. The Badgers’ goaltenders, Daniel Hauser and Alexis Cournoyer, have split time, and both have save percentages north of .940.

Offensively, the Badgers are led by a familiar face. After accumulating 69 points in 77 games with Penn State, JJ Wiebusch transferred to Wisconsin, where he has continued his strong play. The junior from River Falls, Wisconsin, has scored three goals and added eight assists with his new school.

The Badgers’ leading scorer is junior center, Gavin Morrissey. Morrissey also led the Badgers in scoring last season and his 11 assists are tied for seventh in the country.

One of Wisconsin's biggest strengths has been its depth. The Badgers have had 14 different players score multiple goals, making it difficult for the opposition to focus on just a few offensive threats.

When Penn State traveled to Wisconsin last January, the Nittany Lions came away with a weekend sweep at the Kohl Center. However, the series ended on a heated note, as a late-game scrum in the series finale involved 11 players, all of whom received misconduct penalties. Penn State captain Dane Dowiak was one of those 11 and left the ice to a chorus of boos after pointing up at the scoreboard amidst the brawl.

At the game’s end, Gadowsky went to center ice for the traditional postgame handshake, but Hastings never came out to meet him.

If Penn State hopes to turn its season around, a repeat performance in Madison would be a good place to start.

title: Students make room at table for Thanksgiving traditions of their own
author: Ava Troup | For the Collegian
description:
The end of November, in all of its holiday glory, can look different for everyone.

Some take seats at family feasts, kicking back with a bowl of snacks and watching the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. Some might be tuned into the National Dog Show, or one of the many football games playing that day. Regardless of how they celebrate, students have already begun to embrace their own Turkey Day traditions here in State College.

Sofia Moresi, 19, of Philadelphia, said she embraces what she views as the true meaning of Thanksgiving, both at home and at Penn State: family.

“Thanksgiving has always been kind of like a family reunion because me and my cousins and aunts live far away,” Moresi, a second-year studying elementary and early childhood education, said. “We always just have so much fun and have the best food too.”

Each year, Moresi looks forward to reconnecting with her family as they gather around some delicious food.

She added that Thanksgiving isn’t just limited to time with family, and she tries to incorporate her friends too. While there aren’t many Thanksgiving-specific events for the students at University Park, many, like Moresi, have found a way to create their celebrations.

“Me and my roommate do like a soup Sunday event every week, so we get all our friends to come over and we make soup for them,” Moresi said.

Gouri Nair, 22, of Delhi, India, doesn’t celebrate what is considered a “traditional Thanksgiving,” she said, but she’s still excited for the break as she gets to visit home.

Nair is traveling to Delhi to see some of her friends this fall break. She said she has friends who live all over the world.

Her passion for getting together with loved ones extends beyond the Thanksgiving season, though. She continues to enjoy connecting with friends by holding events such as board game nights throughout the whole year, and she recommends that students make traditions of their own.

“There’s a lot of clubs and societies that are out and about, and a lot of them have events almost all the time,” Nair, a first-year graduate student studying economics, said. “I feel like I’ve made a few connections out there, and it’s just really fun to go out there and have a no pressure environment.”

Gabriella Aquilina, 20, of Hazleton, Pennsylvania, is looking forward to the break as a chance to embrace the holiday spirit with her loved ones. Aquilina's family hosts Thanksgiving most years, and she usually spends the whole day in the kitchen, helping prepare for dinner.

Celebrating Thanksgiving can mean many different things to people, and Aquilina has created her own tradition with her mom, who she doesn’t get to see as much during the school year.

“Pretty much from the moment I wake up until the moment dinner starts, cooking with my mom,” Aquilina, a second-year studying kinesiology, said. “She lets me take a lot of free rein, so I can choose some of the items that I want to cook and make them myself.”

When students are at college they see their parents less, which makes Thanksgiving break so special to many.

Liza Lukashin, 20, of San Francisco, California, has a Thanksgiving celebration with her friends — “Friendsgiving” — to get into spirit. However, she said she considers the holiday a time for family above all else.

Lukashin is looking forward to the break from school, since Penn State is so far from her family, and this is a rare opportunity to visit them.

“Being far away from home gives me the benefit of being able to miss my family and being able to make moments with them more special,” Lukashin, a third-year studying supply chain and information systems, said. “I’m able to have that feeling with my friendships here and stuff, and then being able to see my family really makes me feel even more connected with them.”
