title: More bang for your buck | Budget-friendly apartments in downtown State College
author: Serina Chan | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State is known to be one of the most lively and prominent college towns, spanning over 40,000 undergraduates.

Alongside a large number of students comes the need for cheap, accessible housing downtown. Whether you're looking for an affordable place that offers amenities such as a gym and furniture or somewhere that's relatively close to campus (which becomes especially useful during those long, winter treks to your 9 a.m. class), it's important to find somewhere that works with your lifestyle and fits in your budget.

Usually, staying a walking distance from campus makes it hard to have an individual room without spending more than $1,000. Depending on how many roommates you choose to have also drastically affects the amount of money you’re spending.

Finding the right apartment is never entirely simple, but it can be made easier by finding specific management companies that may offer great deals and help you decide what apartment fits your habits and budget without all of the stress.

The Meridian

The Meridian on College Avenue is one of the most affordable apartment complexes close to campus. It’s right next to CATA’s White Loop, which can easily bring you to your desired location on campus or downtown.

There are three general options for rooming: a studio, a one-bedroom and a two-bedroom. In total, the Meridian can occupy five people within one apartment, with the rent decreasing based on each person that's added.

Sharing a room for any of these options brings your rent to around $600 to $800.

Another perk of the Meridian is that it includes a parking lot. Getting a parking spot in this area can be convenient, compared to having to find or purchase a pass farther from your apartment.

The Collegian

The Collegian is located about a block from West campus and provides furnished apartments for five people at maximum occupancy. There are three different floorplans, each of which provides two bedrooms and two bathrooms.

For five people, the total rent comes to $3,080, making each individual cost about $600. This is especially affordable and a relatively short distance from many different food options surrounding the area, like Lupita’s and Vibe Coffee Co.

Fairmount Hills

Fairmount Hills is about half a mile from campus. The apartment offers furnished and unfurnished bedroom floorplans, so you have options depending on what you’re looking for.

A furnished floorplan shared with two other roommates can bring your rent to about $450 to $500. Additional plans, such as two bedrooms with each individual sharing a room, can go for around $700.

Fairmount Hills also offers some amenities that can be helpful such as air conditioning, free internet access and on-site laundry on every floor.

Barcroft Apartments

The Barcroft Apartment complex is directly on the downtown strip, allowing for an easy walk to and from class. This apartment’s location is similar to living in the south dorms, as they’re directly across from each other.

The cheapest option they have is a furnished floor plan for five people. This would include two bedrooms and one bathroom and would be around $600 for each person. Additionally, the unfurnished option at Barcroft allows for two people maximum, with the rent also around $600 for each person.

This apartment is conveniently close to many different food spots such as Teadori, Subway and Osaka Sushi.

Hetzel Plaza

The Hetzel Plaza is similar to the Barcroft apartments. The most popular option is usually a floorplan with two bedrooms and one-and-a-half bathrooms.

The total rent is $2,990, which can be split between four to five people, bringing it to around $650 to $750.

Being in a similar location as the Barcroft apartments, Hetzel Plaza is a great way to stay close to campus, while having many different options of places to eat and shop.

The Blue Loop and White Loop circulate in all of these areas. This can make the walk even shorter onto campus, which is an important factor to be considered if an apartment is a little further from the main downtown strip, as it means you don't have to trade convenience for affordability.

title: Column | State College has an affordable housing crisis. The borough’s priority should be placed on people, not profit
author: Quentin Jurney | The Daily Collegian
description:
Housing, in some shape or form, is essential to any human, regardless of where you’re located. In the society we live in now, we typically pay to own a house (or merely live in it). Housing prices have drastically increased in the United States, but there’s been a constant price hike in State College for decades, notwithstanding national trends.

Penn State has helped stimulate the local economy considerably but has fallen short of being beneficial on quite a few occasions. The dependency State College has on Penn State has been harmful, and in numerous instances, State College has put Penn State over its locals.

This is fairly logical, it's the biggest money maker around and employs the most number of people in State College by a wide margin. I’ll also say the borough helped the area multifariously. Since 2009, the median income of Centre County residents has risen by 10%, according to reporting by WHYY. Having a booming employer like Penn State in your area breathes life into everything; jobs and income have flooded the area, improving life in the community. This is the greatest advantage of having a single dominant employer in a small community like ours.

Nevertheless, the drawbacks are still prevalent. Since 2013, about 200 mobile-home units in State College have been lost because the land surrounding the university has increased in value, according to WHYY. Even though people at all income levels (but, of course, mostly high income) benefit from having students nearby, the people hurt the most are specifically low-income individuals who live in the area.

Affordable housing is disappearing from the State College area because the university and the surrounding land are progressively gaining value. People who can’t afford the increasingly high prices or the newly renovated housing for students in State College are forced to move. They are forced to find housing farther away and commute to State College or they move away completely, disappearing from the area. State College and Penn State are willingly displacing residents who live here for profit.

“(A) 24-acre property was finally sold in March 2013 at a price of over seven million dollars. That’s more than seven times the property’s market value in 1994,” WHYY reported. The pattern persists, as even now, every new high-rise apartment built for students inflates the price of housing around, pushing perennial residents out. So long as students pay for expensive housing, prices will rise.

I think it's perfectly acceptable for State College to indulge Penn State and its students' needs, but not when it’s at the expense of residents who are a part of this community. There’s an ethical obligation that both the town and the university have to the long-term residents here.

Students typically only live here for four years. Meanwhile, residents spend lifetimes within the county borders. They should matter to State College and the university, at the very least, as much as the student body. Without these community members, State College would become a ghost town and I think the university would cease to exist.

It’s the duty of the town and university to take care of the people who reside there regardless of whether it cuts into the profits they reap. There’s an abundance of money to be had. Helping people who live here out isn’t going to cap the cash flow. There are individuals at Penn State making substantially more than they should anyway and it would be a good place to start when budget cuts are made.

In August, the borough purchased Addison Court for $15.75 million. Addison court, which provides affordable housing for seniors and people with disabilities, was going to be demolished and turned into student housing. State College officials clearly have the means and the money to preserve and establish affordable housing tailored toward its residents, it’s just a matter of whether it continues doing so.

State College should enact policy to create and protect affordable housing specifically for residents. I’m not saying to forcefully lower all prices for everyone, even though the university and private developers who make sizable amounts of money would be just fine; it’s not feasible. But it needs to look out for residents impacted by rising prices.

The university should back this as well. As part of the larger community, making sure people can still afford to live here should be a priority for Penn State. Profiting copiously off of the area should not come without giving back.

title: Players to watch | RB Antwan Raymond, LB Moses Walker headline struggling Rutgers team
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Rutgers will travel to Happy Valley to take on Penn State with just two wins on the season.

Without star wide receiver KJ Duff, who’s been ruled out for the season, the Scarlet Knights’ star power has taken a significant drop. Additionally, Rutgers’ top three quarterbacks appeared on the first availability report of the week, with its signal caller on Saturday up in the air.

Here’s some players to watch for Rutgers.

Antwan Raymond, running back

Raymond will be the player to watch on the Scarlet Knights, as he’s their leading rusher and has emerged as the next great running back in a recent history of rushers that have gone to the NFL.

He’s run for 810 yards this season with six touchdowns, playing in all 10 of Rutgers’ games this year. In those games, he’s had at least 11 carries, with a season-high 27 attempts against Boston College in Week 2.

When he faced Penn State last season, he ran 29 times for 189 yards and a touchdown, adding a receiving touchdown as well. He torched the Nittany Lions’ defense as the one-two punch of him and Duff through the pass game kept the defense off-balance.

With Raymond as the lone threat this season, he’ll have a tougher time replicating last year’s mark, especially with Penn State’s growing strength stopping the run.

Moses Walker, linebacker

On the defensive side of the ball, Walker is tied for second on the team in tackles with 45, while also recording 1.5 sacks and two interceptions. He’s tied for the lead in interceptions, as Rutgers has only picked off opposing quarterbacks five times.

Walker will have a big task on Saturday. In the run game, he’ll have to go up against an offensive line that’s figured things out, while also still implementing a lot of pull blockers. He’ll likely be one of the players dealing with the blockers at the second level.

In the pass game, he’ll be up against the running backs, or a matchup nightmare in 6-foot-7 tight end Benjamin Brahmer, who’s proven to be a viable route runner. If he stands up to the task, Rutgers can limit Penn State’s offensive production.

Jesse Ofurie, defensive back

One of Rutgers’ captains, Ofurie has been the starter at the stud position — a hybrid linebacker and defensive back position that allows him to play more in coverage, while also helping out with the run.

Ofurie essentially acts as the nickel cornerback on the defense, and he’s taken a massive jump in production in his first year of consistent playing time.

The senior has 42 tackles on the season, but his numbers have dropped in the last four games, with four or less tackles in each. In Rutgers’ win against Maryland, he notched six tackles, including four solo, and two passes defended.

In the hybrid role, he’ll be asked to do a lot against an offense that’s been complementary in the past couple of weeks.

Sekou Kromah, defensive line

On the defensive line, Kromah is Rutgers’ leader in sacks with three. The Temple transfer matched his total from last season, but already has more tackles this season than in his two years with the Owls.

He’s picked up sacks in two of the last four games for the Scarlet Knights, including one in the victory over Maryland.

Kromah is tied for the team lead in quarterback hurries and has forced one fumble this season. The defensive lineman has been Rutgers’ most productive pass rusher this season, and he’ll likely need success against Penn State’s offensive line for the Scarlet Knights to keep things close.

title: PHOTO STORY | In steep tradition, Nittanyville camps out for Beaver Stadium’s most coveted spot
author: Lucas Yendrzeiwski | The Daily Collegian
description:
The front row of Beaver Stadium’s south end zone is a coveted location for the student body’s most dedicated football fans on game day. Since 2005, members of Nittanyville, formerly titled Paternoville, have set up a community of tents outside of Gate A to secure the spot.

The organization averages 150 camper signups per week. With 50% attendance required at camp, around 70 students can be found at camp behind General James A. Beaver rock on any given night. They wheel out trash cans for pseudo-football games and set up Spikeball nets and cornhole boards. These are just some of the ways students pass the hours between 6 p.m. and 6 a.m., when attendance is required outside the West Shore Home Field entrance.

Hanging a few yards above camp, large, silver letters are stamped onto a navy blue sliver of the stadium: “The best student section in the country, by far.”

Many campers spend their weeknights at camp painting banners draped down the limestone walls of the stadium. The organization provides the supplies, but the campers are responsible for executing the projects. On game day, they don body paint and themed costumes.

Students who don’t feel artistically inclined enough to take on a banner project can be found passing time with their friends in different ways: Around camp, students do homework, play cards and compete in matchups of College Football and Madden on an Xbox.

“It’s amazing to see everyone come together and just have a really fun experience,” Trevor Lavelle, Nittanyville’s public relations chair, said.

Penn State Football has been a defining part of Nittanyville President Aaron Klein’s college experience. He’s spending his senior year as its president.

He’s also spent time responding to online criticism regarding attendance and canceled camping nights. On Oct. 30, the Friday before the game against Purdue, images began circulating on X of an empty camp.

Klein took to X to explain that Nittanyville changed its camping schedule to accommodate campers that wanted to attend a John Summit concert at the Bryce Jordan Center the night before, and enjoy their Halloweekend the night after.

“It’s aggravating that not only someone who’s respected online, and respected on this campus, is — whether or not they are doing it on purpose — engaging in activity that can be negative towards our student organization,” Klein said.

Klein said he stands by his decision. Members of the organization have shown up through pouring rain and falling snow, which says more about the students than the attendance fluctuation, he said.

He added that there are “hot and cold sports fans throughout the world,” yet a set number of Nittanyville members’ dedication often runs hot.

“It’s special to see that core group of people that come every week,” Klein said. “It’s people who truly care about this football team.”

title: Penn State vs. Rutgers preview | A look at both teams, how to watch
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State has officially turned its season around with a third straight win against Minnesota last week. The Nittany Lions are now turning their sights to Saturday, when they’ll face Rutgers at 3:30 p.m. in Beaver Stadium for Senior Day.

The Nittany Lions have dominated the Scarlet Knights throughout their 108-year history, winning 33 of the 35 matchups between the two teams. Penn State will look to win its 19th straight this week.

Here’s a look at how the teams match up, and more information about this weekend’s contest.

Forecast

Saturday’s weather will feel like a typical fall day in Happy Valley.

At kickoff, the temperature will be 62 degrees, with a real feel of 63 degrees. It’ll cool off to 39 degrees and have a real feel of 43 degrees when the sun sets at 4:49 p.m.

There’s no chance of precipitation in the forecast; the game day weather is expected to be partly sunny with 6 mph winds.

Betting, how to watch

The Nittany Lions enter Week 12 as heavy favorites, according to FanDuel, as they are favored to win by 25.5 points.

The over/under is set at 49.5, which would give Penn State a 38-12 victory.

The matchup against Rutgers will be broadcast on Fox Sports 1, while those hoping to attend in person can purchase tickets for as low as $10 on Ticketmaster.

About Rutgers

The Scarlet Knights are experiencing one of their worst seasons in recent years with just two wins entering Saturday’s game. Their two victories this year came against Howard and Maryland.

A major reason for Rutgers’ struggles is due to the many injuries plaguing its starting lineup. Most notably, star wide receiver K.J. Duff hasn’t played since Oct. 24 and was ruled out for the season after he underwent surgery for a high ankle sprain.

The Scarlet Knights have also experienced injuries with three of their quarterbacks. Starter Dylan Lonergan has also been out since Oct. 24, while backup AJ Surace broke three ribs against Wisconsin two weeks later. Sean Ashenfelder started the following game, but was replaced by Surace after Ashenfelder was injured in the first half.

It’s unknown who will start against Penn State, as all three quarterbacks have various designations in this week’s availability report.

With an injured passing attack, Rutgers has had to rely on its run game. Antwon Raymond leads the team with 810 rushing yards and six touchdowns, while Clay Thevenin has 518 yards and five scores.

The Scarlet Knights’ defense has allowed the second-most yards per game in the Big Ten, giving up an average of 413.6 yards. They have the worst run defense, allowing 191.4 yards per game.

About Penn State

The Nittany Lions have played arguably their best football over the last three weeks with a resurgent run game and improved decision-making from Rocco Becht.

While running back Carson Hansen has back-to-back 100-yard games, he left just before halftime against Minnesota and is now questionable on this week’s availability report. Cam Wallace played strong in relief, rushing for 82 yards and catching a touchdown.

In the passing attack, wide receiver Chase Sowell has been Becht’s most reliable target this year, including a 151-yard performance against Michigan and a 125-yard outing against Washington two weeks later. However, he was held without a catch against Minnesota.

Tight ends Benjamin Brahmer and Andrew Rappleyea filled the void, as Brahmer scored on both of his receptions. Rappleyea couldn’t find the end zone, but had four catches for 45 yards.

Penn State’s defense performed the best it has all season in various aspects of its game against the Golden Gophers. The pass rush was effective against Drake Lindsey, recording three sacks. It also held Minnesota to just 41 yards on the ground.

The Nittany Lions have a chance to play a full game against Rutgers, as the third quarter has been a struggle this year — Penn State has been outscored 56-16 coming out of the half.

Regardless of any of Penn State’s past struggles, Saturday presents an opportunity for the Nittany Lions to add to their win column, and potentially give backup players a chance to see the field in what should be a blowout.

title: Harry Styles’ residency: selfish or successful? Students share thoughts
author: Ella Reilly | For the Collegian
description:
In 2019 and 2021, a pandemic delay and an endless Ticketmaster queue left many Harry Styles fans stumbling — and they were ultimately ticketless, stuck listening to him in their headphones in bed rather than out loud in concert.

When 2026 rolled around, a few faithful years post-hiccup, Styles returned from his hiatus and announced a tour, once again. But another roadblock: He played 30 consecutive shows in Madison Square Garden (MSG). The venue gave him his own banner for his residency. Although it’s an impressive feat for an artist to accomplish, the lack of variety in locations made it difficult for some fans to see his show.

Despite many fans' disappointment about his tour decisions, world-famous musician Harry Styles kicked off his Together, Together tour in May. Unlike his previous tours, “Together” began relatively short with 50 shows in seven cities. Due to complaints from fans about the minimal number of cities presented, Styles increased the amount of shows to 107 in 18 cities.

Zachary Calderon, 18, of Wyckoff, New Jersey, said he can understand why a fan would be bothered by the sheer amount of shows played at Madison Square Garden when other venues only got a few nights.

“I would be upset if I wanted to see him and I was on the other side of the country,” Calderon, a first-year studying advertising/public relations, said.

Luckily, Calderon lives relatively close to MSG, making the abundance of tour dates there not as disappointing for him. Despite the distance being better for him than some, Calderon still lives a state away and would need to factor in things like travel costs.

Although Styles’ residency at MSG was disappointing for some, Calderon considered the significance this specific venue would have for any musical artist and Styles himself.

“I think it’s awesome, to be honest, that you can even have the opportunity to do that… that’s a hard opportunity to pass up on,” Calderon said. "From my knowledge, it’s like everyone knows that as his place. That’s his spot.”

Nicknamed “The World’s Most Famous Arena,” MSG has hosted musical legends like Elvis Presley, Elton John and Madonna, making it a desirable spot for musicians to perform. Styles also embraced his time in the Big Apple and was spotted by many fans, wandering around the city when he wasn’t performing, by himself and with his fiancée, Zoë Kravitz.

Ava Daddea, 20, of Pittsburgh, said she understands his decision to play so many shows in New York City, but was still disappointed when his tour dates were announced.

“I get that New York is like his home base," Daddea, a third-year studying psychology, said. "He says all the time, like, he’s grown up in there. It was a little bit, like, ‘Why? Why are you not going to at least do like multiple big locations throughout the whole country if you’re going to pick one spot?’”

Daddea has been a long-time fan of Styles, having seen him in concert several times. This lasting love for him is what made this residency a little bit disheartening.

“Initially, I was upset because it just makes it hard for everybody to go see someone who they love so deeply," Daddea said. "Like, they care. I mean, he is loved by so many people. I think it’s also hard now because in the past, like Love on Tour, he was literally on tour for almost three years straight and went to every single location, like every place, literally everywhere.”

During Love on Tour, which took place from 2021-23, Styles performed 173 shows spanning continents like North America, South America, Europe and Asia and broke several arena and attendance records.

Despite the controversy surrounding his MSG residency, Styles is no stranger to performing at one arena for a long duration. During this previous tour, Styles performed several residencies, including 20 nights at MSG and 18 nights at the Kia Forum in Los Angeles.

Daddea said she's glad that Styles decided to add additional stops to his tour because it showed he cared for his fans and their feedback.

Many fans speculated that the tour’s conclusion would mark the start of a long hiatus or even retirement send off for Styles, but Daddea disagrees.

“I think that this tour, and what he’s doing now, is definitely an indication that he took some time off," Daddea said. "That’s kind of what his whole entire new album is about, and now I think that’s going to be his routine. I don’t think he’s ready to be done.”

Michelenea Caruso-Drennen, 21, of Brookhaven, Pennsylvania, said she refused to believe Together, Together is the beginning of the end.

“I would be devastated,” Caruso-Drennen, a fourth-year studying veterinary and biomedical sciences, said. “I don’t think he’s retired, and I don’t think that was the last tour. I hope it’s not, but I understand if it is. I would have wanted him to say that it was the last one.”

After Caruso-Drennen got past her initial annoyance by the limited venues, she knew she was still making it to the tour, no matter what.

She’s been a fan of Styles since his days in the global sensation boy band, One Direction, and has been dedicated to seeing him live in concert ever since. In August, she got the chance to see him again in concert and said it was the best experience of her life.

“My sisters said that they’ve never seen me that happy,” Caruso-Drennen said.

title: No. 7 Penn State women's hockey returns home, dominates in win against Delaware
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions returned to their home rink after a month-long road trip where Penn State notched a 5-1 record.

The blue and white routed the Blue Hens in a 6-2 win, tying its second-highest mark for goals scored this season.

First period

Before two minutes could tick off the clock, Delaware had already committed a tripping penalty. Wren Abboud was sent to the penalty box, granting Penn State its first power play of the game.

Penn State nearly took advantage of the opportunity, forcing Charlotte Payne to make various saves while skaters crashed for the rebound. The Nittany Lions couldn’t cash in any of their shots.

Grace Outwater followed with a penalty of her own for cross-checking, giving Delaware their first power play of the night. The advantage lasted only 54 seconds before Lexie Lonas joined Outwater for hooking, leading to 4-on-4 play for about a minute.

Neither team scored during that stretch, but Penn State held possession for what felt like the entire two minutes. That was the trend for the first 10 minutes of the period. Penn State didn’t allow a single shot, leading the shot count 10-0.

Penn State’s defense stayed aggressive through the 20 minutes of play, attacking the puck with intention and forcing clearances to the wall.

Payne stood strong amidst the Nittany Lions’ relentless attack. The Blue Hen made crucial saves in the crease to prevent Penn State from opening the scoring.

After Payne saved Sofia Ismael’s shot, officials called a slashing penalty on McKenna Walsh. A short scuffle ensued in front of the net involving Walsh. Penn State challenged the play, arguing for a major penalty on Reese Reid for head contact. The challenge was successful, and Reid served five minutes.

During 4-on-4 play, Grace Outwater scored a power-play goal with thirty seconds left in the period to enter the break with a 1-0 lead.

“It was a good full team effort,” Outwater said. “It was a great play by the (defense) and then also Kylie made a great breakout pass.”

Second period

Entering the second period, the Nittany Lions started with a man advantage for two more minutes, as Reid’s penalty time carried over. Abby Stonehouse increased their lead to two with an impressive shot sent to the top right corner of the net.

Two Nittany Lions were called for penalties: Taya MacDonald for Hooking and Grace Outwater for body-checking. The penalties led to 3-on-5 and 4-on-5 opportunities for Delaware, but the defense held strong on the penalty kill.

Penn State refused to help themselves by tallying another penalty, this time by Grace Tullock for tripping. The blue and white were forced to another 3-on-5 sequence following a penalty on Alanna Devlin for holding.

Delaware finally got on the board when Reid scored a goal to cut into Penn State’s lead. The defender sent her shot from the left side and into the top right corner, making up for her costly major penalty.

“You know they’re bound to get one at some point, no matter how good your kill is,” coach Makenna Newkirk said. “If they're aggressive penalties, and it’s us taking away time and space, it’s easier to go kill a penalty. If it’s more of a lazy penalty, then that’s kind of when we, from a team perspective and coach perspective, we expect a little bit more.

No longer pitching a shutout, the Nittany Lions now led the shot category 22-11, with the defense playing well outside of unfortunate power-play situations.

While on a breakaway, Outwater and Stonehouse strung together a couple of two-man passes to break down the defense before Outwater’s goal. The Nittany Lions took a 3-1 lead with four minutes left in the period.

The two teams went back-and-forth through the remaining moments of the second period, and Penn State headed into the final period up 3-1.

Third period

The Blue Hens came out hot in the third period, as Katie Belk scored on an unassisted breakaway goal that hit the crossbar and in to once again shorten Penn State’s lead to 3-2.

The white and blue returned the favor with a goal of their own from Sophie Morrow, who shot from an awkward angle on the left side to push the lead to two.

The goal-scoring didn’t end there, as Penn State added to their lead with a goal from Nicole Hall after the team put together a couple of passes before Hall finished the play. The Nittany Lions held a 5-2 lead with around 11 minutes remaining.

Kylie Amelcovich sat for two minutes due to a hooking penalty, giving the Blue Hens a much-needed power play. Penn State’s penalty kill unit stepped up once again, preventing a goal for Delaware.

Penn State’s attack compiled multiple stretches where the defense broke down Delaware's defense by simply finding the open skater.

Grace Tullock pushed the puck into the crease, and Abby Stonehouse tipped it into the back of the net for her second goal of the night, putting the game away with less than three minutes on the clock.

“It’s a full team effort, we need our teammates, we’re not just scoring on our own,” Stonehouse said. “I feel like it comes down to the plays made before the goals.”

Outwater ended her night in the penalty box following a hooking penalty. Delaware’s power play was unsuccessful, and Penn State secured a 6-2 win in their first game back from an extended road trip.

Up next

The Nittany Lions return to Pegula Ice Arena for the second half of the series against Delaware at 4 p.m. on Friday.

title: From ‘Hey There Delilah’ to 'Hey There Happy Valley' | Plain White T’s to perform at Penn State
author: Amanda Marion | For the Collegian
description:
The Student Programming Association (SPA) announced Plain White T’s will headline its winter concert Dec. 4 at 7 p.m. in Alumni Hall.

The pop rock band formed in Lombard, Illinois, in 1997 and have since gained 14 million monthly listeners on Spotify and two Grammy nominations.

The group is most notably known for its 2006 hit single “Hey There Delilah,” which went quadruple-platinum and topped the Billboard Hot 100.

In 2023, the band released its self-titled album, “Plain White T’s,” and is also approaching its 30th anniversary as a group in 2027.

Free student tickets will be available through Discover on Nov. 21 at 5 p.m. Additional information about ticket availability and admission requirements are located on SPA’s website or social media.

title: LS Blaise Sokach-Minnick waited his turn to play for Penn State. Now he’ll say goodbye on Senior Day
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Long snapper Blaise Sokach-Minnick waited four years for his time at Penn State to come. Most players nowadays would’ve hit the transfer portal, eager to see playing time and contribute however they could at a different program.

But not Sokach-Minnick, whose childhood dream to don the Penn State uniform kept him loyal to the Nittany Lions.

“You get called old a little bit,” Sokach-Minnick said Wednesday, smiling. “I just think you see the true Penn State, and you see that Penn State at its core is a community that's never going to back down, and they're always going to fight for the right things, and they're going to fight for what truly will be the best for all of us. That's the biggest thing I've learned.”

Sokach-Minnick is one of only three players on the roster to have been with the program for five years alongside offensive linemen Dom Rulli and Jim Fitzgerald, gaining a deeper understanding of his dream school through the trials and tribulations of its football program.

His road to becoming Penn State’s starting long snapper was a long, but not lonely by any stretch. A former walk-on, he sat behind 2022 Patrick Mannelly Award winner Chris Stoll, an honor given to the best long snapper in the nation, and 2025 finalist Tyler Duzansky, both of whom became his biggest supporters and mentors throughout their shared time.

Sokach-Minnick said he idolized Stoll and Duzansky as they set the standard for Sokach-Minnick to follow.

The three have stayed in touch, as Sokach-Minnick and Duzansky text multiple times a week, and Stoll linked up with the redshirt senior in Seattle for the Washington game. Stoll will also be in attendance on Saturday for the Senior Day game against Rutgers.

With two of the best long snappers in the nation ahead of him on the depth chart, Sokach-Minnick didn’t waver. If it meant being a perennial backup, he’d remain grateful for the opportunity to do so at Penn State.

“It's always been my plan to stick it out here,” Sokach-Minnick said. “Growing up in-state, this is the place I've always wanted to be. The place I dreamed of. I wouldn't want to play at any other school. If it was for one game, if it was for four years, whatever it was, I was going to work my tail off to do that.”

Deep down inside, however, all Sokach-Minnick wanted to do was be out there on the field and help the Nittany Lions win.

So when Week 1 of the 2026 season came, and Sokach-Minnick trotted to Beaver Stadium’s 50-yard line for the coin toss as one of four team captains, he couldn’t help but feel emotional. He reminisced on his childhood self sitting on his living room couch on Jan. 2, 2017, watching Penn State play USC in the Rose Bowl, wanting nothing more than to be a Nittany Lion.

“That's the thing that five-year-old me dreamed of,” Sokach-Minnick said. “It was just awesome to see it come to fruition.”

So far this season, Sokach-Minnick has helped kicker Ryan Barker hit 12 field goals and all 35 of his extra-point attempts. He has also aided punter Nathan Tiyce to average 41.2 yards per punt with 15 falling inside the 20-yard line and 11 landing inside the 10.

He was named one of 10 semifinalists for the Mannelly Award on Monday for his efforts, becoming the third straight Penn State long snapper to earn the achievement.

“It's always nice to get recognized for hard work,” Sokach-Minnick said. “But I feel like that's a standard that we've had in the specialist room over the past few years.”

With Senior Day only days away, Sokach-Minnick said he’ll likely be emotional. It’s not quite the end of his college career, with Maryland and a bowl game still left to play, but it’s the final time he’ll play at Beaver Stadium — the field of his dreams.

But it’s his family that’ll make him emotional on Saturday. His mother Mary Beth, father Donnie, grandmother, cousins and brothers Tristan and Stephen, both of whom are long snappers at Albany, will all be in attendance.

“They've been there for me since I was five years old and I picked up a football,” Sokach-Minnick said. “They've been to every single game through the ups and the downs. That's probably going to make me a little emotional.”

After five seasons at Penn State, he never lost the competitive fire which propelled him to a starting role. But most of all, Sokach-Minnick's patience and loyalty to the program afforded him the opportunity to play for the school he grew up watching as a fan.

“I came here knowing that it was going to be a challenge,” Sokach-Minnick said. “I wanted to challenge myself. I wanted to get better, and I wanted to see what I could do. Looking back over the time, I think I really made the most of my time here and that I put myself in a position to live out a dream of mine.”

title: Multiple Penn State women’s volleyball players earn to All-Big honors
author: Joey Bolger | For the Collegian
description:
Multiple Nittany Lions have earned All-Big Ten honors; right-side hitter Kennedy Martin and setter Alexis Stucky were named to the All-Big Ten First Team. Additionally, middle blocker Gabrielle Nichols and outside hitter Whitney Lauenstein were named to the All-Big Ten Second Team.

Middle blocker Kendall Northern also earned All-Big Ten honors, being selected to the All-Freshman team. Northern has impressed all season, totaling 57 blocks and 103 kills.

title: Penn State legend Jack Ham shares he'll return to radio booth against Rutgers
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Jack Ham is making his return.

Ham announced in a statement from Penn State that he'll be back in the booth at Beaver Stadium this weekend as the Penn State Sports Network analyst. He recently had a medical emergency on Nov. 7 at Washington.

"I've spent a lot of Saturdays in Beaver Stadium, first on the field and then up in the booth," the statement from Ham read. "I'll be back alongside Steve (Jones) this weekend, and there's nowhere else I'd rather be."

Ham has been with Penn State Sports Network since 2000 as the color analyst, with the Washington game and last week's contest against Minnesota marking the first two games he's missed.

Matt Campbell visited Ham in the hospital after the game against Washington and delivered updates to the press the following Tuesday, saying he was in stable condition.

Ham flew back to Pennsylvania on Saturday after being released from the hospital.

description:
Penn State’s very own Kennedy Martin has been named Big Ten Player of the Year. The right-side hitter has been dominant in Big Ten play, leading the conference in kills and points.

title: Penn State women’s basketball, Enjulina Gonzalez battle back for first win of Tanisha Wright era
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
In front of its most energetic crowd of the season, Penn State climbed all the way back from 18 points down to defeat Bowling Green on Education Day, 72-70. Enjulina Gonzalez scored all 20 of her points in the electric second-half comeback.

“She was just able to put it all together,” Wright said about her guard. “She came up with big steals. She defended the way she was supposed to defend, and on top of that, she was able to make shots, and so Enji just has to continue to focus on that, not the outside noise, and not worry about misses. When we talk about success, it's all part of the journey, and so she's just continuing on her journey.”

Tanisha Wright rolled out a new starting lineup for the third time, opting for Gonzalez, Skylar Durley, Ava Black, Savannah White and Petra Božan. It’s the first time the Lady Lions have begun a game without Devyn Quigley this season.

It was an ominous start for the blue and white. Durley threw away a cross-court pass, and Bowling Green’s Mafal Monteiro opened the scoring with a fast-break layup.

The Lady Lions settled down quickly with a Božan three-pointer and played the Falcons evenly through the first media timeout. With 4:59 left in the first quarter, Bowling Green led 10-7, and Quigley, Kamrah Banks and Cristen Carter had all entered the game.

A fast and furious final two minutes of the first quarter gave Bowling Green a 17-12 lead at the break. Monteiro swiped the ball from Carter in the final seconds and scored her sixth and seventh points of the game.

After a “six-seven” promotion brought the house down during the break, Black and Gonzalez each picked up their second personal fouls in the first two minutes of the second quarter. Former Penn State assistant Fred Chmiel brought his Falcons out in a zone defense to open the quarter.

Bowling Green went on an 8-2 run early in the second frame, and Wright called her first timeout with 6:42 on the clock, trailing 25-14.

The pause didn’t do much for Wright’s squad. Bowling Green came right out and put heavy pressure on Banks, the freshman tasked with bringing the ball up the floor. The former four-star recruit committed two turnovers and two fouls as the Falcons extended their lead to 36-18.

It wasn’t just Banks; Penn State turned it over 14 times in the first half. Quigley outscored Bowling Green on her own in the final three minutes with seven points, but the Falcons still led 41-25 at the half.

Gonzalez got sneaky with a steal and score on an inbounds pass to cut the lead to 45-30 with 7:27 left in the third quarter, beginning to turn the tide. 20 seconds later, a scuffle broke out under the Bowling Green basket between Quigley and a pair of Falcons. Bowling Green was called for a technical foul after a lengthy review, and Quigley made one of the two free throws.

Gonzalez, the graduate student from Miami, picked off another inbounds pass and dished it to Black, continuing the Penn State run. The Lady Lions cut the lead to four with 4:02 remaining in the third, with help from another steal and five quick points from Gonzalez.

“The coaches keep pouring confidence into me, and since day one, since I've been here, they've continually just believed in me and just keep pouring into not just me, but everybody else. They're such a great staff at trusting us, our work,” Gonzalez said. “So it's just me being patient, trusting God, myself, and my work that I've been putting in. Once I saw the first shot go in, I was like, ‘okay,’ I just kind of got into flow state.”

After nailing a huge triple with 1:42 on the clock, Quigley was called for a technical foul and ejected from the game. The junior finished with 14 points in 24 minutes.

Wright said after the game that, while it was not apparent to the crowd in the moment because her foul in the earlier scuffle cancelled out with a Bowling Green foul, “Devyn received two flagrants, and so that (ejection) was the result of two flagrants."

Bowling Green held a 55-50 lead after the third quarter, but Gonzalez kept coming. She knocked down a jumper on Penn State's first possession, then assisted a Božan three before drilling one of her own to tie the game at 58.

With 7:40 to play, Durley made a pair of free throws to give Penn State its first lead since the 5:24 mark in the first quarter and cap a 12-2 run.

A pair of Božan layups kept Penn State’s lead at one, 66-65 at the final media timeout. Both teams struggled to score in the final stages. Penn State crept its lead up to three, then Durley gave the Lady Lions their largest lead of the game with 52 seconds to play, 70-65.

Bowling Green ended its nearly five-minute scoring drought with a three-point play by Sara Caetano. The freshman made the score 70-68 with 45 seconds remaining.

Penn State went 2-for-4 from the free-throw line in the final 30 seconds, but the misses didn’t bite Wright’s squad. Bowling Green didn’t net another field goal, and the Lady Lions pulled out their first win of the season, 72-70.

Up Next

Penn State is back inside Rec Hall at 1 p.m. on Sunday to take on Saint Joseph’s before heading to the Paradise Jam next week.

title: Former Penn State CB Jalen Kimber selected 4th overall by Dallas Renegades in UFL draft
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
A former Nittany Lion has been drafted to the UFL.

Cornerback Jalen Kimber was chosen fourth overall by the Dallas Renegades in the 2026 UFL Draft.

Kimber was signed by the Tennessee Titans as an undrafted free agent in 2025. After stints with the Buffalo Bills and Cincinnati Bengals, Kimber now has an opportunity for a fresh start.

The cornerback played his final season with the Nittany Lions after transferring from Florida. He played in every game with the Gators in 2023 after playing in just one game across two years with Georgia in 2020 and 2021.

In 2024, he earned All-Big Ten honorable mention honors after playing in 16 games. He notched three pass breakups with 35 tackles in his lone season with the Nittany Lions.

Kimber will become one of just three cornerbacks on the Renegades' roster for the 2027 season, joining Damon Arnette and Ra'Mello Dotson.

title: Preview | Penn State women’s soccer meets Villanova to open NCAA Tournament two decades after last matchup
author: Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian
description:
Monday night set the stage for the NCAA Women's College Cup.

No. 24 Penn State returns to Jeffrey Field after a tough, hard-fought 2-1 overtime loss to Purdue on Nov. 5 during the quarterfinals of the Big Ten Tournament.

“We competed really hard but took some hits with players not being in the game,” Aubrey Kulpa said on the Purdue loss. “We’ve talked a lot about solving problems together and I think that will be our focus for the next couple of matches.”

The Nittany Lions are seeded sixth in the lower left quadrant of the bracket and are set to host Villanova Friday at 6 p.m. in the first round.

It has been almost exactly 20 years since the two programs last faced off. Their last matchup was Nov. 12, 2006, in the second round of the postseason as Penn State took the game 2-0.

The all-time record between the two programs goes to the Nittany Lions at 4-2. The last time the Wildcats beat Penn State dates back to when they hosted the Nittany Lions on Sept. 14, 1997, defeating them 2-1.

What to expect out of Villanova

This Women’s College Cup marks the seventh time in program history and the first appearance for the Wildcats since 2009.

Villanova is coming off a huge 2-1 win against No. 25 Xavier, which awarded the Wildcats their second-ever Big East championship title.

Coming off of the momentum from the title and a 14-1-5 finish this season, the Wildcats are on pace to bring intense competition for Penn State.

Dez Zapata is the biggest offensive contributor to Villanova’s roster. The junior forward from Smyrna, Delaware, has 24 points with eight goals and eight assists and was named the BIG EAST Offensive Player of the Year and to the All-BIG EAST First Team.

Behind Zapata are Morgan Kotch and Avrie Nelson. Kotch has 23 points with eight goals and seven assists and an impressive 73 shots on the season, earning her All-BIG EAST First Team honors. Nelson is third in points with 20 via eight goals and four assists

Beyond their stellar attacking lineup, the Wildcats have notable players on defense.

Starting and playing in all 20 of Villanova’s matchups, Meredith Palmer, the BIG EAST Defensive Player of the Year, is a big factor in the program’s success. The defender from Waxhaw, North Carolina, notched 1,762 minutes in her junior season, the most on the Wildcat’s roster, proving her leadership.

Just behind Palmer is Hannah Dickinson with 1,727 minutes played. The graduate goalkeeper has been Villanova’s first choice in goal, starting in all 20 matches. Saving 85% of shots, the Seattle native has shown to be a wall in the net, securing herself honors including the BIG EAST Goalkeeper of the Year and All-BIG EAST First Team.

The Wildcats are looking not only to continue their momentum coming into Friday’s competition but also to redeem themselves from their last matchup two decades ago.

What to expect from Penn State

The Nittany Lions have shown to be a competitive program all season long. With a 9-4-5 overall finish and a 6-0-3 record in Happy Valley, the blue and white has the home-field advantage hosting the first round of the tournament.

After suffering that loss to the No. 13 Boilermakers in the conference postseason, Penn State looks to Friday with fire under their boots.

“There’s no doubt a fire burning in this group right now; they want to kick somebody else,” Erica Dambach said in Wednesday’s media. “Now we get to really hone in on Villanova today and tomorrow and then go kick somebody else.”

On the offensive side for the Nittany Lions, it’s no shock that Aubrey Kulpa still leads the pack in most statistics. The forward has notched 21 points via eight goals and five assists with 51 shots. The Cromwell, Connecticut, native has recorded 1,359 minutes, starting in all 18 matches for Penn State.

Being 15 days off from playing on a pitch, Kulpa is itching to play.

“15 days away is a long time,” the junior said. “It's been honestly challenging because you get into the flow of the season and wanting to play games, so I'm ready to go; if the game was tomorrow, I’d be fired up.”

Just behind Kulpa is Paige Kalal with 20 points via seven goals and six assists. The senior forward has 32 shots on the season in 1,309 minutes played. Starting in all 18 matches, the Brooklyn Park, Minnesota, native has shown her dominant offensive capabilities in her first season as a Nittany Lion.

Mackenzie Gress and Kayleigh Herr have been the defensive-end dynamic duo. Gress has been a constant in Penn State’s net, totaling 1,545 minutes, while saving 87.4% of shots, 2.4% higher than Villanova’s Dickinson. Herr has been a bulldog in the back line, consistently making impactful blocks and clearances in the Nittany Lions’ final third.

Heading into Friday, Penn State looks to build on its all-time dominance over the Wildcats and show why it’s seeded sixth in its bracket.

“We’re excited to welcome a foe in our state so that we can prove ourselves to be the best in the state of Pennsylvania,” Dambach said.

title: Staff predictions | Will Penn State stay on a roll against Rutgers?
author: The Daily Collegian football staff
description:
Penn State has won three straight games since the bye week, and it has a straightforward path to make it four this weekend against Rutgers.

The Scarlet Knights are 2-8 this season with one win in Big Ten play against Maryland, marking the worst team the Nittany Lions have faced in conference competition so far.

Will Penn State continue its hot streak and put up over 28 points once again? Here’s what we think.

Andrew Deal: Penn State 42, Rutgers 7

This game really shouldn’t be close. Penn State has turned things around, while Rutgers continues to sputter as the season comes to an end.

The Nittany Lions have looked like a better-than-average Big Ten team the past few weeks, culminating in the blowout against Minnesota.

Rutgers is consistent across the board in being bad. It ranks closer to the bottom in the entire country, including ranking No. 122 in run defense in all of the FBS. Penn State should have similar success compared to the past two weeks in the first half.

I expect the Nittany Lions to get out to a hot start behind the passing of Rocco Becht. With the weather expected to be warmer for a November afternoon, the passing game will have more success than it did last week, with Becht eclipsing the 200-yard mark.

Rutgers won’t have much success on offense. Without star wide receiver KJ Duff, who torched Penn State’s secondary for 127 yards and a touchdown last season, the Scarlet Knights’ offense won’t get anything going.

Penn State should be able to get in a lot of depth players, including seniors who may not get time on a regular basis during the season.

Andrew Mercer: Penn State 35, Rutgers 3

Despite Matt Campbell saying “You’d think they’re undefeated” because of the way Greg Schiano coaches them, there’s no reason why Scarlet Knights should even hold a candle to Penn State.

Rutgers is ranked last in the Big Ten and 2-8 overall including a Week 1 loss to UMass, making it clear the Scarlet Knights are bad at football. That UMass team was the worst team in college football last season, going 0-12 on the year. Rutgers lost to them 37-21.

The Scarlet Knights have the fourth-worst pass defense in the conference, and because running back Carson Hansen is still questionable ahead of the game, I have Penn State’s offense coming through Rocco Becht.

Wide receiver Chase Sowell will get back on track after having no catches last week, and tight end Benjamin Brahmer will once again find the end zone after scoring twice.

Meanwhile, if there’s any game for running back Cam Wallace to shine, it’s against the worst run defense in the Big Ten. The Nittany Lions won’t need Hansen to formulate a balanced attack if Taylor Mouser opts to keep the ball on the ground.

I think Rutgers will find a way to get into field goal range, but that’ll be all as Penn State’s strong secondary and improving run defense will keep the Scarlet Knights out of the end zone for a landslide victory.

Lexie Linderman: Penn State 38, Rutgers 10

Rutgers is not a good football team. Penn State has looked like a good football team the last three weeks and just put up 42 points against Minnesota. So, I’m giving the Nittany Lions a heavy edge in this one.

The Scarlet Knights’ season got off to a bad start after losing to UMass in Week 1, and they haven’t recovered since. They were just shut out by Nebraska, who now has the same record as the Nittany Lions.

Penn State has excelled in running the ball lately, and it’ll look to do the same, even if Hansen doesn’t play. Rutgers allows the most rushing yards per game in the Big Ten, so Wallace should still have a good day regardless of whether Hansen is available or not.

Expect Becht to have a similar statline to last week, when he threw for just 84 yards, as he shouldn’t be tasked with doing much considering how poor the Scarlet Knights’ are against the run.

The Nittany Lions will be able to get backup quarterback Alex Manske some burn alongside other depth pieces who haven’t seen much time this year.

Noah Aberegg: Penn State 45, Rutgers 6

Penn State put its dominance on full display last week, destroying Minnesota 42-14 in Beaver Stadium. While the Golden Gophers were coming off same-day travel, Rutgers is a far-worse team the Nittany Lions should be able to cruise past regardless of travel disruptions.

The Scarlet Knights have the second-worst defense in the Big Ten, giving up the fourth-most passing yards and the most rushing yards per game.

Thankfully for Penn State, its run game has gotten going since the bye week. Regardless if Hansen is a go for Saturday, some combination of him and Wallace will likely have a lot of success against Rutgers.

The Scarlet Knights have suffered from the injury bug this season, notably with starting quarterback Dylan Lonergan, who’s been out since suffering an injury Oct. 24. Backup AJ Surace was questionable heading into last week’s game, resulting in third-string Sean Ashenfelder also seeing time against Nebraska. It’s unknown who will start this week.

But Duff has also been out since Oct. 24 after leading the team with 45 receptions, 774 yards and nine touchdowns, accounting for half of Rutgers’ receiving scores.

With the Scarlet Knights’ offense struggling and injured, Penn State’s defense will shut them down while its offense goes wild against the worst defense in the conference, resulting in a blowout win on Senior Day.

title: Penn State’s Don’t Be Strangers club turns out friendships
author: Hailey Weber | For the Collegian
description:
Before college, you probably spent most of your days with the same people, people you've known your whole life, and felt no need to branch outside of your circle. Then suddenly, you leave the safety blanket of old friends and get thrust into a whole new world of strangers.

Although it can feel intimidating, clubs like Don’t Be Strangers, an organization that works towards fostering connections, offers a low stress, low commitment option for anyone who wants to make friends and be creative without all the pressure.

Mickey Ritter, 21, of State College, Pennsylvania, and Mackenzie Morooney, 22, of State College, Pennsylvania, both hold executive roles in the club, but they didn’t start out in those positions.

Ritter explained that a fellow student she knew unofficially started the Don’t Be Strangers club at Penn State.

“There was a girl we went to middle school with who started it, not as a registered student organization with Penn State, but as something she was doing socially, like picnics, ice cream socials,” Ritter, a third-year studying fine arts, said.

Morooney said the founder was inspired to start it because she realized how hard it could be to make friends in college, and she wanted to make things a little easier. Eventually, though, the original founder got too busy to continue to run it. That's when Ritter volunteered to be president.

“It took a while to do all the paperwork and stuff for it. This is our first semester being a registered student organization,” Ritter said.

Don’t Be Strangers offers a different activity every week from movie nights, to holiday themed crafts and even show and tells. If the activity one week isn’t someone's favorite, they can always come back the next week for a fresh start and a new opportunity.

Mackenzie Morooney acts as vice president of Don’t Be Strangers in addition to being the event planner. Morooney enjoys the behind the scenes work of putting the club events together.

Both the current president and the vice president said they believe that clubs with premises like Don’t Be Strangers are vital to every college campus in order to foster a sense of community and, hopefully, make some friends along the way.

"It's so easy to be friendly, but it’s so hard to make and keep friendships," Ritter said. “We've had people show up that are so fun to be around.”

Morooney shared this sentiment, mentioning that the club gives an additional outlet for socialization at Penn State. She believes it's important to have other places to meet people rather than just classes.

Ritter and Morooney urge students to come to a meeting if they’re interested, and then another, so they can understand the full value of the club and all it has to offer.

“I think the problem is that people hear about it and they come check it out and then they're the only person, and, because they're the only person, they don’t try coming back again,” Morooney said. “But if everyone did try coming back, they might realize that it would be fun if they stuck it out a little. I think it's just worth giving it a try. But more importantly, give it a try more than once."

Elizabeth Kern, 21, of Richmond, Virginia, is a manager at the HUB-Robeson Center Starbucks, a part-time graduate student and a proud member of Don’t Be Strangers. Kern heard about the idea from Ritter when the club was considering becoming an official student organization.

“I lived in the same building as Mickey Ritter, he was considering starting the club," Kern said. "He started floating the idea with some of the other people on the executive board of our LLC. I think over the summer Mickey fleshed it out a little bit more. In the fall, they added me to the Discord.”

Kern and Ritter were on the executive board of Ally House LLC. Kern said the work they were doing in the Ally House was similar to the work being done by Don’t Be Strangers. In both organizations, Kern explained they worked towards creating safe spaces for people and harboring connections.

Kern mentioned that one of the activities frequently put on by the club is movie nights and said anyone is welcome to come and watch. Kern encourages people to either rewatch a movie they enjoy or experience a movie they may have not seen. Either way, it's an easy way to make conversation and bond with people.

“The unique thing about Don’t Be Strangers is it's not related to a specific hobby or language or something like that,” Kern said. “It's just: ‘Let's all have a good time!’”

title: ‘Jeff has been unbelievable’ | Kampersal uplifts Penn State women’s hockey to national prominence
author: Mashiah Mitchell | The Daily Collegian
description:
From the moment Jeff Kampersal stepped onto the ice at Princeton 38 years ago, he has done nothing but succeed.

Though Kampersal’s professional playing career may have been short-lived, it didn’t deter him from continuing to contribute to the game that would continue to give back to him. Coming out of Princeton in 1992 as one of the most transformative and polarizing players of the program, Kampersal was drafted by the New York Islanders, who had just come off a 34-35-11 season. He would spend two years in both the AHL and ECHL before returning to his alma mater, this time as head coach.

Kampersal led the Tigers to their first NCAA tournament berth in his 10th season. Prior to that, Princeton had been right on the cusp, and Kampersal was at the forefront with a record of 135-113-21 — shattering the all-time wins record by year six.

He continued his tenure for ten more seasons, amassing one more NCAA tournament appearance before arriving in Happy Valley. Kampersal’s 327 career wins still hold the Princeton record. Then he hit the ground running when he arrived in Happy Valley, righting the ship and turning the program into one of constant contention.

“The amount of players that are committed to being great teammates and being hockey players, taking advantage of the opportunity here,” Kampersal said. “Our players are program-first; they want to win. We saw it early on at open ice when only 1-2 people would show, but now we have most of the team show up to work on something.”

Kampersal has led the Nittany Lions to four NCAA Tournament appearances, five CHA/AHA regular season titles, four AHA Tournament titles, and their first Frozen Four appearance in the program’s 14-year Division I history just last season.

He and the rest of the staff brought a new approach to this year’s team compared to last year, bringing the outlook that “every year (is) a unique challenge.”

“Last year we took a more hands-off approach because of our senior presence. There has been more coaching this year, trying to break old habits and bring in new ones,” Kampersal said. “We’re continuing to shape culture because the majority of our team is still fresh and new, so we want to instill the urgency to win now rather than in their last seasons. We don’t want them skating around on eggshells and putting pressure on them”.

He said being a good teammate is the most important message he received as a player, one that’s carried into his coaching: Star captain forward Grace Outwater has taken the role Kampersal and his staff gave her and translated it into the game through the breakout of freshman forward Sofia Ismael.

Ismael’s stints with Team Canada, along with plenty of other game tape to go off of, made her a top name in the Nittany Lions recruit process during the offseason. Ismael announced her commitment to Penn State in October 2024 and has immediately made an impact. She currently leads the team in points with 17.

“Me and (Grace) are close, and being able to learn from the vets and them introducing us to new things along with the staff has definitely been a motivator,” Ismael said. “They’ve allowed us to make mistakes, and we’re learning from them game by game and getting better.”

Outwater also had success with Kampersal’s help, winning AHA Scoring Champion last year and earning conference Preseason Player of the Year this season as she looks on pace to again lead the AHA in goals.

“Jeff has been unbelievable. Coming in as a freshman, he was a bit intimidating, of course, but he helped with the whole process of coming to college and getting acclimated; he is a funny guy, and he definitely helped me a lot early on,” Outwater said. “He makes you better every day, pushing you to your limit; it has been awesome.”

Kampersal also instills confidence and trust in his coaches, like Moe Bradley. Bradley is still a fresh face in Hockey Valley, now in her second season in her assistant coach tenure.

Bradley’s arrival in State College followed a two-year stint as the head coach of her alma mater, UMass Boston. Bradley’s legacy is felt for the Beacons both as a player and a coach, with her still owning goaltender records and producing talents like Gianna Skrelja.

“(Kampersal) trusts us completely,” Bradley said. “He coaches trust first, and that system has empowered me and the rest of the staff to stick with what we think is the right type of coaching and aspects.”

She also feels like the entire staff has set a precedent for both new and future talent after what the senior-heavy 2025-26 team was able to produce on the ice and wanting to not only build upon that legacy, but exceed it.

“Last year’s team found the level we knew we were capable of being and staying at,” Bradley said. “The message is to be dominant but also stay dominant as well, teams like Wisconsin that are consistently at the top of the rankings. We want to be consistent and be a program that does not fall and sets that standard of people want to come here to win.”

For someone who has been coaching for over three decades now, one might think that the question of retirement would loom in the mind of Jeff Kampersal. It might feel as though next year could be his last. But the man himself, in his 31st season, said he has no problem getting motivated each season.

With 12 Coach of the Year awards under his belt, Kampersal currently ranks ninth in all-time career wins with 519, just four behind the legendary Katey Stone. With 20 games left in this season, Kampersal is almost guaranteed to continue climbing the leaderboard and continue to solidify the legacy he continues to build and will leave behind.

“Working with the players and developing relationships, and them growing into holistic people and being good people, good teammates, and good players, that keeps me in it. The success is nice, but it's the fact that the culture and players are loud; they have a lot of fun, which makes it fun to come to work.”

title: Penn State women’s soccer notebook | Erica Dambach discusses postseason play
author: Lola Brand | For the Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions have spent the season navigating adversity, gaining valuable experience and building confidence against some of the nation’s top competition.

Now, No. 23 Penn State will host unranked Villanova at 6 p.m. Friday in the first round of the NCAA Women’s College Cup, and coach Erica Dambach and junior forward Aubrey Kulpa believe the blue and white is hitting its stride at the right time.

Dambach and Kulpa met with the media over Zoom on Wednesday to discuss navigating adversity and carrying resilience into postseason play, as well as the significance of Penn State heading into the tournament for a historic 32nd time.

Growth through adversity

Penn State has faced tough, top-ranked competition throughout the season, challenging the Nittany Lions to make adjustments, rise to challenges and grow as a team.

Through those experiences, the team has developed a sense of resilience that Dambach believes will be valuable heading into the NCAA tournament. The blue and white had no shortage of opportunities to learn lessons this season, or time to dwell on those moments — with nearly two weeks off from its defeat in the Big Ten Tournament to Purdue.

“It's kind of the analogy of calluses that are built up over time. Since this season has started, we have weathered these challenges,” Dambach said. “We have built calluses; we have challenged ourselves in every way.”

The Nittany Lions have proved time and time again their ability to compete with any opponent, as evidenced by their win over No. 3 Michigan State. In addition, every ranked game for the blue and white was within a goal or a draw. Dambach believes that demanding schedule has prepared the team to handle the pressure and unpredictability of postseason play.

A legacy continues

Penn State will be heading into the NCAA postseason for the 32nd time, making it the second longest NCAA tournament streak in the country. This milestone only adds to a longstanding standard of success within the program, one that carries both the privilege and responsibility of continuing a tradition built by the players and coaches before them.

“We talk to the players a lot about being a part of something bigger than yourself, and I feel that too,” Dambach said. “Obviously, having only been here for twenty of those years, I walked into a really successful program, and with that, you feel the pressure and the privilege, and I think that's what the players feel.”

Dambach brought the program’s only National Championship home in 2015, and she doesn’t take the program’s standard for granted, recognizing the work and challenges that come with earning another tournament appearance and filling that shadow.

“We're part of something really special right now, and I don't take that lightly,” Dambach said. “Every time we get one of those bids, I know it comes with adversity and hard work, and I don't take a single one of those for granted.”

Home-field energy

The blue and white are set to take on Villanova at Jeffrey Field on Friday, opening its NCAA journey on home turf.

Penn State has played its best on its home pitch this season, posting a 6-0-3 record. The expectations in the postseason won’t be much different.

“They come flying out of that building, they feel the energy, they hear the music,” Dambach said. “I think that they've created an opportunity leading into the game to get really hyped and excited, and come flying out of the gates.”

Kulpa

Kulpa has had a tremendous season, notching eight goals and five assists, as well as earning First Team All-Big Ten Honors. She has played a key role in creating scoring opportunities, finishing chances and helping drive the Nittany Lions’ offense.

“I can say I’m itching to play,” Kulpa said. “I’m ready to go. I mean, if the game was tomorrow, I’d be fired up.”

Kulpa and the Nittany Lions are set to take on a Villanova that’s off of winning the Big East crown, entering Happy Valley with a 14-1-5 record.

“I think it's important to note that this group is ticking right now. They are firing on all cylinders. They look good. They feel good. We've used these last two weeks to gain health, to refill our cup, and to get ready for a push here, and all eyes on Villanova.” Dambach said.

title: Penn State men's basketball outlasts IU Indianapolis, continues win streak
author: Myles Hannak | Sports Editor
description:
A win is a win.

After a pair of double-digit victories, the Nittany Lions kept its streak going with a narrow uphill 81-74 win over IU Indianapolis, improving to 5-1 in the process.

The Jaguars came out of the gate with a full-court press that allowed fifth-year forward Josh Reed to find a pair of three-point attempts, which he missed. Scoring started slow for both sides; through the first two and a half minutes, the only ticks on the scoreboard were single free throw makes from Penn State.

IU Indy soon thereafter made a pair of threes after a pair of blue and white blunders. The first six minutes led to a dull 6-6 score with two offenses churning out empty possessions. The Nittany Lions went to the bench to find a sparkplug, but it couldn’t stop an energized Jaguars offense, which at times substituted most of its lineup at once — a frequent trend in the night’s clash.

Ben Howlett’s squad rained threes on Penn State in succession and rapid fashion, which uplifted them to an 18-9 advantage at the 11:04 mark.

Almost a minute later, Penn State got back-to-back baskets, the latter of which was an emphatic Ivan Jurić slam where the 7-footer pulled himself up on the rim. Yet the aggression was fleeting, as the Jaguars’ press forced consecutive turnovers from Reed, and starting guard Dasonte Bowen soon after for scores.

The blue and white trailed by eight with a little over six minutes to play, until a few consecutive scores cut the deficit to three. With it looking optimistic, Jaguars guard Peyton Heiss then hovered over the ball to prevent the Nittany Lions from retrieving it — antagonizing Reed.

It had already been a fast, scrappy game, but it continued, energizing the BJC crowd. Mike Rhoades deployed unique blue and white lineups, including one that utilized both point guards Bowen and Jay Rodgers at once, but it had gotten them to a 37-34 hole with only three minutes to play, as the ball movement helped beat the IU Indy press.

That’s where the Nittany Lions hovered over the next few minutes until Jurić tossed a perfect pass to a cutting Bowen to push it to a one-point game. A half-court heave with seconds expiring from Reed earned oohs and ahhs from the crowd, but the miss kept it at a 41-40 Jaguars’ advantage at the break.

Three-point shooting had been streaky for the blue and white out of the break, and it stayed that way, as they failed to pull even after four minutes of evenly played basketball with plenty of opportunities. As time ticked on, Rhoades’ squad still couldn’t make a push in what had become a war of attrition with few buckets in between.

As the game approached the midpoint of the final half, Penn State’s energy shifted as Thomas Allard sank a pair of threes and Bowen made a layup to flip the advantage to 59-54.

With the momentum finally on its side, the blue and white endured a minor run to take a nine-point lead. Penn State had been out-rebounded for most of the game but finally took the edge with eight minutes left.

The Jaguars continued to press on as their scoring drought ended, pushing it to a one-score game after a few minutes and matching every effort Penn State tried. Ultimately, the Nittany Lions outran the threat down the wire with the win, but IU Indy remained in the rearview the entire time.

Penn State was led by Jurić’s 21 points in 35 minutes, 16 rebounds and four assists. Bowen added 17 points, tying his Penn State career-best, and had five assists. Allard logged 15 points, also a high in his tenure as a Nittany Lion.

Forward Kameron Tinsley led IU Indy scoring with 17 points.

Injury report

The flu sidelined forward Brant Byers for a second consecutive game, but he appeared on the bench. Guard Roberts Blums also remains injured due to a broken finger, appearing in only one game this season.

Rhoades couldn't provide a timeline for return for either.

Up next

After a week off, Penn State heads to the Battle 4 Atlantis in Paradise Island, Bahamas, with the competition set to host its 15th year from Nov. 25 to Nov. 27. The blue and white’s first game is next Wednesday against Penny Hardaway’s coached Memphis squad at 5 p.m. EST.

title: Penn State issues statement following alleged cocaine-ring leader's indictment, calls hazing "unacceptable"
author: Grace Levy | News Editor
description:
Penn State issued a statement following the federal indictment of Agostino Abbatiello, the alleged leader of a cocaine ring tied to Penn State fraternities, on Wednesday.

In the statement, Andrea Dowhower, vice president for Student Affairs, said Penn State’s Delta Upsilon chapter, who was under interim suspension following the alleged trafficking, lost its eligibility following a review that found "profoundly disturbing acts of hazing.”

The chapter is not eligible to return for a minimum four years, allowing students connected to a “problematic chapter culture” to graduate, Dowhower said. Additionally, Penn State will pursue individual conduct actions as needed.

Dowhower reiterated that Penn State’s Sigma Chi chapter, the other fraternity associated with the alleged trafficking, has been suspended since Feb. 2021, and has operated without recognition from Penn State since then.

Sigma Chi is a founding member of the State College Interfraternity Council (SCIFC), a student-run council composed of fraternities in State College. The council is not affiliated with the university.

Dowhower cited Delta Upsilon and Sigma Chi as an “example of a culture that too many people still dismiss as tradition, harmless fun or simply part of the college experience.” However, she said it was “dangerous, unhealthy, and unacceptable."

“Hazing is not a rite of passage. It is not a test of loyalty. Calling it tradition does not make it acceptable, and a student “agreeing” to take part does not make it safe. It is a violation of University expectations and the Code of Conduct and, under Pennsylvania and federal law, hazing is a crime and consent is not a defense,” Dowhower said in the statement.

Dowhower said Penn State will continue to hold organizations and individuals accountable, as well as expand education on hazing and harm-reduction. However, she said while these are “essential,” they are “not enough on their own.”

To prevent hazing, people recognize risks, speak up and support a culture “where respect, belonging and safety are valued more than tradition or status.”

Students are encouraged to report concerns or seek help for other students, and these reports can be made anonymously.

Dowhower said that Penn State does not want to diminish the positive experiences associated with fraternity and sorority life, rather encourage “safety, respect and well-being.”

title: Delta Upsilon loses Penn State recognition for minimum four years
author: Curtis Johnson | For the Collegian
description:
Delta Upsilon, one of the fraternities implicated in an alleged cocaine ring tied to Penn State fraternities, lost its Penn State recognition for at least four years, following an investigation that discovered “disturbing acts of hazing.”

Penn State suspended Delta Upsilon’s eligibility for at least four years to allow all involved members to graduate, according to a release from Penn State on Thursday.

Losing university recognition means Delta Upsilon will lose any privileges associated with being a recognized student organization such as Penn State resources, staff support or university-sanctioned events, such as THON.

The chapter was previously placed on interim suspension on Aug. 17 while the Penn State’s Office of Student Accountability and Conflict Response launched an investigation regarding any off-campus hazing activity during the spring and fall 2024 semesters. This was in response to the Pennsylvania Attorney General’s charges related to cocaine-trafficking filed in August.

Investigations uncovered that pledges were forced to prepare and distribute over 200 half-gram bags of cocaine. Pledges were subjected to intimidation, sleep deprivation, and serious threats to physical harm.

Such hazing activity violates not only Penn State policy, but also state and federal law, including the federal Stop Campus Hazing Act and the Pennsylvania Timothy J. Piazza Antihazing Law.

Andrea Dowhower, vice president for Student Affairs, released a statement explaining the revocation of eligibility for recognition. Dowhower emphasized Penn State’s responsibility to act “swiftly and decisively” against action that can put students in danger.

“What happened at Delta Upsilon … is an example of a culture that too many people still dismiss as tradition, harmless fun, or simply part of the college experience,” Dowhower said.

Once the four year period is over, the international fraternity may seek recognition but will be subject to the university’s approval.

Delta Upsilon was additionally suspended from the internationally affiliated fraternity.
