title: Penn State CB Audavion Collins’ confidence offsets his lack of size, sparks standout career
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Cornerback Audavion Collins said it wasn’t until his second year at Penn State that he felt he truly settled into the program. He appeared in six games as a redshirt freshman, but played in all 16 as a redshirt sophomore.

Transferring from Mississippi State, there was an adjustment period to life at Penn State. Collins’ early conversations with Terry Smith revolved around putting weight on, being more proactive in the film room and working on his consistency.

“I was coming in trying to really learn the program, trying to learn the culture and just the guys I was around, trying to learn from them guys,” Collins said Wednesday. “But I say my second year, I felt like everything started clicking, and I started to get my groove start feeling more, and I started to put more weight on.”

Being undersized never stopped Collins from getting what he wanted out of college football. Not only is he one of the fastest players on the team, he’s a big reason why Penn State’s defensive secondary ranks at the top of the Big Ten.

Because of his 5-foot-11, perpetually undersized frame, Collins found other avenues of differentiating himself from the rest of the pack, including trash talk.

Collins has established himself as one of the most vocal players on the field, contrasting his quiet demeanor off the field. His personality is in full force once his helmet is on, stemming from his abundance of confidence in himself to play lockdown defense.

“When I get out there, I feel like a whole different type of person just talking crazy or whatever I say on the field,” Collins said, grinning. “That's just a whole other side that I always had in me. Even going to camps in high school, I was always the one talking crazy, and it was, ‘man he’s going to be a problem one day.’”

Collins uses his voice in a different way when talking to his fellow defenders, sharing his veteran wisdom as a redshirt senior to mentor younger players.

When Collins was new to Penn State, former Nittany Lion cornerbacks Johnny Dixon, Kalen King and Daequan Hardy were Collins’ biggest mentors, setting an example for him to follow for when he matured into a leader.

Collins said he’s taken safety Ibn McDaniels under his wing in a similar way. He said he “stayed in his ear” and told him his time was going to come eventually, seeing a lot of himself in McDaniels as someone who had to fight to see the field.

Collins developed those leadership skills having gone through the ups and downs of Penn State’s recent seasons.

“It taught me how to be a leader even when it be on low,” Collins said. “Just to have somebody to step up and speak to. That way, if it's a storm, we’ve got to get through it, and I wanted to be the one to help us get through it.”

With only two regular season games remaining in his collegiate career, Collins said he’s focused on playing like himself instead of overextending to impress NFL scouts. He said he’s not thinking about the next step until it’s the right time to move on, and he’s ready to feel all of the emotions of Senior Day against Rutgers on Saturday.

“I’m just trying to take one day at a time, focus on the present moment,” Collins said. “Don't try to look ahead. When that time comes, that time will come. So I just try to stay focused on what's now.”

title: Penn State women’s lacrosse names captains for 2027 season
author: Joey Bolger | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State announced junior defender Lilly Spilker and senior attacker Kelly MacKinney as captains for the 2027 season.

MacKinney had a breakout season last year, scoring 45 goals and totaling 77 points. She was also named IWLCA and Big Ten Offensive Player of the Week during last season.

Spilker was a key piece of the Nittany Lions' defense last season, causing 17 turnovers and leading the team in ground balls with 26.

The blue-and-white look to improve on their 12-7 record last season and return to the NCAA tournament this season.

title: ‘Stay in the moment’ | Penn State seniors prepare for Senior Day ceremony against Rutgers
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Twenty five players will cross the field before Saturday’s game against Rutgers, many walking arm-in-arm with family and friends as Penn State celebrates Senior Day.

The Nittany Lion Senior class is made up of some players who've spent their entire collegiate careers in Happy Valley and others who are much newer to campus, giving Senior Day a different meaning for each of them.

But for many, the ceremony offers an opportunity to reflect on their collegiate careers as they prepare to take the field at Beaver Stadium one final time.

“I don't know if I'm looking forward to it, it's kind of sad to be honest,” tight end Gabe Burkle said Wednesday. “We have such a great senior class, everyone deserves to be celebrated as a senior. I'm glad that it's here.”

Of the 25 players participating, some still have a fifth year of eligibility should they choose to use it, including running back Carson Hansen, offensive tackle Anthony Donkoh and tight end Andrew Rappleyea. Meanwhile, several players listed as seniors aren’t participating in the ceremony, including linebacker Kooper Ebel, tight end Benjamin Brahmer and safety Jamison Patton.

Matt Campbell said Tuesday the option to walk on Senior Day is a personal preference for players, particularly as some players continue to weigh their plans for next season.

“I think college football, you're trying to figure out who the heck's a senior, so it's a global response to it,” Campbell said. “Some guys have eligibility that you know are still working through the process that just didn't feel like they were ready to walk on senior day. Other guys have eligibility that are walking on senior day and probably will wait till the end of the season to to make a final decision if they come back.”

Regardless of whether a player has called Penn State home for several years or arrived less than a year ago, Saturday’s ceremony is expected to be an emotional occasion for many involved.

Wide receiver Chase Sowell was asked which senior would be the most emotional, and he pointed to two longtime Nittany Lions who he believes will “really be hurt.”

“I think (Donkoh) will be one of them,” Sowell said. “I think he's just a guy that just appreciates this place so much, and literally destroyed his body trying to give his everything to this place. And then (Rappleyea) is another one that I know would be pretty hurt.”

Sowell also mentioned offensive lineman Dom Rulli as a player who’ll be emotional pregame, as his family “has a big Penn State tradition through their household.”

Jordan Hill, the director of player development, talked with some of the players about Saturday's game. He said he remembers everything from his Senior Day, including his final bus ride to Beaver Stadium.

“It's going to be pretty emotional for all of us, but we'll get past that, and we'll go out there and win another game for this program,” Rocco Becht said. “This place has meant a lot to me to be able to come here, one of the most prestigious programs, and play here as a quarterback. All the rich history and the traditions that they have here, it's super special to be a part of, and I'm truly excited that I made that decision to come here.”

Senior Day has provided an opportunity for players who haven’t played for the Nittany Lions all four or five years to reflect on both their short time at Penn State, but also their overarching career and everything that came before.

“I reflected just seeing how this place is, and just knowing that like, okay, it's my last year, just my last game, and I got to make it the best I can,” defensive end Ike Ezeogu said. “Just keeping everything in perspective and not really looking too far ahead and looking too back, and just knowing that everything's in front of me. Just gotta just keep my calm, keep my poise, and just stay in the moment.”

As long snapper Blaise Sokach-Minnick walks out Saturday, he’ll have a lot of family waiting for him on the field. His mom, dad, brothers, grandma and cousins will all be at the game celebrating his senior ceremony.

“I think what'll (make me emotional) is my family,” Sokach-Minnick said. “I think that just seeing them, and they've been there for me since I was five years old, and I picked up a football, and they've been to every single game, through the ups and the downs. They've supported me, and that's probably going to make me a little emotional.”

While some players are preparing for their emotional farewell, others are looking forward to celebrating one final opportunity to play in front of the Beaver Stadium crowd.

“I’m ready. I’m ready to celebrate Senior Day,” cornerback Audavion Collins said. “Last home game, last one in Beaver. Man, it means a lot, especially playing in that stadium, especially with them guys. But it most definitely means a lot playing in Beaver. It’s my last one.”

title: Penn State men’s basketball alum Tim Frazier to play for Team USA in FIBA World Cup qualifying
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Former Penn State star Tim Frazier will represent the United States on the Men’s FIBA World Cup Qualifying Team, USA Basketball announced Wednesday.

Frazier played at Penn State from 2009 through 2014, and then spent nine seasons in the NBA with nine different franchises. Most notably, he appeared in 128 games with the Pelicans while starting 53.

At Penn State, the Houston, Texas, native earned first-team All-Big Ten honors in 2012 while averaging 18.8 points per game. Frazier is Penn State’s all-time leader in assists with 641 and sits at 10th all-time in scoring.

Frazier will suit up for Team USA for the first time on Nov. 27 in São Paulo, Brazil, then the team heads to Cali, Colombia, for a second game on Nov. 30.

title: Alleged cocaine-ring leader Agostino Abbatiello indicted on federal charges
author: Grace Levy | News Editor
description:
Agostino S. Abbatiello, one of the alleged ringleaders in the fraternity-led cocaine-trafficking ring at Penn State, was indicted by a federal grand jury Thursday, according to a press release from the Department of Justice.

Abbatiello, 24, of Westbury, New York, was charged with one count of conspiracy to distribute cocaine and six counts of distribution of cocaine in charges announced by U.S. Attorney Brian D. Miller and Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday.

Abbatiello was previously charged with ten felonies related to the alleged distribution of cocaine out of the Sigma Chi and Delta Upsilon fraternities at Penn State spanning Jan. 2023 and Dec. 2024.

According to the press release, Abbatiello sold cocaine in “bulk quantities," purchased the drug from suppliers in Philadelphia and New York and recruited others to assist him in selling.

“This defendant was the top rung of the ladder for a high-level drug trafficking ring that supplied cocaine to Penn State University students, incorporating some fraternity pledges into the packaging process,” Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday said in the release. “We are proud of the fine investigative work involved in building this case, thank the grand jurors for their diligence, and look forward to having a hand in prosecuting with our ready and able partners at the U.S. Attorney’s Office.”

In the state-level case, 13 other defendants were charged alongside Abbatiello, including 12 other former or current Penn State students.

As of today, Abbatiello is listed as incarcerated at the Clinton County Correctional Facility, according to court documents. Previously, he was released on $250,000 bail from the Centre County Correctional Facility.

If convicted in federal court, Abbatiello faces a mandatory minimum of 10 years in prison and a maximum of lifetime imprisonment.

title: Penn State features all 10 wrestlers in latest InterMat rankings
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
Intermat's newly updated rankings shake up the placement of multiple Penn State wrestlers.

While some remain at the top, others rise following their performances through the first two duals of the season. Penn State now has a wrestler ranked in the top 20 of every division.

At 125 pounds, Luke Lilledahl sits atop the division yet again. Lilledahl has started the season undefeated with two wins against unranked opponents. While he's kept it close in both bouts, neither performance warranted a loss of his No. 1 spot.

Following his win against Oklahoma's then-No. 15-ranked wrestler Isaiah Powe, Intermat placed Masanosuke Ono directly above him at No. 16 in the 133-pound division. Ono has impressed so far this season, and his first win against a ranked opponent grants him a spot in the top 20.

At 141 pounds, Marcus Blaze stays put at No. 3 following his statement debut against Oklahoma's ranked No. 11 Tyler Wells. Blaze notched the pinfall victory, proving that his high ranking is legit even with his jump in weight class. With Virginia Tech's Bo Bassett and Lehigh's Luke Stanich, the two wrestlers ranked ahead of him, facing off against each other, Blaze could potentially rise in the next update.

Shayne Van Ness remains at No. 4 at 149 pounds but has a chance to change that at the NWCA All-Star Classic. Van Ness will match up against the No.1 ranked wrestler, Virginia Tech's Caleb Henson. Although the competition is technically an exhibition, it could still put factors into the rankings.

Tyler Kasak's ranking did not shift after the update. The No. 2 wrestler in the 157-pound division has started a bit slow this season with two close decision wins against Blommsburg's Michael Turi and No.16 ranked Rafael Hipolito Jr.

PJ Duke holds his top spot at 165 pounds. Yet Duke has a major test ahead of him at the NWCA All-Star Classic, as he faces Michigan's No. 4-ranked Cam Catrabone after stepping in for Oklahoma's Paddy Gallagher. Duke earned the 12-10 decision against Catrabone during Penn State's dual win over Michigan last season.

Mitchell Mesenbrink, who hasn't lost since his freshman year, owns the No. 1 spot at 174 pounds. With two dominant tech-fall wins against Bloomsburg's Mohamed Abdelhady and Oklahoma's then-No. 31 Tyler Eise, the Dan Hodge trophy winner won't look to sell his spot any time soon.

At 184 pounds, Rocco Welsh keeps his No. 2 ranking. He'll face a top-five ranked talent in Michigan's No. 5 Brock Mantanona at the NWCA All-Star Classic. The matchup will be Welsh and Mantanona's fourth meeting, with Welsh taking the win in all three previous bouts.

Josh Barr remains at No. 1 within the 197-pound division. Barr will be the fifth Nittany Lion to compete at the NWCA All-Star Classic, facing Little Rock's No. 3 ranked Stephen Little. In their most recent meeting at the 2026 Southern Scuffle, Barr got the best of Little in his 9-1 decision.

Cole Mirasola was removed from the rankings now that he is no longer on the roster, as he's taking a religious mission year. His twin brother, Connor Mirasola, moves into the rankings at No. 19 at 285 pounds after his last-second win against then-No.23 Bradley Hill.

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell talks significance of return for 2 senior players
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Penn State will play its final game in Beaver Stadium of the 2026 season on Saturday when it takes on Rutgers.

Matt Campbell met with the media to discuss injury updates, turning the corner on the run game and the return of tight end Benjamin Brahmer and linebacker Kooper Ebel for next year.

Here’s what Campbell had to say.

Injury updates

Cornerback Jahmir Joseph and defensive end Caleb Bacon were late additions to the injury report before Penn State’s game against Minnesota, and both were ruled out ahead of the game.

Campbell gave updates on each ahead of the Nittany Lions’ matchup against Rutgers.

“Jahmir did practice today, so we'll kind of see a little bit more how close he is ready to go,” Campbell said. “I would say both those guys are questionable right now for Saturday.”

Alongside the two defensive players, running back Carson Hansen left the game right before the half. Hansen didn’t return and was given the “questionable” designation from Campbell on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Campbell gave a further update on his top rusher.

“Really super limited so far (in practice),” Campbell said. “Again, I think we'll make that final decision. I would tell you he was last week at this time too, so I think we'll know a lot more probably based off what happens tomorrow in practice. But yeah, (Hansen’s) been super limited so far.”

Run game success

Since the bye week, Penn State’s rushing attack has taken major steps to add another level to the offense, running for over 170 yards in all three games during the win streak.

This new success has stemmed from a bye week in which the Nittany Lions honed in on the run.

“I think you were kind of in that phase in that limbo for a little bit, and so the ability to settle ourselves,” Campbell said. “Have great time to really dig a mile deep into the information and then really reset ourselves fundamentally into, these are the things that we have to do well, and that's why I thought it was such a critical point for us to be able to get that bye week.”

With the offense spiraling during the losing streak prior to the week off, Campbell felt it was necessary to get the run game fixed. Since then, it’s allowed the offense to play complementary football and rely on the run game more.

The offense has run the ball more in each of the past three weeks than it did during the four games to start Big Ten play. The success from both Hansen and running back Cam Wallace has allowed for the pass game to take a back seat at times.

“I think you saw a group of guys straining really hard to try to get things fixed,” Campbell said. “You felt like it was our responsibility to make sure you had the answers to fix it.”

Early returning players

On Tuesday, both Ebel and Brahmer announced that they’ll be returning for a fifth season. Both Iowa State transfers were two of the five players who could opt to play a fifth season with the new five-for-five rule.

Ebel has been one of Penn State’s biggest leaders in his first season in Happy Valley, earning a captain role for every game this season.

“You know what you're going to get in January,” Campbell said. “You know what you're going to get in February, you know what you're going to get in winter conditioning… (Ebel) is the same guy every day, and he brings a sense of maturity and consistency and a demand of his very best. And so, I think that's huge for this team.”

Campbell said very similar things about Brahmer, who’s coming off a two-touchdown game, proving to be a real threat in the end zone.

“Ben, kind of in that same mold on the other side of the football, is a guy that has proven to be at his best,” Campbell said. “One of the best players in the country at his position, on top of this I think unwavering competitive excellence that he wants to not only be the best player but he wants to be a great team.”

title: Penn State women’s basketball notebook | Tanisha Wright talks offense, looks ahead to education day
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State returns home from a 0-3 road trip on Thursday to face Bowling Green. Over the last two weeks, coach Tanisha Wright’s squad lost to Cincinnati, Dayton and Arizona State by a combined 73 points.

The 44-point drubbing by Arizona State on Monday dropped the Lady Lions to 0-4 for the first time in their 61-year history.

Before her first game inside Rec Hall, Wright met with the media to discuss Monday’s loss, her offense and the Education Day matchup coming on Thursday.

Road woes

Penn State suffered its worst loss of the season to Arizona State on Monday, falling 85-41. The Lady Lions shot 16-for-52 from the field, 4-for-15 on three-pointers and 5-for-12 from the free-throw line, all worse marks than the Sun Devils. Penn State also turned the ball over 23 times to Arizona State’s 13.

“I think we're continuing to focus on us getting better,” Wright said. “What we're continuing to learn is what areas that we can get better in, and we're improving in some, and we're still growing in some, and so continuing to focus on those areas until we can put it all together. It's gonna click; it'll click at some point.”

Adding to the challenges, the nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration that shook the country impacted Penn State’s trip to Tempe. The game, originally scheduled for Sunday, tipped off at 4 p.m. ET on Monday.

“I spent 20 years in the W, and we had all kinds of travel and issues and different things like that,” the former Atlanta Dream head coach said. “At the end of the day, you're going to suit up. You're going to play the game, and so you got to be prepared for it. And that's no different than other people who deal with traveling and different things like that when you're going across the country, so it's just a part of it.”

Offensive highs and lows

On the court, the Lady Lions have experienced a wide variety of offensive performances. Petra Božan and Devyn Quigley racked up 27 and 23 points, respectively, against Dayton.

“It showed me that when we're locked in, when we are playing together, when we're focused on the game plan, that we have the ability,” Wright said. “It's not just Petra and Devyn. We have some others that can really (score). It hasn't shown so far this year, and that's why I said they just have to stay the course.”

Guard Enjulina Gonzalez is one of those players who hasn’t showcased a ton of scoring prowess in the early stages of the season. The graduate transfer is shooting 25.7% from the field and is yet to make a three-pointer, but Wright still recognizes her contributions without filling up the basket.

“Obviously, we know her speed,” Wright, a three-time Big Ten Defensive Player of the Year, said. “I think she did a great job defensively this last game, being active, being in the gaps, helping us in that way, and so I think those are all things that Enji (Gonzalez) can bring to the table when her shot isn't falling, and then having the confidence to keep taking the shot when you've put the work in.”

Back at home

The Lady Lions will play a rare Thursday morning game for Wright’s first time coaching in Rec Hall. The blue and white take on Bowling Green at 11 a.m. in its Education Day game.

Wright’s squad has been heavily involved in the community since she took over last March, and she spoke on the impact of hosting local students.

“I think they do a great job already of being solid within our community and understanding the influence that they have on young people's lives, not just young girls, but young boys as well, and so I think that we have, I've said this publicly so many times, we have great kids on this roster,” Wright said.

Another interesting aspect of the battle is the fact that it’s tipping off before lunchtime. Wright stuck with a common theme: whether it’s a national travel panic or a promotion changing their schedule, her Lady Lions come ready to play all the same.

“It's the same way, “ she said. “We're gonna get prepared. We have practice here in a couple hours, so we'll get practice in; we'll prepare for Bowling Green. It's a one-day prep for us, and so we'll get ready the same way we get ready for any other game.”

The Falcons play an unusual number of mid-morning matchups. They are in the midst of five straight 11 a.m. tip-offs, and they have a sixth coming up on Dec. 3.

So far this season, Bowling Green is 4-0, including a 77-73 victory over Cleveland State. The Vikings edged out Penn State inside the Bryce Jordan Center back on Nov. 2 for their lone win in four tries this year.

Bowling Green also touts blowout victories over Georgia Southern, Bellarmine and, most recently, Lawrence Tech.

“Bowling Green is a well-coached team,” Wright said. “They're young, but when you look at who's the head of that snake over there, those two post players are doing a phenomenal job of playing to their strengths, playing to their skills. I think for us, we really have to focus on playing hard and playing the style that we want to play.”

The Lady Lions and Falcons meet in less than 24 hours, with tipoff scheduled for 11 a.m. at Rec Hall.

title: Biggest takeaways from Penn State wrestling’s first weekend
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
After Penn State’s 41-0 rout of Oklahoma on the road, the Nittany Lions began the season 2-0.

Although they’re only a couple of matches into the year, many storylines and things to watch can be pulled from the performances of the blue and white.

Here are some takeaways from Penn State’s first two matches.

Masonuke Ono is the real deal

Ono secured a win against then-No. 15 Isaiah Powe, defeating a ranked opponent for the first time in his collegiate career. After starting the season 2-0, it may be safe to say that Ono’s transition to folkstyle is going as well as it could have so far.

Cael Sanderson said that he had rarely seen Ono get taken down in practice. That has translated to his matches, as Ono has only been taken down twice in his first two bouts. His quickness has allowed him to defend well against attacks from opponents.

The only knock on the Matsue City, Japan, native’s early performances has been his inability to close out matches effectively. In Ono’s bout against Bloomsburg’s Austin Pollard, he was outscored 4-2 in the final two periods, and couldn’t earn the final takedown to win by tech fall.

In Ono’s following match against Oklahoma’s Isaiah Powe, Ono built a 6-1 lead before being outscored 4-1 through the rest of the match. He was penalized for stalling in the final seconds of the third period. His stamina has been a clear issue, which Sanderson acknowledged after the match against Bloomsburg.

If Ono can improve his conditioning, which comes with wrestling more folkstyle matches, then he has a chance to become a real contender in the 133-pound division.

Marcus Blaze’s importance in the lineup

Hayden Cunningham’s loss to Bloomsburg’s Scotty Johnson was a testament to how important Blaze is to the lineup. When he’s out, there’s a hole left at 141. Yet, when he’s in, the Nittany Lions become even more dangerous.

In Blaze’s first match at 141 pounds, he established a 7-1 lead before using a leg sweep to take the No. 11-ranked wrestler to the ground and secure the pin. Blaze used his strength as an advantage, an aspect of his skill set that he’ll need after making the jump to a heavier division.

Rumors circulated about Blaze’s transition to the higher weight class, as Sanderson refused to add much detail surrounding the process. Yet, Cunningham’s loss may have prompted Blaze’s quick return.

Penn State will need Blaze to continue at the pace he’s currently at, as its chances at winning an individual championship at 141 plummet without him.

Multiple close calls show Penn State is human

While the overall score may say otherwise, Oklahoma put up an incredible fight against a couple of the Nittany Lions' best wrestlers. Luke Lilledahl, Tyler Kasak and Connor Mirasola all kept it close in decision wins.

Lilledahl struggled to win big against an unranked opponent in Sebastian Degennaro. Only tallying one takedown on the night, Lilledahl’s attacks were defended well by Degennaro, but he couldn’t find any openings of his own.

While Lilledahl escaped with a win, the manner in which he did so showed that the No. 1-ranked wrestler at 125 pounds may not cruise through the schedule this year.

Kasak created an early 4-1 lead against Rafael Hipolito Jr., but was penalized for stalling twice in order to prevent the late surge of attacks from the Sooner. Looking at both of his performances this season, Kasak hasn’t necessarily impressed so far.

The redshirt junior hadn’t wrestled since the 2024-25 season, so these opening bouts could simply be Kasak wiping off the dust.

Mirasola nearly lost against No. 23-ranked Bradley Hill, but the heavyweight notched a clutch takedown at the end of the period. Mirasola was down early until the third period, when he found success in his attack.

While the other matches would have been upsets had the Nittany Lions suffered a loss, Mirasola came in as the underdog. His late win still shows his susceptibility to a loss when he faces an opponent of a higher caliber than Hill.

title: Dorm-friendly, dining-dollar funded holiday recipes
author: Ally Sons | The Daily Collegian
description:
As Thanksgiving break fast approaches, students are likely looking forward to a break from the dining hall food and a change of pace to a nice home-cooked meal.

It can feel impossible to find any options on campus that aren’t the buffet or the same acai bowl and chicken spots you eat at every day. You might see the dining dollars sitting in your account and have no desire to spend them on anything in particular — which can make you miss home that much more.

A friendsgiving-style holiday celebration with your favorite people on campus can be the perfect way to wrap up. If you’re in the market for some dorm-friendly, dining dollar-funded recipes, look no further.

Powerful proteins

When it comes to main dishes for your dorm-style Friendsgiving, there are more options than you might think. If you want to use your dining dollars for your proteins, some options include getting a takeout box from the buffet and filling it up with chicken breast or any other meat choice the dining hall is offering that day. Keeping this in your mini fridge and reheating it in your microwave or building’s oven is an easy way to be responsible for something bigger than napkins.

Another budget-friendly choice is premade and frozen proteins from the market. Whether that's deli meats, frozen chicken or charcuterie platters, there's a variety of choices at your fingertips.

Fun, fiber-packed vegetables

Vegetable-based sides are a necessary part of any well-rounded holiday meal. Luckily for students on campus, you’re not limited by your meal plan, and there are tons of great choices right near your dorm.

The market offers a large number of frozen, fresh and canned vegetables that you’re able to heat up right in your room. With bags of frozen green beans to cans of corn, you can bring all your holiday meal favorites from home straight from the Findlay Commons.

For some more specific recipe ideas, you can get canned cream of mushroom soup, frozen green beans and a small bottle of Berkey Creamery milk, mix it together and heat it up until fully warmed in a microwave-safe dish. Finally, top it with crispy onions, and you have made a green bean casserole.

Or, if casserole isn’t your speed, creamed corn is another easy favorite made with essentials you can easily find on campus. If you mix together canned corn, butter, milk and cream cheese, you have a simple microwave-ready side dish that is acceptable for any holiday function.

Holiday carbs

One of the most delicious parts of the holiday food spread is, hands-down, the carbs. From potatoes and gravy, mac and cheese and stuffing to the rolls, these items can feel make-or-break for the winter festivities. Once again, don’t let living in the dorms discourage you. There are great recipe options everywhere, if you know what to look for.

The market offers a large variety of instant potatoes and microwavable mac and cheese options. Instant mashed potatoes are easily spiced up with some extra milk, butter and salt and can taste as good as the real thing.

If you’re looking to spice up your cup of Kraft to make it taste a bit more oven-baked, you can sprinkle some shredded or sliced cheese on top, pop it back in the microwave, and it will be close to the straight-out-of-the-oven feel.

The Target on W. Beaver Ave. offers options like instant stuffing and a large number of different kinds of rolls for those willing to tread off campus and brave downtown in this cold. (Depending on what day you go to the market, you may be able to find these things there as well.)

Savory or sweet sauces

Of course, holiday meals wouldn’t be complete without cranberry sauce and gravy. Whether it’s the classic canned cranberry jelly or a more homemade spin, this is a big part of many students' holiday meals.

In order to get or make cranberry sauce, you might need to travel downtown to McLanahan's or Target for the ingredients. However, the preparation and cooking can still be done right in your dorm. All you need is cranberries, sugar, water and a microwave-safe bowl. Then just heat and stir until you reach a consistency you like.

For gravy, your options are a lot wider, with flavor packets sold right downtown, but also with all the necessary ingredients right in the commons. If you simply mix together either chicken or beef broth with some butter and cornstarch, you can have a thin gravy that will work on any protein you pick up or on your mashed potatoes.

Delicious desserts

Arguably, many people's favorite part of their big family meals at home is the dessert. From pie to brownies to cookies, there are so many dorm-friendly choices you can find near you.

Penn State students are lucky when it comes to sweet treats because you can easily find whatever you’re looking for right on campus. Whether it’s the full pies sold at the Findlay Commons in East or the large variety of cookies and baked goods at both South and Pollock, the options are endless.

Whatever you do, though, don’t forget to add a scoop of the Creamery’s Vanilla Bean ice cream right on top of your dessert of choice.

title: Off the Record | Meeting the parents
author: Miss Behave I The Daily Collegian
description:
Editor’s Note: Off the record is a weekly column written by a fourth-year Collegian staffer writing under an alias. It aims to promote a space for honest conversations about love, sex and relationships. Those interested in sharing their experiences or submitting a topic are invited to do so through this anonymous form.

With Thanksgiving just around the corner and the winter holidays to follow, many college students are taking a big step in their relationships: introducing their partner to their family.

Whether you’re bringing your partner home for the holidays or you’re meeting your partner’s family, nerves from all parties are normal.

Nerves mean you care, but I’m still here to ease them just a little bit. Here’s some things to keep in mind as you face the daunting rite of passage in your relationship.

Support your partner

When you’re bringing someone home to meet your family, it’s important to support your partner.

It’s unlikely you’re the only nervous one out of the couple, and having each other’s backs during the process is crucial. Parents, grandparents and siblings are unpredictable. While you can hope they ask about your partner’s major and interests, there’s always the possibility they hound them about things they’re uncomfortable sharing.

It’s important to support each other during uncomfortable situations. You’re in this together.

“Prepare” your partner

While the word “prepare” seems to imply “disclaimers,” that’s not exactly what I mean. If you have a weird uncle who makes strange comments or does a turkey dance where he invites members from the crowd at random to join, let your partner know that. I’m not saying you should talk your family down, but all our families have little quirks, and sometimes it’s helpful to inform an outsider ahead of time.

Any family traditions, judgmental family members and common debates that take place around the dinner table are all things you should warn your partner about. When the craziness ensues, at least they will have expected it.

Be yourself

If you’re meeting your partner’s family this holiday season, my biggest piece of advice to you is to be yourself.

Kinzam Khan wrote a piece for The Good Men Project titled “The Psychology of Planning a ‘Meet the Parents’ Moment in Love.” Khan wrote about the pressure of feeling the need to be perfect rather than prioritizing getting to know your partner’s family.

“People start doing the most unnatural thing possible: they stop trying to connect and start trying to perform,” Khan wrote.

Khan explained how you shouldn’t approach the situation with a script. You’re not auditioning for a part or interviewing for a job, and it’s important to remember that human connection will truly thrive when you let your authentic (and polite) self shine.

Know your audience

Along the lines of being polite, it’s important to respect your partner’s family, just as you wish for them to respect you.

While controversial conversations are a prominent part of many holiday celebrations that bring the family together, I would advise you to not pitch one yourself. If they bring up something that offends you, I’m all for you standing your ground. Maybe just avoid being the one to bring up midterm election results.

Bring a small gift

This doesn’t have to be anything crazy, but a small gift shows that you thought about your visit and put effort into making a good first impression.

A box of chocolates, flowers, wine, or a memento related to a hobby the family enjoys are simple ways to show you are interested in bonding with them and aren’t just there for the free plate of food.

Their family is going to remember you didn’t show up to their doorstep empty-handed, and you’ve laid the groundwork for the type of person and partner you are to their precious child.

My last bit of advice is small, but it’s something I think you should keep in mind: don’t force connection. It’s common for people to become close to their partner’s parents and/or siblings, but it’s also important to remember this doesn’t happen right off the bat and, quite frankly, sometimes not at all.

Let bonds build as they please, and don’t put pressure on unreasonable expectations.

All of this goes to say, congratulations on this exciting step in your relationship! Trust that you don’t have to study or prepare extensively for hours — if you bring your manners and authenticity, I have no doubt you will surprise yourself, and meeting the parents will shortly become a worry of the past.

Until next time,

Miss Behave

title: Through small acts, students hope to make big impacts this holiday season
author: Colleen Cratty | The Daily Collegian
description:
Several Penn State service organizations are heading into the holiday season serving dinner, packing toy boxes and exchanging letters.

The holidays create spirit for some people and a sense of distance for others. Members of each group said their goal is to shift people from feeling alone to feeling cared for, whether they be overseas, in the hospital, or at home.

Dear Hero Program

Students in the Dear Hero Program make care packages for active duty troops every semester to help support them during hard times. These care packages include hygiene products, drink packets and non-perishable food items, as well as handwritten letters from members of the organization.

Spencer Graham, 26, of Clearfield, Pennsylvania, is the president of the organization and joined to support the troops after being a service member himself.

“You miss home, you get homesick and it’s really easy to lose track of the support that you have,” Graham, a fourth-year studying industrial engineering, said. “No one’s patting you on the back.”

He reflected on his experiences and shared that the holidays can be especially tough for those who are actively in service. Graham said that he missed his family and community extra during those times, so sending care packages can brighten people’s days more than one might expect.

Graham also mentioned events they’ve held in the past for Veterans Day, like a collaboration with 814 Cider Works. Last year, they held an event with the cidery where they received a lot of donations and ended up raising enough money to cover the costs of shipping for the care packages.

He also noted the importance of the letters that they send with the care packages. Graham said that they recently worked with Schreyer for Women on writing the cards.

“One of the most important things that I pushed for as president is to get a lot of letters,” Graham said. “Being on the receiving end of those when we were out at sea, I know it makes a big difference.”

Alpha Phi Omega

Alpha Phi Omega is the biggest co-ed service fraternity at Penn State. They hold multiple events during the holiday season to spread cheer around the State College community.

Their most significant event coming up is their Thanksgiving meal for the unhoused that is in partnership with a local homeless shelter called Out of the Cold. The fraternity has hosted many events with the shelter, but this is their second year doing a Thanksgiving dinner with them.

The members go to the shelter, cook food and have genuine conversations with the attendees. President Jay Mattis, 21, of Delmont, Pennsylvania, remarked on the importance of these discussions.

“It was pretty humbling to hear a lot of their backstories and the perseverance that they go through,” Mattis, a third-year studying architectural engineering, said. “It’s become a well-liked event within the fraternity and something we are hoping to make a staple tradition.”

Out of the Cold’s mission is to open doors to any of the unhoused population of State College. The direct focus of the event is to put food on the tables for individuals who cannot afford it or are going through rough times, Mattis said.

He added that this event correlates perfectly with the mission of Alpha Phi Omega. Its three cardinal principles are leadership, friendship and service. The event reflects those values, he said, by leading the efforts of making food and sharing camaraderie with the community.

“It might not seem like a big effort by me or by the fraternity, but even an hour to two hours can significantly change someone’s holiday season,” Mattis said. “Maybe they didn’t have anyone to talk to, and now they have a warm meal and people to talk to to distract from what’s going on in their life.”

Jared Box Project Club

Jared Box Project Club comes together to make and decorate boxes filled with toys, games and other items that are given to families with young children in the hospital.

“The hope is to provide a little bit of comfort and smiles,” Dianna Halloran, 20, of State College, said. “Not only for the kids in the hospital, but also for the families so they know that there’s support, people that back them and someone’s always thinking of them.”

Halloran, the president of the club, said that during the holidays they like to decorate the lids with fun holiday cartoons.

She said the club started in State College with Jared McMullen, a child hospitalized due to a brainstem tumor. The club has since spread all over the nation.

McMullen would fill his backpack with toys and share them with the other children, and the club aims to carry on his legacy, Halloran, a third-year studying economics and supply chain information systems, said.

Halloran said she feels honored to be part of an organization where the sole purpose is just to do good. She added it’s exciting to feel like she’s part of something bigger, as there are so many hospitals around the nation that participate.

“I think so often there is this gloss of the holiday season, everything is cheery, but the reality is that there’s always hardships even during the holiday season,” Halloran said. “If someone is in the hospital during the holiday season, hopefully a Jared Box can bring a smile to a kid’s face.”

Letters to Beverly

The Letters to Beverly club connects generations by pairing students with a resident at a local retirement home to be pen pals. The organization members write letters back and forth across the whole year, with some going out right before holiday break.

Natalie Isett, 22, of Palmyra, Pennsylvania, is the founder and vice-president of the club. She started the organization because she used to write letters to her grandmother, Beverly.

“We just picked up the letters for the first time and I think people are really excited to receive mail and hear from people,” Isett, a fourth-year studying business analytics and information systems, said. “Our whole goal is to bring some happiness to their days and make them feel connected to someone.”

The club’s president, Katherine Potter, 20, of Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, said they also have plans to make Thanksgiving-themed cards to send to the nursing home they are partnered with, Wynwood House.

“I think the holidays are the most important times for family, connection and love,” Potter, a third-year studying finance and accounting, said. “That’s why we started doing the cards this year with each letter. So, in case somebody isn’t able to write back, at least they have the card and they feel loved and thought of.”

Isett added that American culture is so fast paced that people often forget about older generations. She said it’s important to maintain a connection with them, and Letters to Beverly is just a small part of that.

“They have so much knowledge and stories to tell that it’s just beautiful to be able to connect with them,” Isett said.

title: Students reflect on popular fanfiction site going down
author: Hailey Weber | For the Collegian
description:
You excitedly open a tab to your favorite website, ready to continue reading a fan-written story about two characters from your favorite TV series. But there's nothing. No signs of the treasure trove of fan-formed content you once knew.

This scenario played out for many on Oct. 29, 2026, when the creators of a prolific fanfiction website, Archive of Our Own (AO3), announced that its website had experienced “an intrusion” upon its website going offline. AO3 said no user data has been deleted or stolen, according to a message that was displayed on the site.

As of Nov. 15, the AO3 website is back up and running. AO3 published a statement on its website that said no data has been deleted, but some features are temporarily disabled to bring back the site earlier than originally anticipated. AO3 said the missing features will be restored; and readers can refer to a status page to get more information on the site’s return.

Sophia Andahazy, 19, of Mountain Top, Pennsylvania, said she read fanfiction for the first time in middle school. Andahazy said she feels personally connected to fanfiction and enjoys both reading and writing it.

Andahazy, a second-year studying journalism and political science, believes that one of the main appeals of fanfiction is the ability to be creative and explore alternate realities. She finds it interesting to be able to use one’s imagination to create all sorts of different scenarios that might not exist in the actual media.

She said the shutdown of AO3 caused an interruption in people's daily reading routines and caused panic, thinking they would not be able to finish their current story due to the shutdown.

“Maybe you're reading a certain fanfiction, and you’re on chapter four of 17, and then it gets shut down,” Andahazy said. “So now you can’t finish your fanfiction, what are you gonna do?”

Andahazy also said websites like AO3 foster a sense of community above all else. She said reading fanfiction creates a special chance to bond with someone you may not have previously bonded with.

“It's that kind of exciting feeling that you get to talk about something niche or that other people might not get, with someone who really gets it.” Andahazy said.

Elise Crumpton, 18, of Midlothian, Texas, shared a similar story in her experience with fanfiction. She remembered exploring fanfiction the most in 2020 when the COVID-19 pandemic hit and she used fanfiction to keep herself entertained during the shutdown.

Crumpton, a first-year studying nuclear engineering, said her favorite aspect of fanfiction is the community it builds around its readers because people can find a sense of belonging through the shared love of favorite characters and fan theories.

However, Crumpton said fanfiction can get a bad reputation for being too vulgar or overly graphic. She said there is much more to fanfiction than meets the eye and that minority groups have found belonging in fanfiction.

“It's more mainstream than it's ever been,” Crumpton said. “But at its core, fanfiction is built by these communities that are not super respected in the public eye."

Crumpton said fanfiction gives readers and writers the ability to world-build and create representation not explicitly written in the original plot. Crumpton said most readers are drawn to AO3 as opposed to other popular fanfiction sites, like Wattpad, because it’s less commercialized and “gimmicky.”

“Everyone who works on it is a volunteer," Crumpton said. "It's not for profit. The people that are in charge of the website are in the community with you. It's not these corporate people that are separated from you — they're just normal people, which gives AO3 a lot of its trustworthiness.”

Alexandra Snyder, 18, of West Chester, Pennsylvania, said she read fanfiction when she was younger.

“Back in 2020 and 2022, I would read it a lot,” Snyder, a first-year studying advertising/public

relations, said. “It was really cool to see people my age who were writing these in-depth, professional stories. I fell in love with it.”

Snyder really enjoyed the concept of self-insert stories, fanfictions where the reader’s name is included, and they get to become a part of the story themselves. She said being able to create a situation where you’re interacting with a character you love is a very interesting concept.

Snyder prefers AO3 to any other fanfiction website, and she appreciates that the tag feature easily allows readers to find specific stories or tropes they enjoy. She said the large database is what makes it stand out, and people were hurt by the unexpected shutdown because something that was habitual for many suddenly disappeared.

“It's like the equivalent of losing a hobby you once had,” Snyder said. “Now you're in a position where fanfiction was in your routine, and now you don’t have that anymore. I feel like people are valid for reacting so strongly because it's a community that people can have online, and that kind of just disappears so suddenly.”

title: As Bill Pickle’s Taproom turns 21, it’s ‘throwing a party, and everyone is invited’
author: Hadley Louisa-mae Milhomme | For the Collegian
description:
Bill Pickle's Taproom is celebrating its 21st anniversary as a downtown State College staple.

Throughout the month of November, Pickle’s will be featuring a throwback menu, including food, drinks and shots straight off of their original 2005 menu. Other ways Pickle's is commemorating its history is through new merchandise, brand promos and weekly giveaways.

The restaurant was founded in 2005 by Mike Desmond, who converted a long-standing women’s and men’s clothing store called Desmond LTD into Bill Pickle's Taproom at 106 S. Allen St. Pickle’s is owned by Pat Croce and Company Property, along with other popular downtown destinations like the Allen Street Grill and The Basement Nightspot.

Desmond was inspired by local Penn State cult figure William “Bill Pickle” Gilliland. Gilliland was a local legend in the 1800s Prohibition era, working as a janitor and hustler famously suspected of bootlegging liquor to students and alumni on football weekends.

The restaurant has been beloved ever since its opening, with recurring customers returning due to its atmosphere, and the community continues to grow year after year.

Fermin Almeida, 28, of Los Angeles, has been working as the marketing director for Pickle's for over two years and described his time as “two and a half years of a lot of fun.” Almeida said that all of the giveaways, tote bags and events throughout the three week celebration are ways to thank the customers who keep coming back.

“We’ve done weddings, graduations, we’ve had so many memorable memories with people and it’s so diverse too," Almeida said. "You know, it’s from college students to professionals to people who are now near retirement. Everyone is welcome, it’s not for sinners, not for saints. So, it’s for everyone who wants to have a good old time.”

Almeida said the staff is equivalent to a family, and employees are a part of each other’s lives outside of work in meaningful ways. This stands true for employee Emily Knoepfel, 24, of Clarks Summit, Pennsylvania, who worked at The Basement Nightspot for five years but began working at Pickle's in January.

“My coworkers, they are like family to me," Knoepfel said. "It was very easy to feel like a community within our coworkers. Everyone is welcoming here. We do have our own little sense of community.”

Knoepfel said this togetherness is what draws customers in and keeps them coming back. The regulars are what makes Pickle’s feel like home, she added, as customers can bond together to watch the football games or have somewhere to go after the games.

She said this makes celebrating 21 years particularly special.

“I think the fact that Pickle’s has been around for 21 years, that in itself is something you may not see a lot in a town like this," Knoepfel said. "There’s a lot of turnover, a lot of change. I have had a lot of alumni come back, and they were back here in 2005 or 2010.”

Alumni and returning customers are always amazed by how much State College has changed since their last visit, but Pickle’s has stayed a consistent staple in the college town, Knoepfel said.

She also said the staff’s biggest priority is making sure that everyone feels safe, welcome and enjoys their time at Bill Pickle's Taproom.

Conner Dolphin, 21, of State College, said that Pickle’s is the best bar in State College "hands down."

“The drinks here are incredible, the deals are great," Dolphin, a third-year studying communications, said. "I love that they have consistent pricing. The vibe here is always great, the music here is always going. It’s never busy enough that you can’t get in, but it’s busy enough that you have a good time.”

Although Dolphin studies at Penn State’s Altoona campus, he frequently visits State College and plans a stop at Pickle’s.

Whether you have been dining at Pickle’s for decades, or have yet to try the establishment, Almeida said the impact of Pickle’s success for 21 years is something worth celebrating.

“Our staff is throwing a party, and everyone is invited," Almeida said.

title: Preview | No. 7 Penn State women’s hockey looks to defend home ice against Delaware
author: Luci Palacios | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions are looking to get back in the win column as they prepare to host Delaware for a two-game series at Pegula Ice Arena: The blue and white will face the Blue Hens at 6 p.m. Thursday, followed by a 4 p.m. matchup Friday.

Coming into the series, Penn State is 10-4 overall and 8-2 in AHA play. The Nittany Lions currently sit at the top of the conference standings and rank No. 7 in the USCHO Poll for the second consecutive week.

Delaware, meanwhile, has had a difficult start to its season. The Blue Hens enter the series with a 4-11-1 overall record and a 2-8 conference record. They currently sit at the bottom of the AHA standings and are looking to snap a five-game losing streak.

With a 2-5-1 record on the road, Delaware will have its work cut out for it against a Penn State team that has been strong throughout conference play.

The last time the two teams met was earlier this year when Penn State earned a dominant 7-0 victory on Jan. 24. The Nittany Lions also hold a 4-0 advantage in the all-time series since Delaware joined the AHA in 2024.

The Blue Hens have struggled to find consistency this season and will be looking to turn things around against Penn State.

Penn State is coming off a split series against Mercyhurst. The Nittany Lions earned a 7-2 win on Nov. 13 before falling 3-0 the following day. The loss marked the first time Penn State had been shutout since the 2024-25 season. Mercyhurst also outshot Penn State 21-18, marking the first time since Oct. 10 that the Nittany Lions had been outshot by an opponent.

Despite the loss, the blue and white have shown that their offense can be difficult to contain. Penn State has recorded 46 goals this season and averages 3.29 goals and 35.79 shots per game.

Grace Outwater leads the team with nine goals, while Abby Stonehouse follows closely with eight. Just as important as goals are assists, sophomore Sophie Morrow leads the team with 14 assists.

The Nittany Lions have also seen production from multiple players throughout their lineup. During their 7-2 win over Mercyhurst, seven different players found the back of the net, including three power-play goals.

Penn State’s success hasn’t only come from its ability to score. The blue and white have won 413 of their 784 faceoffs, or 52.7% of chances on the draw. Defensively, freshman Megan Hosman leads the team with 22 blocked shots. In net, sophomore Maddy Campbell and freshman Morgan Stickney have shared responsibilities throughout the season.

Campbell has recorded 130 saves with a .929 save percentage, while Stickney has 155 saves and a .923 save percentage. Having two reliable options in goal gives the Nittany Lions another advantage heading into the weekend.

Delaware will need to find a way to slow down Penn State’s offensive production if it hopes to compete with the blue and white. The Blue Hens have scored just 24 goals this season while allowing 44, averaging 1.5 goals and 18.8 shots per game.

On defense, Lexie Lonask leads Delaware with 46 blocked shots, followed by Tiana McIntyre with 30. Despite the lack of offense, the defense is doing what it takes to limit scoring opportunities.

The weekend series also allows Delaware to turn its season around against one of the conference’s top teams. However, Penn State’s offensive depth, strong goaltending and advantage in the all-time series could make that a difficult task.

title: Preview | Penn State women’s basketball searches for first win against Bowling Green
author: Sienna Pearce | For the Collegian
description:
The Lady Lions, who sit at an abysmal 0-4 record this season, will try their luck against the Bowling Green Falcons Thursday at 11 a.m in Rec Hall.

The matchup marks coach Tanisha Wright’s debut in the storied venue. The only other time the two teams have met was in 1995, and Penn State won 88-75. The Lady Lions will either start a winning streak or watch their shots wind up in the gutter.

Penn State

The Lady Lions are adjusting to the new dynamic under Wright. They nearly won their home opener, as the Cleveland State Vikings barely managed a 62-61 victory.

The blue and white fought hard, especially sophomore guard and Vanderbilt transfer Ava Black, who earned 17 points and 10 rebounds for Penn State.

Penn State had a rough few days in Ohio after falling to the Cincinnati Bearcats in a 76-53 loss and wrapping up the road trip with a 77-71 loss against the Dayton Flyers. The Lady Lions were plagued by shooting errors, adding up to 17 turnovers when they faced the Bearcats. However, forward Petra Božan’s performance in the next matchup against the Flyers was a silver lining, as the junior managed a career-high with 27 points.

On Monday, the Lady Lions traveled to the desert to play the Arizona State Sun Devils. The blue and white began to lose momentum in the first quarter after it allowed the Sun Devils to gain the upper hand with a 23-13 lead to close out the first quarter. The Lady Lions failed to bounce back from this rough start, as they began the second half with six turnovers. The last time they lost by 40 or more points was last season against Michigan, 105-65.

Penn State has now lowered its record to 0-2 in its series history against Arizona State with the 85-41 loss, which lowered the program to its worst start in history.

Bowling Green

The Falcons have been flying high this season, going undefeated in the beginning stretch of their season. Bowling Green opened its season with an 82-59 win over the Georgia Southern Eagles.

Freshmen Carol Silva and Sarah Caetano both managed double-doubles and led scoring. Silva scored the most with 25 points, while Caetano put up 10 points.

Bowling Green carried that momentum into the second game that week, winning by four over the Cleveland State Vikings, 77-73. Bowling Green took the lead with a pair of free throws, sealing their victory.

The Falcons left the Lawrence Tech Blue Devils in the dust Monday with an impressive 120-38 victory.

Freshman forward Aurelie Vanderstraeten was a standout, scoring a total of 18 points. Bowling Green also forced 33 turnovers, 25 of which were from steals. Freshman guard Sophie Alexander was responsible for 10 of those swipes alone.

As the Falcons prepare to hit the road for the first time this season, they will need to keep their winning streak alive outside the comfort of Stroh Center. The 2026-2027 season marks the fourth season with Fred Chmiel as the Falcons' head coach. Last season, he led his team to a 17-14 winning record, and had a hand in Johnea Donahue winning MAC’s Defensive Player of the Year.

Before Chmiel coached for Bowling Green, he spent eight years as an assistant coach for South Carolina. The Gamecocks boasted a 247-32 overall record during this time.

Chmiel is also no stranger to Happy Valley, as he was an assistant coach for the Lady Lions from 2010-2014. During his time here, Chmiel was a part of a Penn State team that booked trips to the NCAA Sweet 16 in the 2011-2012 and 2013-2014 seasons.

title: Janecke wins gold, Hall wins bronze at women’s IIHF World Championships
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State forward Nicole Hall and alumni Tessa Janecke represented their respective nations at this year's IIHF Women’s World Championship. Hall represented Team Sweden, while Janecke took the ice for Team USA.

Both teams made deep pushes through the tournament, but both players’ performances were vastly different.

Here’s how both players performed.

Tessa Janecke

Tessa Janecke’s appearance in this year's World Championships marked the fourth of her career. The forward has no shortage of success on the international stage, winning IIHF gold in 2025 and 2023, with a silver in 2024. Janecke also won an Olympic gold medal with Team USA in this year’s games.

Janecke and Team USA kicked off their four preliminary-round matches with a scorching start. The USA defeated their opponents by a combined score of 31-2. Janecke impressed in every game, notching five assists and two goals while going four consecutive games with an assist.

Janecke solidified her role as a playmaker within an established group of forwards. In a group with players like Hilary Knight, Taylor Fox and Kelly Pannek, the depth that Janecke added proved costly through the tournament.

While Janecke contributed no points to the stat sheet, USA still dominated Denmark 14-0 in the quarterfinal. The Orangeville, Illinois, native followed up with a bounce-back performance in the semifinal against Finland, adding two more assists to her tally. The performance earned Janecke Player of the Game.

Janecke delivered one more assist in the championship match against Canada, contributing to a 6-2 blowout win.

The performance resulted in Janecke adding a third gold medal to her trophy room. The forward will soon make her PWHL debut on Dec. 6 with the Vegas Vanguards after she was selected No. 3 overall.

Nicole Hall

Nicole Hall’s first appearance in the senior World Championships was underwhelming to say the least.

While the USA excelled on both ends of the rink, Sweden had an up-and-down tournament. Sweden suffered defeat to Canada in their first preliminary stage match, but rebounded with three wins against Finland, Denmark and Japan to start 3-1.

In Sweden’s 5-1 loss to Canada, it was outshot 41-14, with Hall taking two of them. Hall notched 25 penalty minutes in total and didn’t finish the match after receiving a five-minute major for slew-footing and a game misconduct at 16:46 of the second period.

The forward was absent from the official game lineup in Sweden’s 4-1 win against Finland. There is no confirmed reason why Hall was left off the lineup, but her ejection against Canada may have played a part in head coach Erika Holst’s decision.

Yet, the Stockholm, Sweden, native didn’t allow the ejection to affect her following performance: She posted her best single-game numbers of the tournament. In her third group stage match, Hall finally appeared on the stat sheet with two goals of her own in the 10-0 win against Denmark.

Hall struggled to contribute through the rest of the tournament, while Sweden as a whole reached the third-place game after narrowly beating Switzerland 1-0 and losing 3-0 to Canada.

In the Bronze medal game, Sweden went down 1-0 late in the second period, but equalized with six minutes left in regulation, forcing the game to go to an overtime period. In the shootout, they won 2-1 to secure a bronze medal.

Although Hall had minimal impact, she won her first IIHF bronze medal of her career.

title: Series history | Penn State carries dominance in over 100 years of games against Rutgers
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Penn State and Rutgers will play for the 36th time in the programs’ history on Saturday.

The Nittany Lions hold a 33-2 advantage in a matchup dating back over 100 years. They’ve won 18 straight games against the Scarlet Knights, a streak that began in 1989.

Here’s a look at the lopsided series history between Penn State and Rutgers.

Penn State’s dominance in the 1900s

The two teams squared off 24 times in the 20th century, with Penn State holding a 22-2 advantage during that time.

In the Nittany Lions’ two national championship years, they took down Rutgers in commanding fashion in both. The 49-14 win in 1982 and 31-6 victory in 1986 were two of the largest margins of victories in the series at the time.

The biggest win in the 1900s was a 45-7 win by Penn State in East Rutherford, New Jersey, in Joe Paterno’s first game against Rutgers since becoming the Nittany Lions’ head coach 11 years prior. A 15-12 win by Penn State to open the 1984 season was the closest of the matchups and lowest total score since the Nittany Lions won 7-6 against the Scarlet Knights in 1952.

Penn State’s dominance over Rutgers was also prevalent in the Paterno era, and it only lost to Rutgers one time.

Rutgers’ two wins

Rutgers has two wins in the series that span exactly 70 years apart, with the Scarlet Knights taking the first game ever played between the two squads in 1918 while also winning in 1988.

Penn State fell 26-3 in the first ever meeting, and it wasn’t until 1950 that the teams played again. It is the lowest scoring performance by the Nittany Lions in the series and Rutgers’ largest margin of victory.

The Scarlet Knights’ other win was a 21-16 victory in which they relied on a pass-heavy offense, being one of the first teams to do so.

Penn State even had a chance to win it, forming a lengthy drive that started from the 10-yard line. But a pass from quarterback Tony Sacca to wide receiver Michael Timpson went high and the comeback effort was put to rest.

Since then, Rutgers hasn’t won against Penn State, as the Nittany Lions now have their longest winning streak in the series.

Penn State undefeated in Big Ten

Since Rutgers joined the Big Ten in 2014, it hasn’t beaten one of its closest geographical Big Ten foes. The teams have met 11 times, playing every year except for 2024.

This 11-0 mark has shown the difference between the two squads in the modern era. Penn State has consistently been one of the top teams in the country, while Rutgers has typically been in the bottom of the Big Ten.

The recent history includes a 2022 matchup in which the Nittany Lions won 55-10 on the road. Nick Singleton had a 100-yard kickoff return touchdown, while both Sean Clifford and Drew Allar had rushing touchdowns, with Allar playing late in the game when the score was out of hand. The 45-point margin of victory is the largest in the series.

The last time the programs met in Beaver Stadium was in 2023, where Kaytron Allen notched two rushing touchdowns and quarterback Beau Pribula added another. Pribula was Penn State’s leading rusher in the game after Allar left with an injury.

The James Franklin era of Penn State was dominant against Rutgers. Whether that continues under Matt Campbell is unknown, but he’ll have his first crack at the Scarlet Knights at 3:30 p.m. Saturday in Beaver Stadium.

title: Penn State News Literacy Initiative works to improve media, news literacy among community
author: Jacob Godshall I The Daily Collegian
description:
The news landscape has always been fast-paced and difficult to navigate for some. With the popularity of social media platforms and the increasing frequency in artificial intelligence-produced content, that difficulty may be increasing.

Penn State’s News Literacy Initiative has been working with students and community members to increase their media and news literacy. From Oct. 26 to 30, the News Literacy Initiative hosted its Media Literacy Week, geared toward college and high school students and State College residents.

Cory Barker, the organizer and director of Media Literacy Week, said AI may be one of the most topical issues in news literacy, but it isn’t the only issue or obstacle. Barker said it’s important to realize which companies own what outlets, and what publications are owned by the same company.

“Just understanding the degree at which that concentrated ownership really dictates what we see and how we see it, and how it shapes our beliefs about the world, even if we are not really thinking about it that way (is important),” Barker, 38, of Hartford City, Indiana, said.

Barker said the current issues in the news industry result from structural and financial systems that incentivize news stations to be “loud, dumb, fast and hyperbolic.” He said the difficult part of achieving news literacy is education, because it requires the consumer to put in the extra work on their own and be constantly “diligent and reflective.”

He said people should be able to look deeper into a story and understand why you’re seeing it, but not get to a point where they think “everything sucks.”

“It doesn't mean that you have to hate media, or hate your own taste and only read neoclassic literature or whatever,” Barker said. “That's not what being media literate is.”

As part of the week, students from Penn State visited State College Area High School and spoke to students there about news and media literacy. Veronica Chan, 20, of Mount Pocono, Pennsylvania, who spoke at the high school, said most of the conversations centered around influencers and AI.

The biggest obstacle to news literacy for the average Penn State student is the bias that is present in much of the media we consume, Chan, a third-year student studying advertising and public relations, said.

“If you consume news through a specific person, a lot of the time they're really biased, and they'll cherry-pick what information they tell you. And it's just really easy to believe that influencer or that news station,” Chan said.

Jeff Knapp, 59, of State College, Pennsylvania, said that doing individual research is critical to news literacy. Knapp, the Larry and Ellen Foster librarian for communications, said it isn’t always as easy as people think to determine whether or not a source is trustworthy or biased.

He said people tend to think legacy news publications are more trustworthy or reliable, but that isn’t really the case.

“A lot of them are just creating a lot of what I call SEO content — search engine optimized content,” Knapp said, “If you just happen to say ‘Iran war, what's going on over there?’, they'll have a great story that will be teed up and probably come right to the top of your sources. But the journalism, the writing, it's not as incisive as it used to be.”

Knapp also said that biases in news have and always will be an issue, and readers need to keep that in mind.

Chan added that many people, particularly students, have become “news fatigued,” as they’re presented with so much information that they don’t bother doing extra research on it. She said she worries that some people simply don’t care to do their research to confirm a story or claim, and will just agree and go about spreading misinformation themselves.

“Research anything you think is too extreme to be true,” Chan said. “If there's numbers and statistics involved, definitely look up multiple sources, not just your own.”

title: Sports Editors Weekly | Can Penn State women’s soccer make a deep NCAA Tournament run?
author: Myles Hannak & Gianna Dowling | Sports Editors
description:
For a 32nd consecutive year, Penn State is headed to the NCAA Tournament.

2015 National Champion Erica Dambach’s unit returns after a season in which the Nittany Lions finished 9-4-5 and suffered elimination in the Big Ten Tournament Quarterfinals by Purdue. The blue and white welcome Villanova in the NCAA First Round to Jeffrey Field — where Penn State also holds an undefeated record.

After making it to the national postseason in all but one season since the program's inception in 1995, what should the expectations be for Dambach’s unit?

Gianna Dowling: A run could be made

Penn State is led by a coach who knows the postseason like the back of her hand. Making the NCAA Tournament has become an every-season expectation for the Nittany Lions. However, it’s become a matter of how far they can go.

I think the blue and white have the leadership and star power to compete with almost any team in the 64-team field, but that’s not to say it won’t be easy. Penn State got a tough first-round draw, hosting Big East champion Villanova.

However, entering the tournament, I expect the Nittany Lions to have vengeance on their minds and if Dambach’s squad gets past the first two rounds, a potential rematch with Purdue awaits.

Penn State tied the Boilermakers in their regular-season matchup, but Purdue defeated the blue and white in overtime of the Big Ten tournament opening round. The Boilermakers ended up winning the conference crown, so I have no doubt this is a game the Nittany Lions wish to have back.

Another team I have circled in Penn State’s portion of the bracket is top-seed Ohio State. The Nittany Lions faced the Buckeyes on Sep. 10 and fell by a slight 1-0 margin

My final reason for confidence is that the Nittany Lions have already been battle-tested. They’ve competed with and even beaten top teams in the field. Penn State has the preparation and it should have a vengeful mindset; it's for these reasons I believe the Nittany Lions can surprise a lot of people and make a tournament run.

Myles Hannak: Too tough a field

The blue and white could very well be upset in the first round; Villanova boasts the Big East title in a season in which it was only defeated once over 20 games — what makes the Nittany Lions think they can do the same?

The Wildcats are running off five straight wins, a streak that extends three weeks; the outlook is too insurmountable for a Penn State team that couldn’t turn a strong regular season finish into a Big Ten tournament run. Sure, the Nittany Lions have the edge in freshness, but Villanova has the form.

Let’s say the Park Avenue Army gets the Nittany Lions past a game which looks like a forecasted upset; then the blue and white look scheduled to face Texas Tech, another game that looks like an uphill battle.

I like the pieces on attack and in defense, but I find it hard to believe a team which scored the 86th most goals in the nation and has the 52nd best goals-against average possesses the skills to go deep on the national scene.

title: No. 7 Penn State women’s volleyball offense shines in regular-season finale
author: Joey Bolger | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State returned to Rec Hall for its regular season finale after being on the road the past two weeks, going undefeated with three ranked wins over the span.

The Nittany Lions concluded its regular season with a sweep over the Scarlet Knights, extending its win streak to 10.

“It’s nice to win at home,” said coach Katie Schumacer-Cawley. “And we’re looking forward to what’s ahead with the conference tournament.”

The Nittany Lions are a force to be reckoned with and are a serious contender heading into the inaugural Big Ten women’s volleyball tournament, which will be held on Nov. 20 and conclude on the 25.

The blue-and-white looked unstoppable on offense, with 52 kills and a .416 hitting percentage. Kennedy Martin, Kendall Northern and Emmi Sellman each ended the night with double-digit kills.

“I think that we’re making smarter decisions while hitting, mixing up our shots a lot more,” said Northern. “Just finding different ways to score rather than just like trying to power the ball through the block.”

The Nittany Lions spread the ball around well against the Scarlett Knights, with everyone contributing on offense; this was one of the few matches all season where Penn State had three players with double-digit kills.

“We’re passing well too, and finding ways to, you know, everyone’s getting a piece of it,” said Schumacher-Cawley.

During the first set, the Penn State offense had 19 kills with a .484 hitting percentage. Sellman had six of her 10 kills in the first while Northern had four of her 10. This was the second time all season Sellman and Northern had double-digit kills in a match.

Martin led the team with 15 kills with a .500 hitting percentage. The Big Ten player of the week had three kills in the first set but contributed on defense with an early block. She turned it up in the next two sets, adding 12 more kills and two more blocks.

Martin was recently named a National Player of the Year Semifinalist last week and leads the Big Ten in points, kills, points per set and kills per set during in-conference play.

Another big factor in this offense’s success against Rutgers was setter Alexis Stucky; she ended the night with 43 assists, two kills and 12 digs.

“I think that Stucky moved the ball around well, and we were one-on-one and taking some good high swings, and just worked hard,” said Schumacher-Cawley

The Florida transfer has been on fire throughout the Nittany Lion’s win streak. Stucky only had two games under 40 assists and also notched a season-high 55 assists in back-to-back games against Minnesota and Wisconsin.

The connection between Stucky and Northern on the slide attack was electric, and the Scarlet Knights seemed to have no answer for it throughout the match.

“The slide we worked on a lot and like runs in front,” said Northern. “I think that she just sets me up really well.”

The teamwork for the Nittany Lions could be the intangible aspect needed in their play to propel a deep Big Ten Tournament run.

“I think that they, you know, both worked really hard in transition,” said Schumacher-Cawley. “I thought Gin was, you know, digging and putting the ball in a good spot; we were able to transition and kill.”

Now on a 10-game win streak, the blue-and-white look to keep pressing on the gas pedal heading into the Big Ten and NCAA tournament.
