title: Business owners, entrepreneurs come together, trade advice during fifth annual Business After Hours
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
Around 200 people, many of them small business owners and entrepreneurs, came to the Eric J. Barron Innovation Hub to attend the fifth annual Business After Hours community networking event as part of wider Global Entrepreneurship Week activities occurring in several Pennsylvania counties.

The week, which has been held internationally since 2008 and was picked up by Penn State a year later, is organized and run by the university’s Penn State Small Business Development Center (SBDC). Business After Hours is a joint effort between the SBDC, Invent Penn State, the Chamber of Business and Industry for Centre County (CBICC), Centre Region Entrepreneur Network and Happy Valley Changemakers Collective.

Todd Dolbin, CBICC’s vice president of economic development, said the amount of attendees at Business After Hours shows a desire from community members, as well as Penn State, to support small and “early stage” businesses in State College and throughout Centre County. He said that the event helps show what resources and knowledge the university has to offer entrepreneurs and business owners.

“It shows the breaking down of silos and that we're in this community together and that we're working together to grow our local economic ecosystem,” Dolbin, 46, of State College, Pennsylvania, said. “The university brings an incredible amount of resources to our area, and for our local businesses to be able to tap into the university for that expertise really makes a big difference in helping them grow.”

SBDC Director Tim Keohane said prior to Business After Hours, many of Penn State’s previous Global Entrepreneurship Week events were mainly focused on students before beginning to branch out into surrounding communities. He said this has allowed for students, and especially student entrepreneurs, to speak with business owners and get advice based on their experiences, which Keohane described as “invaluable.”

“For a student entrepreneur or even a community member who's thinking about starting a business, everything looks great on the outside but it's not necessarily as easy as people might think to start a business and operate it successfully,” Keohane, 56, of Lock Haven, Pennsylvania, said. “Having that input from people that have been doing it, and gone through the highs and the lows, and have still come out on the other side and sustained what they're growing with their business, I think, is the real value there.”

Marc Warren, 70, of Boalsburg, Pennsylvania, said he and his friend and fellow business owner, George McMurtry, both chose to attend this year’s Business After Hours to see what new businesses have sprung up in State College and the surrounding areas.

Warren, who along with his wife, Tracy, has run the client and employee feedback and retention company Client Intel, formerly Customer Follow Up, Inc., since 1996, said he is familiar with the obstacles to running a business and found how challenging it can be to overcome them to be why “everybody always quits too soon.”

He said the best advice he could give entrepreneurs and new business owners was to remain persistent and to be clear on why they went into business.

“If it's to show somebody you can do it, or it's something cool about it, that's not enough. Your heart has to be in it,” Warren said. “It gets hard. It gets challenging. But you learn.”

Luke Dudeck said he heard about Business After Hours from a classmate in his MGMT 425 class and chose to attend the event to get feedback on his entry into the class’s pitch competition.

Along with having student entrepreneurs be willing to put themselves out there, Dudeck, a fourth-year studying mechanical engineering, said Business After Hours also showed him the importance of viewing everyone as a potential opportunity to get assistance with their business ideas by first showing interest.

“I think it made me realize that I need to get out there more and put my foot forward first and foremost because sometimes people aren't going to come up to you,” Dudeck said. “I think it's really important to keep a really engaged tone and be more interested in them than you are about yourself, because you want to learn from everyone possible in your life's crossings in business, and just in life in general.”

title: Penn State's Josh Barr focused on self-improvement ahead of NWCA All-Star Classic with teammates
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
With the NWCA All-Star Classic approaching, five Penn State wrestlers will prepare to compete in the yearly competition.

The event will be an opportunity for the Nittany Lions to face the best of the best early in the season. Josh Barr will face a familiar opponent at the NWCA All-Star Classic, as he is set to face Little Rock’s Stephen Little.

“I kind of look at every single match the same," Barr said. "I know it's cliche to say that, but for me, it's not really so much about who I'm wrestling. It's about what I'm doing, where I'm going, and just trying to improve on little things that I've been working on.”

The two faced off at the 2026 Southern Scuffle final last season, where Barr routed Little in a 9-1 win by major decision to take the 197-pound title, his first match of the season after returning from injury. Yet, Barr’s approach to the match is simply as if it were any other bout this season.

Barr is more focused on his personal improvement, noting that he spent an ample amount of time this offseason working on the deficiencies in his skill set. Barr still had nothing but respect for Little, who is a very talented wrestler in his own right.

“Stephen's obviously very tough,” Barr said. “He's ranked, I think, two or three in the country, and yeah, wrestled a couple times. He's been tough every single time we wrestled.”

Little is currently ranked as the No. 3 wrestler at 197 pounds, and undefeated so far in both dual meet and open tournament competitions. At the Cowboy Invitational, Little went 3-0, winning the 197-pound title.

The Trojan cruised through SIUE’s Nico Ronchetti by a 20-5 tech fall, Oklahoma State’s Austin Johnson 11-4 in the semifinals and Oklahoma State’s No. 2 Cody Merril due to medical forfeit in the final.

Barr is grateful for the opportunity to face a competitive opponent not only to earn a ranked win, but to test what's in his arsenal.

“He's a really good guy to try to do stuff on because you know those are the guys that you want the new stuff to work on,” Barr said. “So good opportunity for me to try some things by working on and just excited for it.”

Alongside Barr, PJ Duke was a late entrant into the match. Initially, Oklahoma’s Paddy Gallagher and Michigan’s Cam Catrabone were set to face off as the 165-pound matchup on Nov. 24. However, Duke will replace Gallagher, which sets up a rematch of Duke and Catrabone’s meeting last season.

Duke narrowly defeated Catrabone 12-10, where he picked up a takedown during the final 15 seconds to leave with the victory. Barr said that Duke is “ready to go all the time.”

“Yeah, I think we're just always prepared for whatever's in front of us,” Barr said. “All my teammates are ready to go all the time, so I think it just speaks to our preparation and PJ is just ready to go.”

Preparation is what Duke will need in a matchup against the No. 5 wrestler in the 165-pound weight class. Though, the late switch will now feature the No. 1, which Sanderson argues is how it should be.

“It's the All Star match… the history of the event is you try to get the No. 1 and No. 2, best guys in the weight, and it doesn't always work like that,” Sanderson said. “But you have two contenders for sure.”

title: Penn State notebook | Cael Sanderson talks latest performances, upcoming Black Knight Invite
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
After a 41-0 win against Oklahoma, Cael Sanderson sat down to talk to the media ahead of the Black Knight Invite and NWCA All-Star Classic this week.

Sanderson gave his input on the last two performances, the upcoming meets and set the record straight about the recent “donation” to the program.

Here’s what he had to say.

Reflections on Masanosuke Ono, Tyler Kasak

All eyes have been on the Matsue City, Japan, native after his collegiate folkstyle debut last week against Bloomsburg.

Ono started out the match guns blazing against Husky Austin Pollard, but slowly lost steam towards the end, still managing to get the win. Even though he’s still adjusting to the new style, he was able to improve his speed and endurance during the Oklahoma match.

“He’s just trying to figure out the cadence there and how it looks, but he’s a goer,” Sanderson said. “His shape and everything will continue to improve. His first match was a lot of build-up and recall and I don’t know how it doesn’t steal a little bit of your wind.”

Sanderson regards Ono as “tough” and is confident in his ability to continue to improve throughout the season.

Kasak was a wrestler who made his return to the mat. He’s done enough to clinch wins in his matchups, but has started his season rockier than expected.

“When he needed to score, he went and scored. He can ride when he needs to ride; he’s been off the mat for a while and hasn’t competed a lot. It’s just getting down to weight and I think Tyler’s going to get better every match,” Sanderson said.

After his latest back-and-forth against No.16 Rafael Hipolito Jr., Kasak allowed multiple stalling points, as Hipolito started to take control. He nearly lost the match, but ended up taking it with a takedown in sudden victory.

The Black Knight Invite

The upcoming invitational at Army West Point will be a good opportunity for wrestlers like Nate Desmond to see time on the mat, after sitting out for Ono in the last week.

Sanderson will take 20 of his wrestlers to New York, not including those competing in the NWCA All-Star Classic on Sunday due to the short turnaround time.

“Nate’s a guy we have a lot of confidence in; he filled in for us last year in some big duals and did a fantastic job, having the ability to wrestle three different weights,” Sanderson said. “We’ll just keep taking it one match at a time, but it’s only November, there’s a lot of time to get better and progress.”

Sanderson discussed the difficulty of developing on the mat in a sport where “you can’t pull somebody out in the fourth quarter and give somebody playing time,” and how the invitational will help give back-ups a chance to get comfortable competing.

“We don’t have a lot of opportunities to compete, so they want to compete, and it’s not the most convenient thing. The Black Knight gives the 20 guys the opportunity to compete and get some good competition,” Sanderson said.

Ira Lubert Donation

It was recently announced that former Penn State wrestler Ira Lubert donated a hefty $10 million to the program.

However, Sanderson clarified that the donation is not simply to the program, but for building up the resources in the future.

“We’ve obviously been working on a facility for a couple years and hope at some point to get there,” Sanderson said. “We’re grateful for Ira and all the support he’s given us over the years, but it’s not just a check to the program. It's a gift that will anchor the facility if we get to that point.”

Sanderson and the team have made efforts in the past to raise money for a new facility, including a fundraiser last season.

title: No. 7 Penn State women's volleyball sweeps Rutgers in regular season finale
author: Ashley Felsberg I The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State returned home for its match against Rutgers on Tuesday at 7 p.m. The Nittany Lions entered the contest on a nine-match win streak and hoped to continue it in their regular season finale.

The blue and white extended its hot streak, earning the sweep.

The Nittany Lions took the first lead of set one after a Rutgers attack error. Other than two early points from a Rutgers kill and ace, every two Penn State points seemed to be met with a single Rutgers point. It wasn’t until the 11-8 mark that the Nittany Lions surpassed a two-point run and added four points to their tally, following two Scarlet Knight errors and a kill each from Kennedy Martin and Whitney Lauenstein.

Alexis Stucky’s eight assist to Gabrielle Nichols brought the match to a media timeout.

“I think that Stucky moved the ball around well, and we were one-on-one and taking some good high swings and just worked hard,” Katie Schumacher-Cawley said

Following the media stoppage, the Scarlet Knights snuck back into the set, narrowing Penn State’s lead from five to three; however, a paired kill from Emmi Sellman and Kendall Northern helped the blue and white regain a comfortable lead.

Rutgers regained a single point following Northern’s kill, but Sellman and Northern replicated the exact two plays, adding two more kills to the Nittany Lion’s tally and forcing the Scarlet Knights to call a timeout.

Penn State’s two-point run turned into three after Northern added her fourth kill.

Rutgers crept back after a seven-point deficit, following an attack error from Stucky and a kill each for Natalie Robinson and Malia Romes. A Whitney Lauenstein kill halted the momentum and the Scarlet Knights called another timeout, keeping a five-point distance as the blue and white were within two points of set point.

Martin’s third kill clinched the set for the blue and white.

Rutgers gained an early two-point lead in set two after a service ace and a Penn State attack error, however, a Stucky kill gave the blue and white a slight redemption.

A pair of kills from Martin and Northern allowed Penn State to creep back into an even score after a persistent neck-and-neck one-point battle. Following the 9-9 mark, the two teams alternated single points for six points straight.

Rutgers continued its offensive momentum, and Penn State was unable to gain a comfortable lead as it had in a majority of the first set. The Nittany Lions and Scarlet Knights traded one- and two-point runs until 17-17, when Penn State went on its first three-point run of the set, fueled by three Rutgers attack errors.

Despite two Robinson kills that prevented any true offensive momentum for the blue and white, four Rutgers errors brought Penn State to set point. Ultimately, an Avery Jesewitz attack error sealed the deal and gave the Nittany Lions a two-set lead.

Lauenstein came out swinging in set three with a cross-court kill to give Penn State the first lead; however, Lily Bolen quickly replicated it for the Scarlet Knights.

Two Nichols kills and a block gave Penn State a 4-3 lead after a persistent back-and-forth. Sellman added to that momentum with a kill; however, former Nittany Lion Karis Willow responded with a same-side kill of her own.

After a Rutgers timeout, a paired block between Stucky and Northern, along with Launstein’s eighth kill, pushed Penn State’s lead to five.

“I think that (Stucky) just like sets me up really well, puts me in good positions to score,” Northern said.

.

Ryla Jones subbed into the match and received a standing ovation in Rec Hall. Jones knee injury sustained against Michigan State kept her out of play since Sept. 27, so her return was highly anticipated.

“I think it was great to see her back. I know she’s been working very hard in rehab and treatment and all that stuff for the past month and a half or so,” Northern said.

After six straight one-point trades, Rutgers went on a three-point run with a Launestein error, a Brooke Baldwin ace, and a Willow kill. Martin answered back with her 12th kill, and Northern and Sellman followed up with a paired block ahead of the media timeout.

“They, you know, both worked really hard in transition, and that’s something we’ve been talking to Kendall about for a while,” Schumacher-Cawley said.

Sellman and Northern continued to be a force, each adding a kill after the stoppage and pushing Penn State’s lead to five. Another Martin kill followed, forcing Rutgers to call a timeout and temporarily halting a five-point run.

The run extended to six as Martin put up her 14th kill. The run stopped after an Imani Howell kill, which George then followed up.

A Northern kill was followed up by a Sellman ace to bring Penn State within three of set point.

Despite Rutgers adding two more points to their total, a Lauenstein solo block brought the set to match point, and a Rutgers attack error officially sealed the Penn State sweep.

Up Next

Penn State will prepare for the first-ever Big Ten Tournament in Fishers, Indiana, which begins on Friday.

title: U.S. officially loses measles elimination status
author: Kevin Harris | For the Collegian
description:
After 26 years, the United States lost its measles elimination status since the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) declared continuous virus transmission had lasted over 12 months.

The decision from PAHO comes after a notable increase in measles cases across the United States over the last two years.

Over 5,400 cases of measles have been documented across the U.S. in 2026, the highest number of outbreaks since 1991. Pennsylvania has reported 1,561 cases, 309 hospitalizations and seven confirmed measles-related deaths. Within the last year, Centre County has 44 reported cases.

“Losing measles elimination status is much more than losing a public health designation. It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization and death,” Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, said in a news release.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro acknowledged the loss of status and called for increased vaccination across the state in a Facebook post Tuesday.

“Measles is preventable. We eliminated it in this country once, and we can do it again. I continue urging all Pennsylvanians to speak with their health care providers about getting vaccinated and protecting themselves and their families,” Shapiro said in the post.

title: Penn State men's hockey notebook | Guy Gadowsky talks struggles amid losing streak
author: Chase Fisher | The Daily Collegian
description:
The media met with Guy Gadowsky on Tuesday, three days removed from his team’s second straight winless series.

The Nittany Lions, ranked 57th out of 62 teams in the NPI ratings, the metric used to determine the 16 teams that make the NCAA Tournament, were outscored 14-6 against second-ranked Michigan in Ann Arbor.

Here’s what Gadowsky said on Tuesday about Penn State’s two losses to the Wolverines, which extended the team’s losing streak to five games and added to the program’s worst 12-game start in its history.

Penn State gave up 14 goals, it was a ‘team issue’

Penn State entered this season with goaltending as a clear strength. Netminder Josh Fleming returned to the team after a dominant 2025-26 campaign, while freshman goalie Ryder Fetterolf, the reigning CHL Goaltender of the Year, joined Fleming to make a dynamic tandem.

That duo has been underwhelming statistically 12 games into the season. Fleming has seen his save percentage drop to .896 after a strong .924 mark last year. Fetterolf boasts a troubling 4.596 goals-allowed average, which ballooned on Saturday after surrendering eight goals.

Gadowsky, however, has nothing but praise for them week after week. He said again on Tuesday that he thought both netminders “played well” against Michigan, adding that he thought the team’s defensive performance on Saturday was “very unfair” to Fetterolf.

Gadowsky was alluding to the 10 penalties the Nittany Lions took in Game 2 against the Wolverines. Michigan scored seven goals from those 10 infractions.

“The goaltending was not the issue by any means,” Gadowsky said on Tuesday evening. “I give Fleming a lot of credit for getting down early (on Friday). I don't think that was a Fleming issue; I thought that was a team issue. A lot of players obviously have never been in that building, and they come at you pretty fast. And I like how we adjusted, but for him to really dig in after that, I thought it showed a lot of credit or a lot of character for him.”

‘Not happy with the results’

Gadowsky hasn’t been pleased with the outcomes of his challenges this season. Penn State lost another on Saturday in the first period after appealing what Gadowsky and his video team thought was a missed major penalty on Michigan.

The well-seasoned coach said on Tuesday, however, that he wholeheartedly supports every time his video coach says a play is challengeable. “You can’t just look at what you see in the stands,” Gadowsky said.

“This year we have not been successful, and look, it's not just us,” he added. “I think it's very difficult. If you look at the rule book, there's 52 times that say referee's discretion. So it's really difficult to challenge something that in the rule book says is the referees' discretion because you can always come back and go well, it's my discretion, so it's a tough one.”

‘It’s an execution thing’

Twelve out of Penn State’s 24 active roster players weren’t with the program a year ago. Gadowsky said on Tuesday that most of them have never played in the NCAA either. The team is still in an adjustment period because of it.

With that comes difficulty communicating on the ice, and a strain to get on the same page from the coaches to the players. Gadowsky said that isn’t a problem; however, execution is the overarching issue.

He said that’s why players get better as time goes on. “Everybody’s coming from different leagues,” Gadowsky said.

“We're trying to establish a bit of a gritty, like back to what you guys have all seen in the past, pretty gritty hockey team,” he added. “You have to walk that line, be really gritty, but stay out of the box. It's not easy, so it is an execution thing, but it's not like ‘Oh, just do this.’”

title: Penn State issues Timely Warning for a sexual offense, first since 2024
author: Neel Ved | The Daily Collegian
description:
Editor's note: This story was updated Wednesday morning with a statement from a UPPS spokesperson.

Penn State reported its known first sexual offense of the semester, according to a University Park-issued Timely Warning issued at 4:02 pm on Tuesday.

The incident reportedly occurred at a tailgate area near Beaver Stadium on Saturday between 5-8 p.m. The individual involved has not been identified, according to the warning.

It’s unknown if the student knew the perpetrator, and “it can be assumed that conditions continue to exist that may pose a threat to members and guests of the University community,” according to the Timely Warning.

Though the report is available online, several students have reported they did not receive the timely warning via email or text.

In the past, Timely Warnings were sent out via text alert.

Jacqueline Sheader, UPPS' chief information officer told The Daily Collegian in an email on Wednesday that UPPS is "doing a review to ensure information is fully distributed."

Sheader also said that Timely Warnings are distributed to all faculty, staff and students through their official Penn State emails by "default," however, this process is separate from PSUAlert which distributes emergency alerts via text message or phone call.

The warning is the first Timely Warning sent out since Feb. 19, 2025, and the first for a sexual offense since Nov. 19, 2024.

Anyone with information is being asked to contact University Police.

title: Penn State women’s hockey notebook | Assistant coach Jennifer Wakefield talks player updates, regrouping
author: Brady Welsh | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State women’s hockey hosted a media session Tuesday morning for the first time since the series split against Mercyhurst this weekend. Coach Jeff Kampersal was unavailable and assistant coach Jennifer Wakefield spoke on his behalf.

Matilde Fantin injury update

Forward Matilde Fantin has yet to play a game in her sophomore campaign due to a lingering injury she sustained towards the end of last season. In September, Kampersal mentioned she would be out “at least through Thanksgiving,” and the topic has gone cold since.

However, with Thanksgiving a week away, a vague but positive update on Fantin was provided.

“She's doing great, progressing well, and we'll kind of just leave it at that,” Wakefield said.

Fantin played 26 games for the Nittany Lions last year, potting 10 goals and 23 points. She also competed in the 2026 Milan Cortina Olympics for Team Italy, where she scored three goals. There is still no timetable for Fantin’s return.

IIHF Women’s World Championship review

Junior forward Nicole Hall missed the last four games of Penn State’s road trip as she was selected to team Sweden to compete in the IIHF Women’s World Championship in Denmark that wrapped up Monday.

The team is still awaiting her arrival from Denmark.

“It depends on any flights or delays, kind of out of our control,” Wakefield said about Hall’s game status.

However, if everything goes to plan, and Hall arrives back in the U.S. in time for Thursday’s game, she will be active against the Blue Hens.

Sweden defeated Finland 2-1 in a shootout Monday to take home the tournament’s bronze medal. Although Hall didn’t register a point, she was a big part of Sweden’s penalty kill being as good as it was en route to taking home the country’s first IIHF Women’s World Championship medal since 2007.

“Nicole’s development since I've been here has been insane,” Wakefield said. “It's been super nice to watch, you know, her confidence level when she goes with the national team.”

Former Nittany Lion captain Tessa Janecke took home the gold with Team USA, putting up 10 points in seven games. The 2026 third overall pick in the PWHL draft earned her second international gold of the year, as she also competed in the Olympics in February.

“I don't think people know how good (Janecke) is until they can see her live, ” Wakefield said. “There's not really one way to stop Tessa, and that's why I think she's gonna blow a lot of people away during her first year of the PWHL.”

Looking back

The Nittany Lions went down 2-0 in the first period in Game 1 against Mercyhurst on Friday, but then exploded for seven unanswered goals scored by seven different players. The team also went four-for-four on the power play, something Wakefield acknowledged as being one of their biggest strengths this season.

The momentum changed Saturday as Penn State’s scorching offense was suddenly stopped in its tracks 3-0, its first multi-goal and shutout loss of the season.

“You definitely have to give Mercyhurst their praise for coming out and playing us as hard as they did,” Wakefield said. “We knew we were going to get that, and we didn't respond well to the kind of pressure they put on us.”

The game propelled Mercyhurst into the USCHO top-15 for the first time this season, which Wakefield mentioned was “nice to see” from a fellow AHA competitor.

Penn State won’t let Saturday’s game keep them down, as the short week doesn’t give the Nittany Lions much time to. Wakefield is a former player who won gold with Team Canada at the 2014 Sochi Olympics, and from her experience, she prefers it that way.

“It's exciting to have a short week after a loss, especially when you have higher expectations of your performance in game two,” Wakefield said. “I think the short week gives an opportunity for players to turn their game around quickly.”

Thursday against Delaware will be the Nittany Lions’ first home game in over a month, but Wakefield doesn’t believe that any potential “road fatigue” had anything to do with Saturday’s result.

Looking ahead

The main thing that the team wants to see more of in the Delaware series is urgency, something that Wakefield mentioned every team needs to play with to avoid being “exposed.” The Nittany Lions will also need better defensive play, sharper transitions going into this series, with the power play still expected to play a big role.

Wakefield praised Delaware head coach and former Penn State assistant Allison Coomey when discussing how to keep the power play as an advantage in this series.

“Coomey is super smart, so I'm sure she'll have a game plan,” Wakefield said. “I'm sure (Makenna Newkirk), who is responsible for our power play here, will have something to combat that.”

Puck drops at 6 p.m. for Thursday’s Game 1, with a 4 p.m. start scheduled for Game 2 on Friday.

title: Penn State LB Kooper Ebel’s return offers early glimpse into Matt Campbell’s offseason roster building
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Linebacker Kooper Ebel said Tuesday at the Beaver Stadium podium that he’s planning on returning to Penn State next year for his fifth season.

Matt Campbell has emphasized for the last two weeks that conversations regarding players’ futures with the team won’t take place until the weeks following the regular season. Ebel got a head start on that with his announcement and said he hasn’t spoken to Campbell about his decision one-on-one.

“There's like a three-week gap that I think really that's where you got to put your time and effort into meeting with each player,” Campbell said. “‘Where are you? Where are we going? What's best for you? Where is this program going?’”

Campbell is no stranger to the transfer portal and offseason recruiting, as 27 players on this year’s squad came from various teams around the country last offseason. This year, he’ll have the opportunity to not just recruit from the transfer portal, but also work through the retention of his current players.

“I think the more retention of the right humans that fit on the roster, the better we're going to continue to be,” Campbell said. “I think there's been so much growth. We're nowhere near where we want to be yet.”

But now there’s the new five-for-five rule, which permits athletes to compete in college sports for five years rather than four, adding a wrinkle to that retention process.

Ebel is just one of the players who has the option to return next year, as tight end Benjamin Brahmer, safety Jamison Patton, running back Carson Hansen and others are also eligible for their fifth year.

“I certainly think there's the possibility that some of that senior leadership or veteran leadership in our team is going to have a chance to be probably pretty special for us,” Campbell said.

While the Nittany Lions would likely benefit from a majority of their seniors returning for another year, Campbell made clear it's a decision that comes from what’s best for each player.

He referenced former Iowa State running back David Montgomery, who’s now a Houston Texan. Montgomery was eligible to return for a fourth year, but Campbell knew his potential and what was best for him and his future.

“You need to go and maximize your opportunity,” Campbell said. “I just think everybody's got to make the best decision for them, and I feel like my responsibility is to give everybody and try to get the best information so them and their family can make a great decision for them.”

While Campbell will begin building a roster made of current and future Nittany Lions once the regular season is over, Ebel also said he’ll begin conversations with players as well.

“When the season's over, whenever that is, I plan on doing everything I can to bring in the right people, the right players into this program, and continue to build with coach Campbell,” Ebel said.

With Penn State’s recent turnaround and three-game winning streak, Ebel believes the team is building something special — a major reason he decided to come back.

Ebel’s choice to return also provides the Nittany Lions with a veteran presence as Campbell continues to establish his culture within the program and build the team for years to come.

“It brings a definite feel of certainty behind that,” wide receiver Chase Sowell said. “You get a group of guys that have been in his system for a while now and know what he's looking for, and know what he wants out of his program and out of his team. And then on top of that, just bring more experience.”

title: Rocco Becht is ‘taking what the defense gives them’ in post-bye week resurgence
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
A third Rocco Becht passing touchdown against Minnesota put Penn State up 35-0, eventually cruising to a 42-14 victory — a score that didn’t seem even remotely realistic before the bye week.

But it was a testament to how Becht and the offense have played since the week off. The Nittany Lions’ veteran quarterback had five turnovers in the three losses before the bye, yet he hasn’t given away the ball since.

Becht has managed the offense significantly better en route to Penn State’s three-game winning streak.

“I think Rocco's done a good job of keeping us on track offensively and taking what the defense gives them,” Taylor Mouser said Tuesday. “There's times where anybody, where the game starts to get away or you start to get stressed or you try to do too much and he doesn't do that a ton.”

Becht’s ability to adapt to what the defense is doing has allowed the offense to catch fire. Since the winning streak started, Penn State has scored 28 or more points in every game, something it hadn’t done since the blowout win against Buffalo in Week 3.

The quarterback said he’s “playing the play” more instead of trying to do something during the moment that’s potentially not there or not set up in the play that’s called. Becht cited using what the defense gives as a reason why there’s been no turnovers from him over the last three weeks.

“There was times in the first couple games where we're trying to force something, we're trying to make something happen, we're trying to make the big play happen instead of just letting it happen and letting it come to us,” Becht said.

A major part of the turnaround also comes from his leadership and the experience he has. Matt Campbell consistently mentioned his veteran presence as a reason for continuing to play him when things weren’t going well.

That decision paid off, as Becht’s experience from last season helped him get out of his rut during the losing streak this year a lot faster compared to when he had a four-game skid at Iowa State last season.

“That's when I finally figured it out was toward the end of the year when we were finally getting on a win streak, how to get out of that,” Becht said. “Also just trust the people around me, trust my family, listen to those that I love, and I think for me it's kind of just moving on.”

Becht admitted he didn’t think he’d have to use the experience from last year so quickly, but he was ready for it to happen when it did. Now, Penn State looks like a completely different team.

Mouser has also said Becht’s adjustments at the line of scrimmage result in success for the offense, including in the run game. In the last three weeks, the rushing attack has not only had more explosive plays, but it’s also rarely run for negative yards.

“If we have a sensitive run into a sensitive front or sensitive pressure, Rocco, you see him out there directing traffic,” Mouser said. “There's a lot of checks, a lot of kills. We put a lot on his plate, even on the ones that aren't passes.”

Not only is Becht a quarterback who can place the ball in different windows, but he’s also proven to be smart in where he goes with the ball. He’s found his form lately, tripling his touchdown total in Big Ten play over the last three weeks.

“I think for him, he's played patient, he's played confident, he's trusted his eyes and gotten the ball to the right place,” Mouser said. “And when it hasn't been there, like it was for Ben's first touchdown, like it wasn't the defense we wanted, but he put the ball where only Ben could get it, and he's the kind of quarterback that can do that.”

title: Penn State softball releases 2027 Schedule
author: Riley Warner | For the Collegian
description:
This season, Penn State hosts 21 of its 53 games at Nittany Lion Softball Park and Beard Field. Following an impressive season record of 33-21, Penn State, led by coach Clarisa Crowell, looks to repeat such success in the 2026-2027 season.

The season starts with a trio of non-conference tournaments over the course of February, many of which will be against 2026 NCAA tournament teams. Starting in Boca Raton, Florida, the blue and white will once again be competing in the Paradise Classic. The four-day tournament takes place Feb. 12-14. Penn State will play Southern Illinois and host team FAU on Feb. 12, Miami (Ohio) and Boston College on Feb. 13, and will end the tournament facing Boston College on Feb.14.

Days later, Penn State will head to Arizona for the ASU/GCU Invitational hosted by Arizona State and Grand Canyon University on Feb. 18-21. The Nittany Lions will compete in six games across the two campuses. The tournament will feature games against 2026 NCAA contenders, including both host teams as well as Kansas, and games against BYU and Missouri.

The Nittany Lions end February in Charlottesville, Virginia, with the Minuzo Classic at Palmer Park. From Feb. 26- 28, the blue and white will play one game against Delaware, two against tournament hosts Virginia, and two against Princeton.

Action at Beard Field begins on March 5 with the Penn State Invitational. The Nittany Lions will play three games against Saint Joesph’s and two against Dartmouth, with the tournament ending on March 7.

From March 9-14 the Nittany Lions will be away in California. The team will play two non-conference matches against Loyola Marymount on March 9 and Cal State Fullerton on March 10 before playing an in-conference series with UCLA on Mar. 12- 14.

After the week in California, Penn State will return for its Big Ten home opener against Purdue in a weekend series with games on March 19-21. The weekend thereafter, conference play will continue with the Nittany Lions hosting Ohio State on March 26-28. After these two series, Youngstown State will come to play at Beard Field on March 30.

The Nittany Lions travel to Maryland from April 2-4 before coming back to Beard Field to play Bucknell on April 7. What follows is a Big Ten series against Rutgers from April 9-11 before a solo home game against Pittsburgh on April 14.

The Nittany Lions close out April on the road with games at Iowa from April 16-18 and Michigan State from April 23-25 and a solo home game against Akron on the 28th.

Regular season play ends in May with a doubleheader at Villanova on May 1 and a closing series at Beard Field from May 7-9 against Michigan.

title: Penn State selected as academic partner for proposed U.S. Space Academy
author: Katie Kolovos | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State has been selected as Pennsylvania's academic partner for the proposed U.S. Space Academy, according to a release from the university on Nov. 16.

The university, along with Gov. Josh Shapiro, Sen. Dave McCormick (R-PA), the Keystone Space Collaborative and the Pittsburgh International Airport proposed the establishment of the academy in southwestern Pennsylvania. Penn State was chosen to deliver the proposal to federal officials on Nov. 16.

The proposal is in response to a Aug. 2026 Executive Order seeking the establishment of a permanent United States Space Academy (USSA). As space technology becomes more integral to everyday life, Penn State hopes to support a modern workforce trained in engineering, robotics and policy. Penn State will work alongside six other research universities across the Commonwealth to help develop the proposal.

“Penn State is honored to have been selected to support the Commonwealth’s pursuit of this initiative and to lend our expertise in research, academics, and workforce development,” President Neeli Bendapudi said in a release from Gov. Shapiro. “Working in collaboration with research institutions across Pennsylvania, we can provide the framework needed to train the next generation of astronauts, scientists, engineers, operators, entrepreneurs, and civil servants. Our proposed curriculum would provide students with critical hands-on experience and the skills they need to meet the rapidly changing workforce needs.”

If Pennsylvania is selected to host the academy, Penn State will serve as the degree-granting institution and transcript issuer until the academy gets its own accreditation. Representatives from Penn State will help guide the planning process of the curriculum and campus.

The proposed academic plan includes bachelor’s degrees in space engineering, space science and space operations. Students would also have the option for a technical concentration within their major, with experiential learning as a pillar of the proposed curriculum.

The academy aims to have graduates leave prepared to enter the space industry with hands-on experience and specialized expertise.

Penn State’s Cocoziello Institute of Real Estate Innovation led the architectural planning for the campus. Faculty and student research groups from the Cocoziello Institute, Penn State’s Office of Physical Plant, university planner Neil Sullivan and the architecture firm NBBJ worked together to develop concepts for the campus.

Penn State is also working with Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Pittsburgh on the proposal.

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell says RB Carson Hansen is questionable for Saturday against Rutgers
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
After gaining bowl eligibility with a win over Minnesota, Matt Campbell spoke to the media on Tuesday for his weekly press conference at Beaver Stadium.

Campbell gave an update on running back Carson Hansen’s availability, shared his thoughts on senior day and discussed the team’s growth in the third quarter.

Here’s more on what he said.

Carson Hansen update

Campbell said Hansen is “questionable” heading into Penn State’s Week 12 matchup against Rutgers after only playing the first half against the Golden Gophers, limping to the locker room after 126 rushing yards and a touchdown.

Without Hansen, Campbell said Cam Wallace will be the No. 1 running back. However, he also said he feels confident in the depth of the running back room including Quinton Martin Jr. and James Peoples, claiming it’ll be a “committee of guys” if Hansen doesn’t play Saturday.

“Cam has stepped into a major role and has proven that he's been ready to go and his opportunities have come his way,” Campbell said. “I thought James Peoples really did a great job in the second half coming in, and obviously James has had some positive moments, and I've said this a lot about Quinton, he’s proven that he's got the ability to do it.”

Wallace has been the No. 2 running back since the Purdue game when it was previously Peoples, and when Wallace took over, Peoples didn’t have a carry for two straight weeks. With Hansen out, Peoples got four carries for 12 yards and also linked up with backup quarterback Alex Manske for a 22-yard touchdown.

Meanwhile, Martin hasn’t had a carry since Michigan, when he got the ball twice.

Who walks on senior day?

Campbell said he has a hands-off approach to senior day in general because of eligibility, but especially this year because of the new five-for-five rule, which has given some players an extra year. Thus, Campbell said he doesn’t exactly know who’s leaving and who isn’t.

He said it boils down to “personal preference” who walks and who doesn’t, and all meetings related to returning for another year will happen after the season’s conclusion.

“It's a global response to it,” Campbell said. “Some guys have eligibility that are still working through the process that just didn't feel like they were ready to walk on senior day. Other guys have eligibility that are walking on senior day and probably will wait till the end of the season to make a final decision if they come back.”

Campbell said there’s the possibility for a veteran leadership group to return for the 2027 season, something he called “pretty special.” However, he said the desire to come back must come from the players, and he can’t force anyone to stay.

He referenced former Iowa State running backs Breece Hall and David Montgomery, who left college early to play in the NFL, saying the players have to make the right decision for themselves.

“You need to go and maximize your opportunity,” Campbell said. “I just think everybody's got to make the best decision for them. I feel like my responsibility is to try to get the best information so they and their family can make a great decision for them. I think the more retention of the right humans that fit on the roster, the better we're going to continue to be.”

Third quarter toughness

Penn State has been outscored 56-16 in the third quarter this season, and Campbell was honest about why he believes the scoreboard doesn’t favor the Nittany Lions coming out of halftime.

“I think it is a mentality piece,” Campbell said. “I think it's a mental toughness piece. I think it's a demand to play your best 60 minutes and play to a standard rather than playing to a scoreboard, and so I think those are things that we're continuing to grow in.”

However, Penn State did much better in the second half against Minnesota compared to how the team played against Washington. After a 28-0 first half, the Nittany Lion tied the Golden Gophers 14-14 in the second half to win the game 42-14.

Additionally, Campbell praised how the offense quickly scored on the first drive of the second half, saying he thought his team made some strides.

Campbell noted there are still issues the team needs to fix, such as staying focused on third down to force changes of possession, but he has faith the Nittany Lions can continue growing as the regular season comes to a close.

“Do I think those things can change? You're darn right, I do,” Campbell said. “I think you got to demand it every day. It's how you practice, it's how you show up in a meeting, it's can you consistently do your job for 60 minutes? I still don't think we've proven that we can do that to the consistency level that we would want to do that, but I do think we've grown every week.”

title: Penn State notebook | OC Taylor Mouser still looking for growth in run game despite recent success
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State earned its best Big Ten victory on Saturday when it dominated Minnesota, 42-14, behind a 28-point first half.

Taylor Mouser met with the media on Tuesday to discuss the run game, backup quarterback Alex Manske’s development and more.

Here’s a look at what Mouser had to say.

Run game success

Coming out of the bye week, Penn State has had a revitalized run game that’s averaged 224 yards per game in the last three contests.

That success has come from better results from running backs Carson Hansen and Cam Wallace, who’ve been the two primary backs over the last month.

Despite the growth, Mouser isn’t complacent with the run game.

“I think we have to be just as desperate to grow as we were three weeks ago,” Mouser said. “We have to have more urgency than what we played with, and we have to have more attack than what we played with, and we have to have our best week this week.”

Shortly before halftime against Minnesota, Hansen suffered an injury that kept him out of the second half. While Mouser said “we hope Carson can come back sooner than later,” Wallace stepped up and carried the ball the rest of the game.

“(Wallace is) taking his game to a new level and doing it every single day,” Mouser said. “His game stands out. You go watch him in practice, it stands out. When you watch him in the game, it stands out.”

Navigating first season

Mouser’s first season at Penn State has had its highs and lows for both him and the rest of the new players and staff in Happy Valley. The Nittany Lions started the year ranked in the AP Poll, but lost four straight to open Big Ten play before turning it around with a three-game winning streak.

“It's certainly been frustrating at times just because I want to do well for the guys, the fans and the people,” Mouser said. “It means a lot to be the offensive coordinator here, give people good memories and winning."

Mouser added, "There's been generations that have come before me that built the standard to be able to go into games and expect to win. So when you don't do that, more than anything, you know you're not living up to the standard, and that weighs a lot on me too.”

Mouser’s path to Happy Valley hasn’t exactly been an easy path either, as he struggled to find a coaching job out of college. After Matt Campbell took him in at Toledo, the two have been together since.

“I don't try to forget how lucky I am to be in this spot, even when it's you know going bad like the man in the arena, and I don't forget that. I get to be surrounded by people I love with all my heart.”

Manske’s growth

After Mouser praised Manske early in the season, he only saw the field in garbage time during nonconference play. As Becht struggled early in Big Ten play, calls for Manske to get a chance rang loud, but Manske remained on the bench.

Against Minnesota, Manske took the field for the first time in 56 days and delivered a strong performance in the final stretch of the game, throwing his first career touchdown pass.

“I think just really he's such a talented guy, and hopefully, you guys got to see that a little bit,” Mouser said. “There's been flashes of it.”

While Manske hasn’t had much playing time since coming to college, he’s taken every opportunity to grow, including on the practice field and his brief moments on the field.

“Manske's done a good job in the two years I've been with him,” Mouser said. “He’s never complained about being on the field whether we've been good or haven't been good. When we give that kid reps, (he’s) one of the most competitive guys that we have, one of the best spirits that we have.”

Manske finished Saturday’s game with two completions for 38 yards and a touchdown, and Mouser was impressed with how he handled himself. The redshirt freshman “knows that it’s Rocco’s team,” according to Mouser, but “his time is coming.”

“Manske doesn't go in and we run those plays if we didn't trust him as a football team to be able to do that,” Mouser said. “When your number gets called, you have to go in and do well.”

title: Big Ten roundup | Rutgers remains undefeated, Wisconsin sinks in Florida
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
While Penn State is 2-0 after a pair of resounding victories against Bloomsburg and Oklahoma, some of its Big Ten opponents haven’t been so successful.

Rutgers put up a strong performance to upset Lehigh, while Wisconsin struggled in back-to-back duals in Bradenton, Florida, including consecutive upsets allowed by the Badgers’ heavyweight.

Here’s how the conference performed in the 2026-27 campaign’s second week.

Illinois

After a smooth season opener against Hofstra, the Fighting Illini hit the road for a dual against The Citadel. Illinois dropped its first matches of the season, but still earned an efficient, 38-6 victory in South Carolina to remain undefeated.

Despite two wins in the first half of the match, Illinois responded with big victories, including a fall by Greyson Clark and a technical fall from Michael Gioffre to take a 13-3 lead.

Illinois picked it up in the back half of the match with five straight bonus point victories to close out the match in commanding fashion.

Indiana

The Hoosiers split a pair of opening-week matches but got back in the win column after defeating Central Michigan 27-9.

Indiana won the dual’s first eight matches. Jackson Blum, Tom Crook and Orlando Cruz all earned major decisions while the rest of the lineup worked to decisions over the Chippewas.

Central Michigan got on the board with an Indiana forfeit at 197 pounds before Carter Neves closed the dual with an hard-fought upset win over No. 17 Connor Barket at heavyweight, grinding out a 15-14 decision.

Iowa

Iowa opened its season in dominant fashion, shellacking Bellarmine to a 44-(-1) final score.

The Hawkeyes won every match, headlined by a tech fall by Leo DeLuca at 125 pounds. The Knights lost a team point due to an illegal uniform infraction in the 149-pound match.

In the back half of the match, 184-pounder Angelo Ferrari pinned his opponent to further extend the Hawkeyes’ advantage, showcasing the overall dominance Iowa put on against Bellarmine.

Michigan

The Wolverines improved to 2-0 with a 44-0 beatdown of Columbia.

Michigan used a trio of dominant matches from 165-184 pounds, with back-to-back tech falls from Cameron Catrabone and Beau Mantanona.

Beau’s brother, Brock, pinned his opponent in the first period. 197-pounder Hayden Walters earned a major decision and Niko Sahakian worked to an upset decision to seal a second-consecutive shutout for the Wolverines.

Michigan State

Michigan State went west, splitting a pair of Californian duals against Cal Poly and CSU Bakersfield.

The Spartans struggled against Cal Poly, winning just two matches. They got victories from Evan Gosz at 149 pounds and Josh Terrill at heavyweight, as they fell to the Mustangs, 33-7.

The Spartans trailed in the second dual against CSU Bakersfield, but came back to earn their first win of the season 24-13.

Gabe Ramirez got the Roadrunners started with a pin before Michigan State’s Caleb Weiand cut the deficit in half with a decision. Gosz and Darius Marines delivered a decision and a major decision, respectively, to put the Spartans up 10-9.

Gabriel Schumm worked to a 10-2 major decision that briefly reestablished the Roadrunner lead, but Michigan State claimed three decisions and a technical fall over the final four matches to avoid another loss.

Ohio State

The Buckeyes got their season underway with a 34-10 win over Columbia in Columbus.

125-pounder Sulayman Bah earned a 9-3 decision to score the first points of the night for the Lions. National contender Ben Davino responded with a 20-5 technical fall at 133 pounds that Brogan Fielding followed with a 4-2 decision.

Brandon Cannon pinned his opponent before Ethan Stiles and Jaxon Smith each earned technical falls to take a commanding lead in the dual.

Ryder Rogotzke pinned his opponent and Nick Feldman worked to a major decision that sealed Ohio State’s 34-10 victory in the Covelli Center.

Rutgers

The Scarlet Knights are still undefeated, and passed a major test against Lehigh on Sunday.

Anthony Knox opened Rutgers’ scoring with a major decision, but Lehigh jumped into the lead with back-to-back victories, including a tech fall from Luke Stanich.

Brandt and Conner Harer each earned decision wins at 149 and 157 pounds, and Andrew Barbosa followed up on the brothers’ success with an 11-2 major decision.

Brady Collins edged a 6-5 decision to cut the Rutgers lead to 14-11. Shane Cartagena-Walsh scored a decision to put the Scarlet Knights on the brink of victory before 197-pounder Remy Cotton sealed the upset, without having to worry about the result of heavyweight.

Wisconsin

The Badgers had another two-dial week, dropping both to Penn and North Dakota State in Bradenton, Florida.

Penn won the first six matches of the clash with the Badgers, using three major decisions and a technical fall from Sean Seefeldt to take a commanding lead over Wisconsin.

The Badgers got on the board with a three-match winning streak, as Luke Condon won a decision, Wyatt Clayton won in sudden victory and Wyatt Ingham pinned John Pardo, but Braxton Amos was upset by Penn heavyweight Martin Cosgrove to wrap up the 26-12 defeat in the Sunshine State.

It was another tough start for Wisconsin against North Dakota State, as the Bison won the dual’s first five matches before Caleb Dennee got the Badgers on the board with a late pin.

After a North Dakota State decision, Clayton and Ingham earned a decision and major decision, respectively to improve to 2-0 on the day. Amos was upset again in a 7-3 decision loss to Shilo Jones that concluded the 25-13 Bison win.

title: Recruiting roundup | Flip targets headline Penn State visitors in Week 11
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Penn State has put together three straight wins and has started to gain ground on some flip candidates in the 2027 class and highly ranked recruits in the 2028 cycle.

From four committed players in the upcoming signing class to some major future targets, there were big names visiting despite a smaller overall list to see the Nittany Lions trounce Minnesota.

Here’s who was in Happy Valley over the weekend.

Commits return to their future home

Penn State had four players in town who’ll be enrolled in under two months, if they choose to head to Happy Valley early.

Offensive tackle David Tarawallie headlines the group, as he’s quickly become one of the top players in the class. The 4-star has continued to bulk up, and now ranks as the No. 99 player in the country, the No. 11 offensive tackle and No. 5 player in Ohio.

The Nittany Lions also had two in-state commits in town. 3-star offensive lineman Jon Sassic, who’s missed his entire senior season with an injury, visited for the fourth time since Week 1. The No. 61 interior offensive lineman has visited the most of any commit in the 2027 class.

From the Philadelphia area, defensive lineman Stanley Montgomery also saw Penn State’s third consecutive win. Montgomery is the No. 7 player in the state and is just outside the top 100 nationally at No. 112. He fits in with the new prototype for defensive lineman at Penn State, listed at 6-foot-3, 300 pounds.

The final commit in town was 3-star cornerback Ka’Ron Ceaser. The No. 19 player in New Jersey is a two-way athlete at Winslow Township and is planning to play cornerback at Penn State.

Flip target on campus

The Nittany Lions had a major flip target on campus from the 2027 class. A player who’s recently had some big-time offers, Boston College 3-star commit Jayden Paulino made his way to Penn State for the weekend.

Penn State offered the defensive lineman on Nov. 3. One day later, the current Boston College pledge added offers from Michigan and Missouri. Of the four, Penn State is the closest to his home, as he plays for Passaic County Tech in New Jersey.

The No. 27 player in New Jersey visited for the second time in three weeks as he was in State College for Penn State’s first win of the streak against Purdue.

Paulino is one of multiple Boston College commits, or former commits, the Nittany Lions are targeting to flip ahead of the early national signing day.

2028, 2029 candidates

Despite only having three players committed in classes beyond 2027, Matt Campbell and his staff continue to push for some of the top players in their growing pipelines.

The first of the group was 4-star athlete Brandon Murphy Jr., who is the No. 151 player in the country and No. 4 player in Pennsylvania in the 2028 class. Murphy has visited Penn State three times this season and is planning to visit again for the Nittany Lions’ final home game of the season against Rutgers.

3-star linebacker Cyrus Zuah also made his way to Happy Valley from Baltimore. The No. 31 linebacker in the 2028 class has offers from some of the top programs in the country including Ohio State, Florida, Alabama and Notre Dame.

One of Penn State’s most targeted players, 3-star tight end Quinn Weber was back in attendance on Saturday. The No. 24 tight end and No. 15 player in New Jersey visited for the second time this season, making the trip to Penn State for the Nittany Lions’ loss to Wisconsin on Sept. 26. He also has a visit set up with Tennessee for the Volunteers’ upcoming game against LSU.

In the 2029 class, highly ranked defensive lineman Kennedy Hurte-Jones visited. While he doesn’t have a 247Sports composite ranking, he’s a top 100 recruit on multiple sites. The staff appears to be getting in early on the sophomore, who’s already listed at 6-foot-4, 280 pounds.

Alongside Hurte-Jones was another highly ranked defensive lineman in Cardell Beck. Similarly, Bech is ranked as one of the top players in the country in his class, including as the No. 1 player in Maryland, according to 247Sports.

title: Penn State Figure Skating Competition Team kicks off season with Exhibition Skate
author: Sienna Pearce | For the Collegian
description:
Each time a Penn State Figure Skating Competition Team member took the ice for its Exhibition Skate Fundraiser Friday night, teammates drummed their fists against the glass and cheered.

The sounds rolled throughout Pegula Arena, which was filled with families, friends and fans. The event was raising funds to support the team in their season ahead. Unlike traditional figure skating teams, Penn State doesn’t compete for individual placements, and instead competes for an overall team score.

The team is led by President Veronica Bellorin, a fourth-year studying biobehavioral health. Her responsibilities include maintaining Penn State’s status as a club sport, handling community service hours, utilizing IMLeagues, planning ice time for the year and overseeing all of the other positions.

“The biggest thing is that, at competitions, we’re all one. So even if it isn’t our day, we still support each other, and we all want what's best for each other,” Bellorin said. “You really form that bond, and it feels like family.”

Bellorin is also responsible for motivating her teammates and imparting words of wisdom.

“It’s always an honor to represent Penn State, and that's the biggest thing I tell everyone, is to have fun and relax. Even though we're all standing behind you, focus on yourself in the moment," Bellorin said.

Last season was especially exciting for the blue and white. At their qualifying competition hosted at Case Western Reserve University, they earned a total of 257 team points, the most they’ve ever scored at a single competition. That accomplishment helped them finish second in the Southeast section, the highest sectional finish in team history.

Penn State carried that momentum through the year and ended its season on a high note, competing in the 2026 National Intercollegiate Final, where it finished as the highest-placing Big 10 school.

Its goal this upcoming competition season is to qualify for the National Intercollegiate Final this year, which will be hosted at the University of Delaware this April.

Bellorin works hand-in-hand with Vice President Christina Romonoski-Dao to create a welcoming and supportive environment, she said. Romonoski-Dao, a third-year studying biomedical engineering, oversees away games, including planning out travel logistics and registering for competitions.

Romonoski-Dao said her teammates are what make the experience worthwhile.

“You want everyone to perform their best, and you always want to cheer on your teammates,” Romonoski-Dao said. “My favorite part is to travel and compete with so many people I’ve grown close with.”

Alexa Winter’s experience as a seasoned member has allowed her to develop an easygoing and laid-back pre-skate ritual. During competitions, or rather right before they start, she said she takes a second for herself: She jumps around, tries to calm her breathing and doesn’t “overdo anything.” It helps her get in the zone, she said.

Winter, a fifth-year team member studying architectural engineering, said there’s an undemanding, supportive energy she feels when competing with her teammates.

“It’s very different for most people when they come in, because you're used to being in the sport alone,” Winter said. “I think a lot of people don't realize how close you guys get just from training together and being at comps the whole weekend.”

title: Nittany Lions in the NFL | WR Parker Washington’s career day highlights Week 10 performances
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
While Penn State earned bowl eligibility with a win over Minnesota, various alumni got to work in Week 10 of the NFL season.

Wide receiver Parker Washington had a career-best performance, tight ends Brenton Strange and Pat Freiermuth made the most of their few targets and linebacker Chop Robinson’s pass rush was greatly effective.

Here’s a deeper look into how they performed this week.

Parker Washington, wide receiver, Jacksonville Jaguars

Washington had a career day in the Jacksonville Jaguars’ 40-23 victory over the Tennessee Titans. With 152 receiving yards and a touchdown on seven catches, Washington was the heartbeat of the Jaguars’ offense and helped quarterback Trevor Lawrence total 352 passing yards.

His career-high 152-yard performance included a long of 50 yards, his second-longest reception of the season.

Lawrence found a leaping Washington in the back of the end zone, who fully extended to bring in a high pass while staying in bounds on third-and-goal in the first quarter to open the scoring.

It was Washington’s second game in a row with a touchdown and his sixth of the season. He leads Jacksonville in touchdowns, receiving yards and targets as the team’s primary offensive weapon.

Brenton Strange, tight end, Jacksonville Jaguars

Lawrence found another former Nittany Lion for a touchdown on Sunday as well.

On fourth-and-2 in the third quarter, Lawrence found a wide-open Strange in the end zone for an easy 3-yard touchdown, increasing the Jaguars’ lead.

It was one of only two receptions on the day for Strange, who finished the game with nine yards and his second touchdown of the season — his first since Jacksonville’s 34-10 victory over the Cleveland Browns in Week 1.

Strange also has the third-most receiving yards on the team with 365.

Pat Freiermuth, tight end, Pittsburgh Steelers

Freiermuth was another former Nittany Lion to find the end zone despite having only two catches.

In the fourth quarter against the Cincinnati Bengals, quarterback Aaron Rodgers found his tight end along the sideline. Freiermuth staggered forward with a pair of defenders desperately trying to drag him down, but fell with the ball extended over the goal line for a 27-yard touchdown.

It was Freiermuth’s fifth touchdown of the season and his first since Oct. 11 when he scored twice against the Indianapolis Colts. Despite his previous scoring slump, he stills leads the Steelers in touchdowns and ranks fourth on the team with 270 receiving yards.

However, Freiermuth’s score didn’t make too much of a dent on the Bengals 38-18 victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers.

Chop Robinson, linebacker, Miami Dolphins

Robinson played a part in keeping the Miami Dolphins neck-and-neck with the Colts, getting home for a sack on quarterback Daniel Jones while also forcing a fumble.

In the first quarter, Jones scrambled out of the pocket for two yards but Robinson punched the ball free. However, it rolled untouched out of bounds, allowing the Colts to punt the ball away.

As for Robinson’s sack, the pocket collapsed around Jones on a second-and-25, with Robinson bringing him down to force a third-and-29.

Robinson finished the game with five tackles, his plays directly contributing to two punts, giving the struggling Dolphin offense more chances to take the lead.

Robinson leads the Dolphins with five sacks on the season. He also has 20 tackles, five tackles for loss and a pass breakup.

title: Where are national outlets predicting Penn State will play this postseason? Duke’s Mayo Bowl the favorite pick after Week 11
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
It’s official: Penn State secured bowl eligibility with its 42-14 win over Minnesota on Saturday.

Now the question turns to which bowl game the Nittany Lions will play in. Many national media outlets have projected Penn State to play in various contests, with most of the projected destinations located far south of Happy Valley.

Here are the current bowl projections after Penn State beat the Golden Gophers in Week 11.

ESPN, On3: Duke’s Mayo Bowl

The most common of the projections continues to be the Duke’s Mayo Bowl, as ESPN once again has the Nittany Lions traveling to Charlotte, North Carolina. Now, On3 also projects them making the trip as well.

This would be the first time in school history Penn State would compete in the Duke’s Mayo Bowl, which is slated for 3:30 p.m. on Dec. 26 at Bank of America Stadium.

ESPN writer Kyle Bonagura continues to have Clemson as Penn State’s projected opponent, which would mark the second straight year it faces the Tigers. The two teams faced off in the Pinstripe Bowl last year with the Nittany Lions winning, 22-10.

Meanwhile, ESPN’s Mark Schlabach has Penn State squaring off against North Carolina for the first time since 1943, when the Tar Heels won 19-0 at home. North Carolina is in its second year under former New England Patriots head coach Bill Belichick and has a 5-5 record.

On3 projects the Nittany Lions to face SMU, which is a rematch of the first round of the 2024 College Football Playoff. Penn State won 38-10, as Tony Rojas and former linebacker Dom DeLuca each recorded a pick six against quarterback Kevin Jennings, who’s now in his final season with the Mustangs.

Sports Illustrated: Cactus Bowl

If Sports Illustrated’s bowl projection holds true, Penn State may be making a second cross-country trip of the season, as it has the Nittany Lions battling UCF in the Cactus Bowl in Tempe, Arizona.

The Cactus Bowl will be played at 7:30 p.m. on Dec. 26 at Mountain America Stadium, home of Arizona State. Penn State hasn’t participated in it before.

On the other hand, the Nittany Lions have played the Knights in the past, although it’s been 12 years since the two teams went toe-to-toe. Penn State won 26-24 with a last-second field goal in 2014 at the Croke Park Classic opener in Dublin, Ireland.

The Knights are 5-5 on the year, including an upset over then-No. 10 BYU on Oct. 24.

CBS: ReliaQuest Bowl

Penn State’s first bowl game projection in Florida comes from CBS, which predicts the Nittany Lions will face Ole Miss in the ReliaQuest Bowl at noon on Dec. 31. The game is played in Raymond James Stadium, the home of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

This is the first time Penn State would play in the ReliaQuest Bowl, although it’s played in the Outback Bowl five times before it was rebranded to the Tampa Bay Bowl and ultimately the ReliaQuest Bowl. The Nittany Lions have a 3-2 record in the Outback Bowl, last losing to Arkansas in 2022.

Penn State has only seen the Rebels in action once before, also in postseason play. The Nittany Lions lost to Ole Miss, 38-25, in the 2023 Peach Bowl.

Ole Miss is also in Year 1 under a new head coach, with Pete Golding replacing Lane Kiffin after he left for LSU during last year’s postseason.

The Rebels started the season on a strong note with two ranked wins over Louisville and the Tigers but have since struggled. Ole Miss is on a two-game losing streak with four losses this year.

The Athletic: Music City Bowl

The Athletic projects Penn State to head south for the Music City Bowl against South Carolina. It would be the Nittany Lions’ first appearance in that bowl, which will be played in Nashville, Tennessee, at 3 p.m. on Dec. 30.

The two teams haven’t faced each other since 1941, with Penn State holding a 2-0 all-time lead in the series history.

The Gamecocks have had a back-and-forth season, currently sitting at 6-4 and sixth in the SEC. After losing three straight games from the end of September into October, South Carolina beat then-No. 16 Florida and then-No. 11 Tennessee.

Those wins created a four-game streak that continued against Oklahoma and Texas A&M. However, South Carolina was blown out against Arkansas last week without quarterback LaNorris Sellers.

Former Penn State coaches Stan Drayton and Deion Barnes are currently on the Gamecocks’ staff.

title: Penn State LS Blaise Sokach-Minnick named semifinalist for Patrick Mannelly Award
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State's long snapper has been promoted to semifinalist status.

Blaise Sokach-Minnick was named one of 10 semifinalists for the Patrick Mannelly Award, given annually to the nation's top long snapper.

He's the third Penn State long snapper in a row to be named a semifinalist, following in the footsteps of Chris Stoll and Tyler Duzansky. Stoll became the lone Mannelly Award-winning Nittany Lion in 2022, while Duzansky was a finalist last season.

title: Penn State trustee emeritus Ira Lubert, wife Pam Estradt gift $75 million to university
author: Anna Nagle | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State alum Ira Lubert and his wife, Pam Estradt, have become the second largest donors in Penn State history with a commitment to donate $75 million in 2027.

The donation will go toward academic programs, the Beaver Stadium Revitalization project, the wrestling team and “future priorities.”

“This commitment is a transformative investment in our mission, and it will enhance the education we offer, strengthen many important programs and community pride, and deepen our impact in the Philadelphia area and beyond. It will also be a powerful catalyst for a fundraising campaign that promises to set a new standard for giving to the University, inspiring even greater ambition for Penn Staters past, present and future,” President Neeli Bendapudi said in a press release on Friday.

In 2024, the couple donated $1 million to Penn State Abington and have previously supported the campus via scholarships and emergency assistance, according to the release. Lubert previously served on Penn State Abington’s advisory board.

$49 million will go toward establishing the President’s Endowment for Academic Programs, creating a permanent fund for Penn State presidents to use to support academic excellence, student access and strategic initiatives.

$10 million was given for improvements to Penn State's wrestling program. Lubert, who wrestled at Penn State from 1970 to 1973, the release read.

$10 million is also slated to go toward creating the Lubert Family Welcome Center as a part of the Beaver Stadium Revitalization project.

In 2024, $4 million in real estate value was slated to be allocated for later goals.

Lubert graduated in 1973 from the College of Health and Human Development and led a career in private equity and real estate, as well as currently serving as a trustee emeritus for the Penn State Board of Trustees. After retiring from his career, Lubert has pursued a number of philanthropic goals, and has supported scholarships, student food security and Penn State Athletics in the past. Lubert was awarded the Alumni Fellow award in 1995 and the Distinguished Alumni Award in 2006.

While Estradt did not attend Penn State, she has a “long kinship” to the university, according to the release. Estradt's parents met at University Park and her twin daughters graduated in 2020; and she graduated from Moore College of Art and Design in Philadelphia in 1983.

The couple’s gift comes at the start of Penn State’s 2027 fundraising campaign.

“With the public launch of a new fundraising campaign on the horizon, we wanted to challenge ourselves and all Penn Staters to invest deeply across the university, from our academic excellence to our athletic traditions to our presence in commonwealth communities. Our gifts now will help shape what Penn State is for future generations,” Estradt and Lubert said in a statement.

title: Penn State women’s basketball loses to Arizona State, marking worst start in program history
author: Myles Hannak | Sports Editor
description:
Penn State officially had the worst season start in program history after its worst loss of the year.

The Lady Lions dropped a road contest to Arizona State, 85-41, falling to 0-4 on the season — something that had never happened in any season in history dating back to 1965.

First-year coach Tanisha Wright’s unit got off to a slow start, falling behind 23-13 after a sloppy first quarter. The Sun Devils were able to generate massive amounts of turnovers from the Lady Lions, as they logged seven over the first frame and allowed 11 points off those blunders.

Shooting figures were nearly identical between the two sides, but that trend was brief. Penn State started the second half with a bucket, but then went on a three-minute scoring drought that allowed a 12-0 Arizona State run.

The energy soon thereafter amped up for Wright’s squad up to the half, with graduate student guard Enjulina Gonzalez leading the charge, despite 2-of-9 shooting at the break. Guard Skylar Durley had a team-high six points on 3-of-4 shooting at halftime, followed by Ava Black’s five points on 100% shooting.

The Lady Lions became susceptible to Arizona State guard Madison Morson and forward Ayanna-Sarai Darrington, who each had 10 points and hadn’t missed a shot over eight combined attempts. Senior Sun Devils guard Rashunda Jones had dished eight assists and had three steals at the break, as Penn State trailed 45-24.

By halftime, Wright’s squad had shot 37% from the field and 16.7% from the free throw line, as its 3-of-8 mark from three-point range had been the only statistical advantage for Penn State. The Lady Lions trailed in rebounding by five, assists by eight and had 11 turnovers to Arizona State’s six.

The break wasn’t the solution, as Penn State started the second half with six turnovers to Arizona State’s one, which ballooned the lead to 33 for the Sun Devils. As things snowballed, Penn State’s scoring drought continued through most of the fourth quarter.

Penn State missed easy layups at the rack as it got outworked for a full 40 minutes, and it showed. Mentally, the Lady Lions appeared frustrated as the result became solidified.

For Arizona State, six players had double-digit scoring in its win. Durley led Penn State in scoring with eight points, while Gonzalez scored once the second half and finished 3-of-12 from the field. The Lady Lions shot 30% from the field, 26.7% from three and 41.7% from the charity stripe.

Wright’s unit committed 10 more turnovers than Arizona State and was out-rebounded by 12 in a drubbing where it led for only 1:04 minutes of total game time. The last time Penn State lost by 40 or more was Jan. 8 of last season, when then-No. 9 Michigan took down the Lady Lions, 105-65.

Up next

Penn State returns to Happy Valley on Thursday for the first time since its season opener at the Bryce Jordan Center on Nov. 2. The Lady Lions face Bowling Green for Education Day, with tipoff for Wright’s coaching debut at Rec Hall at 11 a.m.
