title: Penn State women's soccer earns No. 6 seed in NCAA bracket, hosts first round
author: Gabriel Kovadlo | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State is heading back to the NCAA Women’s College Cup for the 32nd consecutive time, dating back to 1995, the year after the program began varsity play.

The Nittany Lions have had approximately two weeks to prepare for the NCAA postseason, as the first round takes place this upcoming Friday, Nov. 20, through Sunday, Nov. 22.

The blue and white earned the No. 6 seed in the bottom left quadrant of the bracket and will take on Villanova at Jeffrey Field. The Wildcats finished 14-1-5 and won its program’s second-ever Big East title this year.

Penn State closed its regular season on Oct. 30, winning in dominant fashion against Indiana, 4-0. This resulted in the Nittany Lions finishing the season with a 9-4-5 and a Big Ten record of 7-2-3. The blue and white were also undefeated at home, going 6-0-3.

The blue and white is coming off an early exit in the Big Ten tournament, where they lost in the quarterfinals to then-No. 16 Purdue in an overtime clash, 2-1.

The Nittany Lions won their first and only NCAA title back in 2015, when they defeated Duke 1-0. The program’s all-time record is 60-26-3 in NCAA tournament play, and this year’s team looks to expand the win column and fight to become the next national champs.

title: Former Penn State men's soccer goalkeeper Kris Shakes earns yearly USL Championship award
author: Luci Palacios | The Daily Collegian
description:
Kris Shakes was named the USL Championship Goalkeeper of the Year while playing for New Mexico United. Shakes has continued to build on his success since his time with the Nittany Lions, earning one of the league’s top individual honors.

In his third professional season, Shakes recorded 117 saves and finished the regular season with a 78.5% save percentage. His performance helped him stand out among the league’s top players.

title: How Penn State men’s basketball’s offense can reach another level this season
author: Will Horstman | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is playing well offensively this season, but it still has room to grow.

Due to availability issues, Mike Rhoades and the Nittany Lions have turned to an offense that revolves around scoring inside with center Ivan Jurić, forward Roko Prkačin and forward Josh Reed. It worked against New Haven on Sunday at the Bryce Jordan Center, as Reed scored 20 points to lead Penn State to an 86-52 win over the Chargers.

But it only worked because New Haven doesn’t have the personnel to match up with Penn State’s frontcourt. Anytime Jurić (7-foot, 250 pounds) or Prkačin (6-foot-8, 230 pounds) had the ball, the Chargers, who don’t have anyone taller than 6-foot-9, would double them. It didn’t matter because Jurić and Prkačin still combined for 30 points.

Once Penn State plays a Big Ten team, that kind of production inside will be much harder to get. The Nittany Lions need sharpshooters Brant Byers and Roberts Blums back on the court to provide more perimeter shooting, which will bring this offense to a higher level.

“We had 17 assists on 27 baskets,” Rhoades said. “I still think it could even be better. I think we need to play with more of a hot ball. Having those guys out there, guys are going to find more assists and give those big guys a little more space.”

Rhoades runs an inside-outside scheme on offense, which means Penn State prioritizes scoring inside. If that’s not there, whoever has the ball can find an open shooter outside, as an opposing defense would usually help inside.

Against New Haven, there wasn’t much of a need to pass outside. Not only were Byers and Blums not active, but Jurić and Prkačin each drew six fouls to lead Penn State to shoot 27-for-31 at the free throw line.

The Chargers essentially threw everything they had at Prkačin and Jurić. Prkačin still had 16 points and 10 rebounds, while Jurić had 14 points and 10 rebounds.

With the success inside, Penn State took only 14 3-point attempts, making five of them. It continues a trend of minimal 3-point shooting for the Nittany Lions, who are averaging just 16.4 3-point attempts per game this season.

“I would like to shoot more threes, but I'd like to make sure we're making the right plays,” Rhoades said. “When teams start taking away our inside stuff, and maybe not foul us, then we'll find more threes. I think better defense can create some transition threes. That will get that number up a little bit more, too.”

Reed and guard Thomas Allard are Penn State’s best 3-point threats with Byers and Blums out. Reed shot 2-for-4 from three against New Haven, while Allard hit 2-for-7. Other than them, no one else looks willing to shoot 3-pointers, relying more on Jurić and Prkačin inside.

Byers and Blums will add more 3-point shooting once they’re back on the court because they shot over 39% from three at Miami (Ohio) and Davidson last season, respectively.

Byers, who missed the New Haven game due to having the flu, is expected back for Wednesday’s game against IU Indy. Rhoades said he might have a new update on Blums, who’s recovering from a broken finger, in the coming days, too.

Once both shooters are back on the floor, Jurić and Prkačin will have more opportunities to set others up for shots. Jurić had three assists against New Haven, but he should’ve had even more. Allard missed a layup and guard Reggie Grodin missed a three off of quality passes from Jurić. Prkačin had two assists as well.

Jurić is averaging 15.8 points and 12.6 rebounds per game, recording a double-double in each of Penn State’s first five games. Once those shooters return, expect Jurić to have more than the 1.2 assists per game he’s averaging right now, too.

Prkačin is shooting 81.1% from the floor even while getting doubled. More outside threat would open up more looks for Prkačin without having to be doubled.

Jurić and Prkačin give the Nittany Lions a strong presence inside. Reed has shown he’s a reliable, versatile scorer. If Byers and Blums reach their potential as 3-point shooters this season, Penn State’s offense could make a lot of noise in the Big Ten schedule.

title: Preview | No. 10 Penn State women’s volleyball closes regular season out against Rutgers
author: Madelyn Lawlor | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State continues to tear through the Big Ten, sustaining a nine-match winning streak.

The blue and white looks to finish the regular season strong with its final match before the Big Ten Tournament. The Nittany Lions have stacked up impressive conference wins in the closing stretch, but face one final home clash as they look to solidify a top-four seed and double bye in the tournament.

The blue and white swept both Maryland and No. 25 Illinois on the road, powered by strong offensive showings from right-side hitter Kennedy Martin and setter Alexis Stucky. The Nittany Lions improved to 21-5 overall and 13-3 in conference with the victories. The win against Illinois marked their sixth-straight ranked win.

Penn State has continued to build momentum through the gauntlet of Big Ten play, coming into form at the business end of the season. The last time the blue and white accumulated a win streak this long came in 2024. The Nittany Lions finished the season on a 12-game winning streak that started in mid-November and ended with a victory in the national championship game.

Penn State hosts Rutgers on Tuesday at 7 p.m. in Rec Hall. The Nittany Lions will then head to Fishers, Indiana, for the Big Ten Tournament, which begins Friday. They’re currently tied for second in the conference with No. 12 Oregon and No. 9 Wisconsin. The blue and white can lock up a double bye if it comes out on top against the Scarlet Knights. Penn State would then play Sunday in the quarterfinals.

Rutgers currently sits tied for 14th in the Big Ten, with a 4-12 conference record and a 13-15 mark overall. The Scarlet Knights have lost to every ranked team they have played thus far. This includes defeats against No. 1 Nebraska, then-No. 15 Indiana, No. 19 Minnesota, No. 18 Washington, Oregon and then-No. 11 Purdue.

Rutgers’ best conference win came against Michigan at home Nov. 5. Besides that victory, the Scarlet Knights have failed to beat teams ranked ahead of them in the conference standings.

Rutgers split its last two matches, getting swept by Wisconsin but defeating Maryland 3-2 in a close-fought battle, both at home.

The Scarlet Knights' offense is powered by freshmen right-side hitter and middle blocker Malia Romes and setter Brooke Baldwin. Romes leads Rutgers in kills per set and points per set, averaging 2.81 and 3.15, respectively. Baldwin fuels the attack, leading the team in assists per set with 5.44.

Rutgers remains in the lower tier of the conference in most statistical metrics. It’s not strong offensively or defensively, averaging a hitting percentage of .221, which ranks 15th in the conference, while also generating low numbers in blocks and digs. The Scarlet Knights’ strongest number is service aces, averaging 1.62 per set and ranking fifth in the conference. Outside hitter Karis Willow, a Penn State transfer, leads the squad with 38 on the season.

The blue and white has historically dominated Rutgers. The Nittany Lions have never lost to the Scarlet Knights, winning 24 straight since the first matchup in 2000. Many of these matches have ended in sweeps. Penn State has swept its past five matches against Rutgers.

The Scarlet Knights haven’t won a set against the blue and white since October 2021. The Nittany Lions will look to keep the streak going and close out the regular season with a victory at Rec Hall.

title: Sports, holiday spirit | Here’s what’s happening in the valley
author: Sarah Price | The Daily Collegian
description:
After 13 consecutive weeks of nonstop work, there's just one more week until Penn State students finally have a break.

If you’re looking to soak up the last few moments of the fall semester, here’s what’s happening in the valley.

Monday, Nov. 16

Campus Orchestra Concert

Join the Campus Orchestra for an evening of music at Eisenhower Auditorium at 7:30 p.m. The program features music from Mozart and Beethoven and concludes with Rimsky-Korsakov.

Tickets are available through the Arts Ticket Center.

Tuesday, Nov. 17

"The Nightmare Before Christmas"

Whether you’re still craving the Halloween aesthetic or already making your Christmas list, The State Theatre is playing “The Nightmare Before Christmas” at 7:30 p.m. Why pick between the two when you can have both wrapped up in one, perfect movie?

The 1993 stop-motion animated film is based on a 1982 poem by Tim Burton, who helped pioneer goth subculture in Hollywood. The film was directed by Burton’s friend, Henry Selick, known for his work in stop-motion animation and for films such as “Coraline.”

Tickets can be purchased online or at the theatre.

Penn State women’s volleyball vs. Rutgers

If you haven’t made it to Rec Hall for a women’s volleyball game this semester, this is your last chance to join the wRECking Crew, the official student section of Penn State volleyball, for their final home match against Rutgers at 7 p.m.

The blue and white-clad team currently sit 21-5 overall, and 13-3 in Big Ten play, after sweeping Illinois on Saturday and has clinched a spot in the 2026 Allstate Big Ten Volleyball Tournament in Indiana.

Tickets are free for Penn State students as the Nittany Lions face the Scarlet Knights.

Wednesday, Nov. 18

Penn State men’s basketball vs. IU Indy

It’s finally basketball season in Happy Valley, with Penn State men’s basketball currently 3-1 this season. You can join Legion of Blue, the official student section of Penn State basketball, for the Nittany Lions' game against Indiana at the Bryce Jordan Center at 6:30 p.m.

Tickets can be purchased on Ticketmaster.

Thursday, Nov. 19

Light Up Night

If you’ve recently walked downtown at night, which now falls upon us around 5 p.m. thanks to the end of daylight savings, you might’ve noticed lights strung up in the trees. It’s the first sign that the holidays are near, which means winter break is on the horizon.

Start your Christmas cheer with Light Up Night from 5 to 8 p.m. in downtown State College on Fraser Street’s MLK Plaza and the 100 block of Allen Street.

Enjoy the winter carnival as the night concludes with Santa lighting the evergreen tree at the Allen Street Gates.

Friday, Nov. 20

Improv Comedy Show

Join The Blue Brick Theatre at 7 p.m. for their Friday night improv comedy show that features three long-form improv sets, with an intermission between each, and ends at 8:30 p.m.

Tickets for their Friday Night Improv can be purchased on the theatre’s website, with student discounts available — just make sure to bring your student ID. You can also purchase at the door with cash or card.

Saturday, Nov. 21

Winter Reflections Craft Show

Are you in need of handmade gifts this holiday season? Take the short drive to South Hills School of Business and Technology for their annual Winter Reflections Craft Show. Shop local vendors for handmade goods, gift items, homemade food and more.

The craft show will be held from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. with free admission and parking, located at 480 Waupelani Drive.

Penn State Football vs. Rutgers

After a much-needed 42-14 win over Minnesota, Penn State will face Rutgers for the last home game of the season. After Saturday’s win, the Nittany Lions are officially bowl eligible at 6-4.

The game will start at 3:30 p.m.

title: What if ‘Dancing With The Stars’ had a Penn State week? Imagining the season 35 dances
author: Rebecca Fein | The Daily Collegian
description:
“Dancing With The Stars” pairs professional ballroom dancers with celebrities to compete for the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, and to compete across our television screens some autumn Tuesdays.

Picture a night where the show’s often blue-lit studio takes on the feel of an orange-hued, fall day in State College. You can probably see a blur of white in Beaver Stadium, smell the steam emanating from the many grills crammed in tailgate-designated lots. Maybe you hear feet shuffling out of the Forum Building, feel early November’s remaining rain dampen the hems of your jeans.

I’m prompting you to visualize all of this to pose one question: What if “Dancing with the Stars” had a Penn State-themed week?

In this fantasy world I’m inviting you to, the show would be scored by its existing judges and would find a guest judge in Penn State alum Stephen Nedoroscik, the 2024 Olympic bronze medalist in men’s pommel horse. (Nedoroscik’s a season-33 “Dancing With The Stars” alum, too.)

Let’s see what season 35 couples would dance to if a Penn State-themed “Dancing with the Stars” week became a reality.

Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson

Shum and Johnson, who are among the most technically skilled of this year's couples, would perform a crisp Argentine tango to “Seven Nation Army” by The White Stripes.

After week five's Super Bowl Night samba to “Yeah!” by Usher, we know Shum is capable of revealing his seductive, more serious side. This dance would be one of the cleanest of the season, with, of course, the classic Argentine tango foot crosses.

Shum would be in a suit colored pink and black, an homage to the original Penn State colors.

Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov

Glenn and Pashkov would perform a quickstep to “Kernkraft 400” by Zombie Nation, a classic Penn State football song.

Pairing this fan-favorite couple with the iconic “We Are Penn State” chant will secure high scores from the judges and the fans.

On the show, Glenn has done a beautiful contemporary dance and spun across the floor in a cha-cha and rumba, but one of her lower-scoring dances this season was her Week 8 quickstep to “A Star is Born” from “Hercules,” so why not give her a shot at redemption?

Due to Glenn’s athleticism, the number would be full of technical tricks that are sure to be trending on TikTok later that week, including the Penn State Drum Major flip, the Penn State Cheerleaders’ backflips and, of course, a show-stopping Lionette kickline.

Jenna Dewan and Val Chmerkovskiy

The rookie herself will perform a rumba to the song “In The Air Tonight” by Phil Collins.

Dewan and Chmerkovskiy would leave the audience on their feet after knocking this dance out of Beaver Stadium, including a perfect execution of the signature Cuban hips.

There are copious dating rumors about Dewan and Chmerknovskiy floating around online (even though both individuals are happily married), and the rumba would put their physical and emotional connection to the ultimate test.

Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach

Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach would dance a cha-cha to “Mo Bamba” by Sheck Wes.

The two would begin at the top of the stage with an impressive lift. Then, when the beat drops, they would prance across the floor and rock out to the chorus, making us feel like we’re right at home in Beaver Stadium.

Karagach would be sporting a short fringe dress the color of none other than Penn State’s navy blue. The dress would feature sheer, bedazzled sleeves that spell out “For The Glory” in gems.

Frech would don a white button-down, also completely decked out in sparkles, but with tear-away fabric for him to rip his shirt open during the dance's finale.

Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold

For the comedy king, Wood and Arnold would go a bit of a different route for this week. They would dress Wood up as the Nittany Lion, while Arnold sported the signature look of a Lionette, and the two would dance a jazz routine to the “Lion King Remix.”

Arnold’s choreography would draw inspiration from how members of the student section shake their pom poms to this song. She would not be afraid to teach Wood how to flip and spin her.

This couple would be sure to secure votes with this spectacle.

Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik

Ravnik’s outstanding choreography is going to be put to the test when this couple dances a Viennese waltz to none other than the Penn State alma mater.

I can picture Ali in a long, white dress with a sheer train. She’d be covered in sparkles, and the lyrics to Penn State’s alma mater would be gracing the trim.

Despite the challenging song, this couple would tear up the dance floor and make the audience tear up with this beautiful tribute to “dear old state.

Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas

After Higgins’ successful paso doble from dedication week, during which she dedicated her dance to her home country of Ireland, another paso doble to “Fight On State” by Joseph Sanders would be sure to impress the crowds.

Fans have been questioning Higgin’s power and say she only does well on “pretty dances,” so this will become her test to prove the people wrong.

There's straight 10s across the board for these dances! If Penn State week on “Dancing With The Stars” ever does happen, it’s safe to say “we are” in for a treat.

title: Big Ten roundup | Backup QBs shine, Nebraska shuts out Rutgers in Week 11 action
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
In a week when multiple teams gained bowl eligibility, there weren’t many upsets outside of Maryland’s comeback victory over Wisconsin, a rare occurrence considering the volume of upsets and drama this season.

Various backup quarterbacks got their chance to shine, including a record-setting performance from Maryland’s Cardell Williams. Oregon and Iowa beat up on their unranked opponents, while Nebraska had the lone shutout on Saturday.

Here’s a deeper look into how the Big Ten did in Week 11.

Backup quarterbacks build steam

Many starting quarterbacks are injured, including UCLA’s Nico Iamaleava, Indiana’s Josh Hoover, Ohio State’s Julian Sayin and Maryland’s Malik Washington.

On Friday, Bruins’ backup quarterback Ty Dieffenbach went 13-for-20 with 232 passing yards and two touchdowns to beat Illinois, 22-14. Wide receiver Aidan Mizell had a monster day for UCLA, tallying 176 receiving yards and a touchdown.

Curt Cignetti to give Grant Wilson the nod, who led the Hoosiers to a comeback victory over Minnesota in their last matchup.

Wilson threw for 305 yards, two touchdowns and an interception against No. 18 USC on Saturday, but it was Indiana’s three interceptions that led it to a 27-13 victory.

The Buckeyes went with Luke Fahey for the third straight game after he put up 260 yards against USC and 360 yards against Oregon despite losing both contests. He finally got Ohio State back in the win column with a 28-19 victory over Northwestern.

117 of his 201 passing yards were to wide receiver Jeremiah Smith, who also had a touchdown. Fahey also found running back Isaiah West and wide receiver Devin McCuin in the end zone, but threw an interception as well.

Cardell Williams’ record-setting Big Ten debut

Williams, a Sacramento State transfer, got his first start as a Terrapin, leading the team to a 24-21 victory over Wisconsin.

He went 21-for-23 with 183 yards, his 91.3% completion rate ranking second among debuting Big Ten quarterbacks since 1996, and he set a school record for consecutive completions with a series of 19 passes to close the game, which are the most by a Big Ten quarterback this season.

Williams accounted for all three of Maryland’s touchdowns including a passing touchdown and two rushing touchdowns. Kicker Sean O'Haire sealed the deal with a game-winning 30-yard field goal.

Ranked domination

No. 15 Iowa and No. 16 Oregon both destroyed their respective unranked opponents.

The Hawkeyes and Ducks each led Purdue and Michigan 21-7 at halftime and didn’t allow another touchdown, coasting to victory. Iowa won 28-7, while Oregon tacked on a field goal to win 31-7.

Oregon quarterback Dylan Raiola’s four touchdown passes were the highlight of the game, all four of which were to different targets. Raiola finished 20-for-28 with 341 passing yards.

Meanwhile, Iowa primarily used a rushing attack to beat the Boilermakers, as three different players found the end zone on the ground: running back Xavier Williams, wide receiver Tony Diaz and quarterback Hank Brown.

Nebraska shuts out Rutgers

A Cornhusker touchdown in all four quarters and two interceptions on defense were the highlights of Nebraska’s 31-0 win over Rutgers at SHI Stadium in Piscataway, New Jersey.

Quarterback Anthony Colandrea found the end zone with his legs and hit tight ends Carter Nelson and Luke Lindenmeyer through the air for touchdowns, closing the game with 188 passing yards.

Scarlet Knight quarterback AJ Surace was replaced by Sean Ashenfelder after completing just four of 12 passes for 24 yards and two interceptions. Ashenfelder went three-for-four with 18 yards.

Nebraska earned bowl eligibility, improving to 6-4 overall and 3-4 in the Big Ten.

Washington gets back on track despite rough morning travel

It’s one close game after another for the Huskies, as they faced Michigan State coming off a three-point loss to Penn State in Week 10.

Washington got back in the win column with a 21-14 victory over Michigan State despite arriving in East Lansing around 2:20 a.m. after the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide ground stop Friday night. As a result, the game was moved to a 5:30 p.m. kickoff.

After the Huskies and Spartans entered halftime tied 14-14, both offenses stalled throughout the second half. Running back Jayden Limar’s 1-yard rushing touchdown late in the fourth quarter sent Washington through with a win and bowl eligibility.

Limar was Washington’s leading rusher despite only having 29 yards. It was all quarterback Demond Williams Jr., who had 288 passing yards and two touchdowns, both to wide receiver Chris Lawson.

title: As Penn State alum Yash Patel grows in content creation, he does ‘it in a happy way’
author: Alli Satterfield | The Daily Collegian
description:
Yash Patel, who graduated from Penn State in 2024 with a degree in finance, landed sixth place on Season 28 of the reality TV show “Big Brother,” and the 24-year-old of Monroe Township, New Jersey.

He survived the social experiment and competition television show for 73 days, living with and competing against strangers with no connection to the outside world for a $750,000 prize. The show allowed him to leave his nine-to-five job to focus fully on his content — which is mainly lifestyle for men — and create his social presence.

“I felt very much like a square peg in a circle mold … that’s how I felt sitting at my desk, nine-to-five finance job,” Yash said. “So I was like, ‘Let me start making content.’”

Yash wasn’t a content creator or campus celebrity when he was a student at Penn State, though. He was a normal student who joined a business fraternity and completed a semester abroad.

Darsh Patel, 26, of Monroe Township, New Jersey, said he was always the experimental brother. He would try things, fail and pass what he learned onto Yash.

But Darsh learned early on that there’s more room for financial growth in content creation than there is in a typical nine-to-five job. Darsh works with content creators as a consultant, and he encouraged his younger brother to get into the social media business.

“He was working a normal job, and he was not making insane money," Darsh said. "He was doing a very normal thing. When you see potential in someone, you want them to achieve it.”

The two brothers worked together to create a content-growth plan for Yash, Darsh said. Initially, Yash’s content was just taking his camera along for the ride of his day — and it still is, for the most part — but “Big Brother” was an unexpected boost that both of them were excited about.

Since Yash was originally an alternate for the show, he watched one or two seasons to prepare, and when he ended up being selected, he was excited about the social nature of the show’s competition.

Yash said he ended up becoming close with a lot of contestants, including his co-star Melody Morris. His “10 out of 10” experience at Penn State, as he described it, and time on “Big Brother” helped him develop into the person and content creator he’s continuing to become.

Sam Johki, who graduated from Penn State in 2024 with a degree in finance, was Yash’s travel buddy during their semester abroad. He said Yash was already disciplined, dedicated and encouraging during their time in Barcelona, and recalled sitting together on the beach in Greece and talking about their goals.

“He’s always been someone you can have a really good time with, but you can also have those intellectual conversations with,” Johki, 24, of Kennett Square, Pennsylvania, said. “He’s always been a good person to bounce perspectives off of.”

Darsh and Johki both said they could picture Yash going on “Survivor” or “The Traitors.” Yash said the only opportunity he would be skeptical about is a dating show, but generally, he’s open to any new adventure.

What’s coming next for Yash, he said, is the million dollar question. But he knows he wants to continue growing his social media platforms and enjoying the publicity that is coming from “Big Brother.” He said he’s interested in possibly exploring other competition-based reality TV shows too.

He just hopes to keep connecting with other people and showing his followers how hard work can pay off with the power of positivity, he added.

“Go put yourself out there, and do it in a happy way,” Yash said. “I promise you, life’s better with a smile. Be grateful, be positive. It’s changed my life, and I fundamentally believe it has the power to change everybody else’s too.”

title: No. 1 Penn State wrestling shuts out Oklahoma in first road dual
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State traveled to Norman, Oklahoma, to face the Sooners at Lloyd Noble Center for their first road meet of the season.

The Nittany Lions pitched another shutout in a 41-0 win against Oklahoma, with multiple wrestlers in blue and white gaining wins against ranked opponents.

Here’s how each match went down.

125 pounds: No. 1 Luke Lilledahl (PSU) vs. Sebastian Degennaro (OU)

The bout stayed at a standstill through the duration of the first period, with neither wrestler scoring. Lilledahl scored an escape point to begin the second period, before quickly notching a takedown.

Degennaro notched two escape points, one in the second period and another to begin the third. Lilledahl’s riding time continued to pile up, giving him a point for riding time, as the opening match finished with a 5-2 decision.

Penn State opened up with a 3-0 lead.

133 pounds: Masanosuke Ono (PSU) vs. No. 15 Isaiah Powe (OU)

Ono and Powe opened the first period with hand fighting while on their feet, and both wrestlers patiently waited for an opportunity to earn a takedown. Ono reached for Powe’s ankles, bringing the Sooner to the mat for a takedown, and Powe earned an escape point.

Ono quickly snatched the ankle again, a skill that he’s proven to have within his first two matches of the season, to notch two takedowns in the opening period. Throughout the rest of the match, Ono was consistently dealing with a bloody nose, something that forced the clock to stop multiple times.

The Nittany Lion extended his lead with an escape point to begin the second period. Powe nearly took Ono to the ground, but he kicked out of the grip. However, the Sooner stayed relentless, earning a takedown in the final seconds of the second period.

Ono’s quickness continued to be an issue for Powe, as he grabbed a hold of his ankle again, but couldn't finish the job with a takedown.

Ono came out on top in his first matchup against a ranked opponent, defeating Powe 7-5. His decision victory doubled Penn State’s lead to 6-0.

141 pounds: No. 3 Marcus Blaze (PSU) vs. No. 11 Tyler Wells (OU)

Blaze made his debut at 141 pounds against Oklahoma, and immediately used his strength to grab the lower body of Wells and score the first points of the bout with a takedown. Blaze showcased his power, riding out Well to end the first period.

During the second period, the wrestlers repeatedly pushed each other out of bounds while fighting for position. Both were brought to the mat, and Blaze was awarded the takedown in the final seconds of the period.

After a leg takedown from Blaze, he pushed Wells’ shoulders to the mat for the pin. Blaze made a statement in his first match of the season with a win, extending the Nittany Lions’ lead to 12-0.

149 pounds: No. 4 Shayne Van Ness (PSU) vs. No. 14 Jack Gioffre (OU)

In the opening minutes of the first period, action was stopped for a potentially dangerous hold on Jack Gioffre. After review, neither a takedown nor a potentially dangerous hold was awarded to either wrestler. Van Ness pushed through a hard-fought battle on the mat to score his first takedown.

Gioffre didn’t make it easy for Van Ness, scoring an escape point after Van Ness racked up riding time. Van Ness closed the period with an unanswered takedown and added more riding time to the count.

The two started neutral to start the third period. Gioffre tried to attack, but Van Ness countered and took position to add another takedown to the stat sheet. Van Ness pulled away in the third, adding two more takedowns and a point for riding time to bring the final score to 16-4.

Van Ness gave Penn State its first major decision of the night, pushing the lead to 16-0.

157 pounds: No. 2 Tyler Kasak (PSU) vs No. 16 Rafael Hipolito Jr. (OU)

Hipolito attacked the right leg of Kasak, bringing him to the ground, but Kasak didn’t give up a takedown while on the mat. Kasak brought down Hipolito for his first takedown, but Kasak couldn’t prevent the escape.

Hipolito began on top after a stoppage, but Kasak immediately secured an escape point after returning to his feet.

After a battle on the mat, Hipolito eluded Kasak’s grip to cut into the Nittany Lion’s lead. Hipolito was given a point due to Kasak’s stalling, as he started to build momentum with 30 seconds left in the third period.

Hipolito tied the match with another stalling point within the final seconds, sending the match to overtime.

After backing away for much of the match, Kasak finished the job with a final takedown in the first 30 seconds to end Hipolito’s late push and avoid a last-second loss with a 7-4 win in sudden victory.

165 Pounds: No. 1 PJ Duke (PSU) vs. Bryce Burkett (OU)

Duke got a hold of Burkett early, winning a takedown early in the first period. Later, Duke grabbed the leg of Burkett, and pushed him to the ground after being off balance. Burkett escaped both holds to earn two points.

Duke remained persistent, bringing Burkett back to the mat not too long after the escape. Burkett broke free for another escape point. While both wrestlers were on the ground, Duke took top position on Burkett to notch his fourth takedown of the first period.

Inching close to a major decision, Duke compiled two more takedowns by using his strength against Burkett to put him on the mat. Burkett earned his fifth escape point, but Duke nullified the point with his seventh takedown to earn a 21-5 tech fall.

174 Pounds: No. 1 Mitchell Mesenbrink (PSU) vs. No. 31 Tyler Eise (OU)

Mesenbrink stayed on top of Eise for a takedown before a stoppage was called for a stalemate. After starting in the middle, Eise fled the grip of Mesenbrink for an escape point. Mesenbrink shot at the legs of Eise and worked his way to the top for another takedown in the opening period.

On his third straight attempt, Mesenbrink finally did enough for the referees to award a takedown to end the second period.

After starting on bottom, Mesenbrink powered his way out for an escape point. Mesenbrink followed by taking both of Eise's legs and driving him to the mat for another takedown. Nearing a tech fall, Mesenbrink turned to Eise for his fourth takedown.

Mesenbrink finished with a 20-4 tech fall win.

184 Pounds: No. 2 Rocco Welsh (PSU) vs. Brian Soldano (OU)

Welsh and Soldano battled on their feet during the opening minutes, with neither wrestler tallying a point in the first period.

Welsh finally got a hold of Soldano, but Soldano quickly escaped for the first points of the match. Welsh continued to find success in the second, raising Soldano and taking him to the mat for a takedown. He did the same a bit later, as he grabbed Soldano’s hips and pulled him to the mat for a second takedown, leading 6-2.

Welsh once again took down Soldano, and his power started to overwhelm Soldano, as he allowed two more takedowns. Soldano’s escape wasn’t enough, and Welsh was granted a riding time point to bring the final score to a 16-5 major decision win.

His win gave Penn State a 33-0 lead.

197 Pounds: No. 1 Josh Barr (PSU) vs. Jersey Robb (OU)

Barr held the body of Robb and drove his legs, using Robb backwards momentum to knock him off his feet. Then, Barr took Robb’s left leg and kicked down the other to add three more points to his score.

Barr’s defense got him another takedown. Barr did a great job of taking position while on the mat again, building on his lead with a fourth takedown. A fifth takedown for Barr was won the same way, as he found the recipe for success.

Barr escaped Robb, then gained a hold of Robb’s legs to win a total of four points in the third period and take the 19-4 tech-fall.

285 pounds: Connor Mirasola (PSU) vs. No. 23 Bradley Hill (OU)

In the final bout of the night, it was a slow start, with neither wrestler scoring in the first period.

Mirasola started on bottom at the start of the second period and escaped Hill’s grip. Hill scored a takedown after diving at the left ankle of Hill and driving him down.

Hill came closer to Oklahoma’s first win of the night after notching an escape. A surge of scrambling from both wrestlers, with counters and takedown attempts coming from both sides, all led to a stalemate.

Penn State challenged the no-call from the referees, arguing that Mirasola won a takedown during the stretch. The call was overturned, awarding Mirasola a takedown and an escape from Hill to bring the score to 5-4.

In need of a takedown, Mirasola reached for the right leg of Hill and dragged him to the mat to secure the takedown with 10 seconds left. Mirasola defended the final attacks of Hill, bringing the final tally to a 7-6 decision win.

title: Penn State men's basketball drubs New Haven behind complete team performance
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
Many words describe Penn State’s defeat of New Haven on Sunday, but “easy” probably isn’t one of them.

The Nittany Lions persevered through another slow start, using 20 points from fifth-year forward Josh Reed to secure an 86-52 victory over the Chargers in the Bryce Jordan Center.

“I don't give a damn about the scoreboard,” Mike Rhoades said. “(That) will take care of itself. It's about the standards. There's a certain way this team has to play to beat teams in the Big Ten. It has to start well before that. There's gotta be a standard of high-level basketball no matter who the opponent is; that's how we're gonna get better.”

Penn State’s offense was sluggish to open the afternoon. After a mid-range basket by Teshaun Steele, Roko Prkačin responded with a layup in the paint.

The Croatian got to the charity stripe on the Nittany Lions’ next possession, but missed both shots. Dasonte Bowen missed a layup of his own, and Thomas Allard failed to connect on a pair of three-point shots, allowing Penn State to take a slight edge at the first media timeout.

After several free throws from Bowen, François Wibaut and Josh Reed, a wide-open three-pointer by Reed and a contested layup by Ivan Jurić erased Penn State’s deficit.

Reed converted on a smooth jumper to cap a 14-0 run for the Nittany Lions, and after a single free throw from New Haven ended the streak, swished a long-range shot to hit double figures near the first half’s midpoint.

The Chargers responded with a three-point shot of their own before Prkačin made a pair of free throws and Bowen netted a tough layup. Already holding a significant advantage, Penn State further pulled away when Wibaut made his first field goal with a flashy euro-step.

New Haven struggled from beyond the arc in the opening 20 minutes. Kheni Briggs made the Chargers’ second three-point shot of the contest after a 1-for-8 start, but Allard quickly answered.

Jay Rodgers continued the Nittany Lions’ hot first-half shooting with a long-range shot late in the period, the last field goal that Penn State would record before halftime.

“Definitely his best game since he's been here, and I'm really proud of him,” Rhoades said of Rodgers. He's a game manager. He's a really good passer. He sees the floor. We need him to play high-level defense, especially against the teams on our schedule coming up.”

Juric made a pair of charity-stripe shots to give the blue and white a 41-28 lead at the break.

After Prkačin got the scoring started, Reed built on his standout first half with a driving layup to open the second. Two Bowen jump shots sandwiched one from Steele in a stretch of end-to-end scoring while Penn State maintained a healthy lead early in the frame.

Back-to-back blocks by Wibaut in a single possession highlighted a tight defensive streak by the Nittany Lions, but New Haven hung around with consecutive two-point buckets.

Prkačin converted from the line, Reggie Grodin made the first two field goals of his career and Juric smoothly scored a breakaway layup to stretch the lead to 19 and force a Charger timeout with less than 10 minutes to play in the contest.

“I tell him, ‘You’ve got to be like a crazy dude when you go out there,” Rhoades said of Grodin. “Just don't care, fly around and create great energy and juice for your team. And he did that today, and he does that in practice,”

While it was a tough afternoon for Allard from beyond the arc, he found nylon on a corner shot to find his second make of the game after starting 1-for-5 from long range.

Rodgers and Reed made layups and the former sank two shots from the free throw line as the clock wound down. Juric snagged a defensive rebound to reach 10 for the afternoon, giving the Croatian center a fifth consecutive double-double in the young season.

Reed stole the ball in the defensive end, charged down the court and rose up for an emphatic, one-handed slam to deliver an exclamation point on his 20-point performance.

“That's my first one here at Penn State, so it was pretty cool,” Reed said. “Overall tonight, I thought we played really well. I don't think we’ve played a full 40 minutes of basketball this year yet, and I feel like we did that tonight, and the results showed (that).

Injury report

Guard Roberts Blums remains sidelined due to a broken finger, as Rhoades said the junior will be out for a “couple weeks” after Penn State’s Nov. 5 clash with Chattanooga.

Forward Brant Byers wasn’t seen on the bench for the Nittany Lions. After the game, Rhoades confirmed that the Miami (OH) transfer has the flu.

Up next

Penn State will wrap up its three-game homestand with a matchup against IU Indy on Wednesday. Tipoff is set for 6:30 p.m. in the Bryce Jordan Center.

title: Week 11 report card | Run game takes over, defense stands tall in blowout win over Minnesota
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Penn State has put together three straight wins after dominating Minnesota in Beaver Stadium on Saturday. The Nittany Lions once again got out to a scorching start and cruised to a 42-14 victory.

There was significant improvement in the second half, as Penn State kept the Golden Gophers comfortably at bay despite slowing down after a 28-0 first-half lead.

Here’s how I’d grade each part of the Nittany Lions’ win over Minnesota.

Overall: B+

Penn State was dominant. It was all Nittany Lions in the first half, and even with the score in the second half being 14-14, they still had control of the game. It’s never going to be perfect in college football, but Penn State played its best game of the season against a sneaky good Minnesota team to lock up bowl eligibility.

Coaching staff: B+

Both Taylor Mouser and D’Anton Lynn’s playcalling were stellar on Saturday.

Mouser has clearly found what’s working for the offense, while Lynn continues to add complexities to the defense, featuring a three-linebacker formation for much of the game.

The only real negative was Matt Campbell’s decision to keep some of his starters in, like Rocco Becht, who was slow to get up late in the game and still remained in the game. Campbell eventually put in Alex Manske, but it wasn’t until Becht had taken multiple snaps after.

Offense: B+

Penn State’s offense is putting it all together. It didn’t need Becht to be the hero, relying on a strong run game mixed with minimal passing when needed. Despite stalling a bit in the second half, the offense still put up 42 points in a blowout win.

Pass game: C+

Becht had very low numbers, some of which is likely due to the weather conditions, as it rained throughout the game while the temperature neared 32 degrees.

However, in his 15 passes, he had three touchdowns and nine completions for 84 yards. Additionally, Manske entered the game and was efficient, completing both of his passes, including a lob pass off his back foot to running back James Peoples for a touchdown.

Becht didn’t do much, but he also didn’t have to, and that’s what leads to this passing grade.

Run game: A

The run game was the aspect of the offense that carried Penn State’s unit. Whatever adjustments were made at the bye week have certainly paid off, as the duo of running backs Carson Hansen and Cam Wallace have found what the coaching staff has been looking for.

Hansen played in just the first half after leaving the game at the end of the half limping. However, he ran wild, rushing for 126 yards and multiple explosive runs.

Wallace also had a couple of big runs himself in his 82-yard day, and the holes the offensive line were creating allowed the running backs to thrive.

Offensive line: B

The offensive line had a mix of good and bad in its performance. On one hand, the run blocking was impressive, but Becht was sacked three times, which doesn’t count the couple of scrambles he had for short gains.

In pass protection, Penn State’s unit struggled to pick up stunts, but despite those struggles, the run game was the story, and a big part of that was because of the offensive line.

Defense: B

The defense limited Minnesota to 14 points, with both of the touchdowns coming in the second half. It dominated the line of scrimmage and also prevented consistency in the pass game despite some lapses in the second half, causing the grade to drop a bit.

Pass rush: B

The pass rush showed significant improvement, having multiple sacks for the first time in Big Ten play.

That came from multiple different position groups, as Lynn schemed up different ways to get pressure. The rush continued to close the pocket on Minnesota quarterback Drake Lindsey and controlled the line of scrimmage throughout.

Linebackers: C+

The linebackers had an interesting day. The tackling and run defense was very strong, as the unit deployed five different linebackers during the game.

This included a breakout performance from Cam Smith, who tallied eight tackles.

However, both Tony Rojas and Marcus Neal Jr. were the players in coverage on Minnesota’s two big pass plays to running back Darius Taylor. Neither of which kept up with Taylor, and those plays were big in the Golden Gophers scoring both of their touchdowns.

Secondary: B

The secondary, despite not having a key depth piece in Jahmir Joseph, had a strong game. It limited Lindsey to 185 passing yards and only struggled in coverage a couple of times.

This did include a touchdown pass in which cornerback Josiah Zayas was beat, but outside of that, the stellar cornerbacks had another strong performance to prevent Minnesota’s passing game from gaining rhythm.

Special teams: A

The special teams had a clean day across the board. Kicker Ryan Barker went a perfect 6-for-6 on extra points, and punter Nathan Tiyce had an average of 44.6 yards per punt. Wide receiver Zay Robinson only had two punt returns, one of which set Penn State up with great field position on a 19-yard return.

title: Stock up, stock down | Penn State’s pass rush succeeds, pass game quiet against Minnesota
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State continued its hot post-bye week stretch with a third straight win on Saturday, defeating Minnesota, 42-14.

The Nittany Lions dominated the first half with four touchdowns, as running backs Carson Hansen and Cam Wallace scored alongside tight end Benjamin Brahmer and Rocco Becht. The defense also played one of its best games with three shutout quarters and a strong pass rush.

Here’s who’s trending up and down after Week 11.

Stock up: Alex McPherson

Penn State’s pass rush has struggled to affect opposing quarterbacks this season, with Tony Rojas having nearly half the team’s total sacks.

In arguably Penn State’s best game of the season against the Golden Gophers, the Nittany Lions had three sacks and played at a season-best level. Defensive end Alex McPherson led the charge, earning a sack and two tackles for loss.

McPherson’s 10-yard sack against Drake Lindsey was his first as a Nittany Lion and the first solo sack of his career. He’s consistently grown over his sophomore year, evident by starting in Penn State’s last three games.

Stock up: Carson Hansen

While his dominant performance came from just one half of play, Hansen produced his second straight 100-yard game as he continued to solidify himself as worthy of the starting role.

On the Nittany Lions’ second offensive play, Hansen broke free for a 34-yard pickup, making his way into the red zone. The following drive, he continued to pound the rock, finding the red zone once again for Penn State.

Hansen’s biggest play of the day came on a 46-yard rushing touchdown as he made four defenders miss en route to the end zone. Less than 10 minutes later, however, he limped off the field to the locker room. He didn’t return for the second half.

“I do think he'll be all right,” Campbell said. “I don’t think it’s a significant injury, but we’ll certainly know more probably earlier this week about what his availability will be next week.”

Stock down: Pass game

The Nittany Lions recorded just 122 yards through the air against Minnesota, with 38 coming in garbage time from backup quarterback Alex Manske. Becht completed just nine passes, throwing the ball just 15 times.

Wide receiver Chase Sowell didn’t contribute to the passing attack, as he was targeted just once but couldn’t haul in Becht’s pass. He recorded a combined 276 yards in his last two contests, which were against Michigan and Washington, making Saturday a stark difference from Sowell’s recent success.

Tight ends Andrew Rappleyea and Benjamin Brahmer were the only players with multiple catches, although they recorded a mere 68 yards. It was a quiet week overall from the passing attack that generated under 200 yards for just the third time this year.

Stock up: Cam Smith

After he was sidelined for the first three games of Big Ten play due to injury, linebacker Cam Smith saw his most playing time of the season against Minnesota.

The Nittany Lions ran a three-linebacker formation for much of Saturday’s game, resulting in Rojas, Kooper Ebel and either Smith, Marcus Neal Jr. or Cael Brezina taking the field together. Smith saw the most time as the third linebacker.

“It was really great to see Cam be able to capitalize on some of his moments tonight,” Ebel said. “He's had a whirlwind of a season just with injuries, so to be able to get out there and then make the most of it, man, that's how you get more opportunities if you capitalize on those opportunities you're given.”

Smith finished the night with eight tackles, including five solo tackles, the most among the Nittany Lions.

Stock down: Third quarter defense

For the second straight week, Penn State’s defense faltered in the third quarter. It gave up 11 points last week against Washington and 14 points to Minnesota this week.

Although the Nittany Lions were able to rebound and stop the Golden Gophers after their two scoring drives, it still showed their defense hasn’t been as strong out of the break.

Tony Rojas had some of the biggest miscues in the third quarter, as he was burned on a 58-yard passing play to Minnesota receiver Darius Taylor. He would’ve scored if it wasn’t for safety Jamison Patton catching up and making the tackle. Lindsey then targeted Rojas again on Minnesota’s first touchdown of the day.

Penn State has been outscored 56-16 in the third quarter during Big Ten play, something Matt Campbell said last Tuesday is a “real problem.”

Stock up: Benjamin Brahmer

It’s been a relatively quiet senior year for Brahmer, who came into the season on the John Mackey Award watch list. After scoring three times in the first two games of the year, he was unable to find the end zone for seven weeks.

Against Minnesota on Saturday, Brahmer recorded a touchdown for the first time since Week 2, reeling in two touchdowns from Becht.

It was an incredibly efficient day for the Brahmer, as he caught the ball just twice but scored on each of the receptions. He nearly had a third receiving touchdown, but the call was overturned by the referees.

With two weeks to play in the regular season, Brahmer leads the team with five receiving touchdowns and sits third with 323 receiving yards.

title: Penn State TE Benjamin Brahmer’s 2 touchdowns against Minnesota ‘showcase his God-given talent’
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Three of tight end Benjamin Brahmer’s four targets in Penn State’s 42-14 victory over Minnesota on Saturday night were in the end zone while he was heavily guarded, as he finished with two touchdowns on just two catches.

As Brahmer has morphed into a premier red-zone threat for the Nittany Lions, Rocco Becht has relied on his tight end’s towering frame and secure hands to make plays only he can make.

“You’ve just gotta not think about it and go make the play,” Brahmer said postgame. “Matt (Campbell) always tells us you’ve got to be the one to go up and get the ball, and then come down with it too, obviously.”

In the first quarter, Becht placed a bullet pass above Brahmer’s head in the back of the end zone for a 19-yard strike and Penn State’s second touchdown. It was a ball the tight end had to leap for through double coverage, but he still came down with it despite taking a shot to the hip.

Brahmer had a one-handed grab late in the second quarter, toe-tapping the back of the end zone for what would’ve been his second touchdown of the game. However, the officials said he didn’t have full possession of the ball and the pass was ruled incomplete.

It didn’t matter, as he went back out in the third quarter and found an open gap in the middle of the end zone for a 4-yard touchdown reception.

Becht was relieved at the success of his tight end, as they’ve put in the work to have results like Saturday.

The quarterback recalled the times he’d overthrown Brahmer, contributing to his quiet outings. So Becht leaned into Brahmer’s ability to catch through traffic and trusted his own skills as a passer to get the ball in the best spot for him, even if it meant threading the needle.

“Finally we were able to connect in the end zone,” Becht said with a smile. “I know we've been trying to do that for the past couple of weeks, but I think for me it's whether he's covered by one guy, two guys, just being able to put a ball where he's able to go get it.”

Campbell praised Brahmer’s work ethic postgame, specifically how he’s not an outspoken person. Instead, Brahmer has a blue-collar, hard-nosed style of football fueled by relentless effort that helps him capitalize when his number is called.

Even in the postgame press conference, Brahmer barely spoke about himself. He spent the time mostly discussing running back Carson Hansen or the team’s resiliency to bounce back from its four-game losing skid.

“Ben's an elite worker, he doesn't say a word,” Campbell said. “He's the same guy every single day in practice, and he only continues to showcase his God-given talent every time he gets the opportunity to do it, and we're really proud of him. I thought he was outstanding tonight. I thought he had an unbelievable game.”

Campbell also said he’s “fortunate” to have been with Brahmer since he came out of high school. Watching his collegiate journey unfold, Campbell has grown accustomed to his freakish talent, and it was only a matter of time before he had a day like Saturday.

“(Brahmer) never shocks me in terms of what he does,” Campbell said. “His level of excellence is as high as he wants to take it.”

title: Column | It’s time to give credit to Penn State’s coaching staff for turning this season around
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
As Rocco Becht spoke to the media with tears in his eyes after Michigan, it felt like Penn State had hit rock bottom. Four straight losses. An offense struggling to score points. Zero semblance of a rushing attack.

Nearly a month later, Becht was all smiles after a third straight win. His offense had just put up 42 points despite him having just 84 passing yards. The Nittany Lions reached bowl eligibility, and the offense has scored 28 points or more in each of the last three games.

It’s clear something changed during the bye week for Penn State, as it’s looked like a completely different team since. And that’s a big testament to Matt Campbell, who could very well end his first year at the helm 8-4.

“I said it from the beginning, that we weren't going to shortcut this process,” Campbell said postgame. “We weren't going to try to win at all costs. We were going to try to build the right foundation, and we were going to do it the right way.”

Campbell has been very honest in his assessment of his team from the beginning and also transparent that his goal this season is to build a foundation for a program he hopes to bring success down the line.

After destroying Buffalo in the final game of the nonconference slate, Campbell said he didn’t think Penn State was where it needed to be heading into Big Ten play. That proved true with a loss to Wisconsin, which then snowballed into three more losses and heavy questioning about whether Campbell was really the right guy for this job after all.

But now Campbell might finish with the same record as many other big-shot first-year head coaches. See Lane Kiffin at LSU, which is now 6-4, just like Penn State (albeit a bit of a harder schedule). Will Stein and Kentucky now have three losses. Kyle Whittingham has Michigan in utter chaos. And James Franklin just lost to Stanford.

So while it seemed bad for a bit, there are plenty of other programs dealing with the same thing. Not everyone can be Bob Chesney at UCLA.

“We've worked really hard to try to lay those foundations, and we're going to continue to work really hard to lay those foundations,” Campbell said. “I think that's more important than even a win or a loss as to how we do it, and you earn the right to win football games, and this group is certainly doing those things right now.”

The reasons for Penn State’s turnaround are endless. Carson Hansen looks like a completely different running back. Cam Wallace has emerged as a legit Big Ten rusher. The pass rush has picked things up. Becht hasn’t turned the ball over. The offensive line is clicking.

There are plenty more nuances to name, but behind all of those is a group of players that have become a team. It just took a bit to get there.

“I think you've seen it the past two games and even this game, we're playing as a team, and you can see it out there,” Becht said. “We're playing for one another, special teams, offense, defense. We're all playing together, and we're all convicted. I think we had a full team game today. I think we're just so connected right now, and coming up towards the end of the year, this is when we're playing our best football. ”

Penn State wouldn’t have reached this point, though, if it wasn’t for the way this coaching staff carries itself. Wallace said Campbell has been the same person throughout the hard times and the better ones. Tight end Benjamin Brahmer said Taylor Mouser “had fun today” and is “the hardest worker I know.”

“Just the late nights he spends with all the coaches on the offensive staff, and just continue to refine what he can do in the details, and continue to make this offense better for us,” Brahmer said.

Of course, there is the “what if” of it all. What if Penn State had held onto its lead against Wisconsin? What if Becht hadn’t turned the ball over three times against Michigan? What if the Nittany Lions offense had scored a touchdown in the second half against USC?

Yes, there is a world in which Penn State’s still playing for a spot in the College Football Playoff. There will be a “what could’ve been” surrounding this team for the rest of the year. But the Nittany Lions are rolling, and kudos to Campbell for how dramatically things have changed.

“This group chose to stay together and find solutions and work through it,” Campbell said. “We'll see where this group ends. We still got eight guaranteed quarters to us left. And where do we end this season? Who do we become? Can we continue to grow and get better? I think there's still great challenges for us. So we've made great steps forward, which is awesome, but I think there's still a lot for this football team to decide who it wants to be and how it wants to finish.”

title: Penn State gains bowl eligibility in win over Minnesota after staying 'process-oriented'
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State will be playing a 13th game after beating Minnesota, 42-14, for their sixth victory of the season.

The Nittany Lions are now bowl eligible after what’s been a tumultuous season with many highs and lows — the “storm of the college football season” as Matt Campbell had described it on numerous occasions leading up to the season.

Campbell knew the team was going to face adversity, and he said making a bowl was a testament to the team staying committed to the process.

“I don't think I've ever wavered from my beliefs in what this football team could become and who they were,” Campbell said when asked about bowl eligibility postgame. “I think there's been a lot that this group, coaching staff included, has had to work through to navigate this whole journey.”

Even when the team lost games to USC and Michigan, Campbell felt there was improvement and held onto his faith in his players. After dominating Minnesota, he noted the team’s collective improvement since its loss to Northwestern in Week 5.

Linebacker Kooper Ebel said he’s proud of the team’s commitment to improving day after day instead of pinning the blame on any aspect of the team in particular, crediting comradery as the biggest influence on getting out of Penn State’s four-game slump.

“No one ever complained,” Ebel said. “No one ever pointed fingers. There was a lot of inward looking, ‘Man, what could I do better?’ I felt like everyone came to practice every day, win, loss, whatever the result was. We weren't result-driven. We were just process-oriented, and man, it's paying off.”

Ebel and his teammates had a common consensus after beating Minnesota — defeating Rutgers and Maryland, the final two games on Penn State’s regular season schedule. But Ebel understood the weight of making a bowl after everything the team has gone through.

“It's awesome, (the bowl) means everything to us,” Ebel said. “It's been a whirlwind of a season. This is great momentum. We obviously have a handful of regular season games left but we're gonna use this momentum, capitalize on it and finish this thing the right way.”

Defensive tackle Dallas Vakalahi said the team’s goal was always to beat every opponent in front of them, and “a byproduct of winning was going to be the bowl.”

Rocco Becht echoed that sentiment, and his plan isn’t to sit back and wait for the bowl game — he’s gunning to finish the regular season 8-4. He said the Nittany Lions are “playing our best football” down the stretch and they're going to carry the momentum through to the end.

But first, Penn State has to host the Scarlet Knights next week and pay the Terrapins a visit two days after Thanksgiving before any bowl trophies are involved.

“We're going to take it game-by-game now,” Becht said. “We’ve still got two more games. We want to win eight games this year, and that's the goal right now. That's where our eyes are. It's awesome that we are bowl eligible now, but we’ve got to be prepared for next week and the week after.”

title: ‘It starts up front’ | Penn State’s DL controls line of scrimmage in dominant win over Minnesota
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
When defensive end Alex McPherson wrapped up Minnesota quarterback Drake Lindsey for a sack, it marked the defensive end’s first sack as a Nittany Lion and his second straight play with a tackle behind the line of scrimmage.

McPherson’s performance was part of a dominant showing from the defensive front that controlled the line of scrimmage consistently for the first time all season. The Nittany Lions had eight tackles for loss, their most in Big Ten play.

“McPherson's an elite football player,” linebacker Kooper Ebel said. “I think a lot of people forget that he's really a true sophomore. He doesn't play like it, and the way that he leads and he carries himself in the facility and how he goes about his business, you would never know, but he's been a great game changer for us.”

Ebel said McPherson’s process as a football player is the thing that stands out about him, truly making him “elite.” That includes how he handles himself in the weight room and nutrition.

“Everything that he does is like a pro, and that's really impressive for a young guy to have that figured out as soon as he does,” Ebel said.

McPherson felt it was a long time coming to notch his first sack in a Penn State uniform. It was also the first solo sack of his career. But it all comes back to the consistency of his work, knowing “it’ll pay off eventually.”

The sophomore’s performance was just part of the strong showing from the front seven. Defensive tackle Dallas Vakalahi also recorded his first sack as a Penn Stater, and it was the first time he sacked a quarterback in almost two years.

“I saw the tackle, his set kind of showed me pass,” Vakalahi said. “I thought to myself, ‘I'm gonna get back there.’ I pictured it. I was going to, and I got there. It's kind of one of those moments that made a full circle for me, just knowing that what I'm doing in practice is paying off for me.”

The defensive line limited a Minnesota team that trotted out four different running backs to 41 yards rushing. While it was already struggling in the run game, averaging 98.56 yards per game, Penn State lowered that number with its performance on Saturday.

It’s an improvement from the week prior, where Washington, which also struggles to run the ball consistently, ran for 134 yards on the ground.

“Week by week, I think we progressively got better each and every week, and it shows on tape,” Vakalahi said. “I think this was probably one of our best weeks yet, and hope to see more production from all of us as a whole.”

Even with the high numbers of tackles for loss, Matt Campbell doesn’t think the interior of the defensive line gets enough credit for what it’s done. Campbell felt they got vertical in the win over Minnesota and overall “did a great job.”

Eight different players recorded a tackle for loss on Saturday. Three different players got credit for sacks, which doesn’t include the 12-yard sack Tony Rojas had that was wiped away by a defensive holding penalty on the Golden Gophers’ opening drive.

“We know we have a very talented group, and it shows up in practice,” McPherson said. “At the beginning of the season we just needed to finish a little bit more at the end of our rushes. But we're a very talented group, and I have had faith in us the whole time, and so has our coaches, and so has everybody else in the building, because they know how talented we are at the defensive line position.”

Penn State’s front seven understands the talent it has on paper. It showcased what that talent can do when it all gets put together on the field. Now, it comes down to carrying that level of play into the final weeks of the season.

“I think one of the big things is it shows us where we can be every game and striving for that standard every game now, going forward, knowing that we have the ability to make TFLs and sacks to disrupt offenses,” Vakalahi said. “Because at the end of the day, it starts up front with us seven.”

title: ‘Everything's just clicking now’ | Penn State RB Carson Hansen has explosive showing against Minnesota
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
As Carson Hansen took the handoff from Rocco Becht just across midfield, he immediately shed a tackle and made three more Minnesota defenders miss on his way to a 46-yard touchdown.

Hansen, a Lakeville, Minnesota, native, was a 3-star recruit coming out of high school, with 16 offers from various schools across the country. But despite growing up just 30 minutes away from campus, he wasn’t offered by the Golden Gophers.

Saturday night was his first career game against Minnesota, and he made the most of his moments against his hometown team. Hansen finished the day with 12 carries for 126 yards and a touchdown, averaging over 10 yards per carry for the first time this season.

“He's confident in himself every single day,” Becht said postgame. “He comes to work every single day. He's a great leader. Nothing's changed. I think he's just been able to make it happen now, and super proud of that guy and what he's been able to do.”

Hansen’s first season at Penn State was a tale of two halves, as he averaged just 39.7 yards per game in the first seven contests of the year. He’s flipped that script since the bye week, now averaging 113.7 yards in each of the last three games.

“I've seen that guy for years run the ball, so I know what he's capable of,” offensive lineman Trevor Buhr said. “Seeing him be able to take that step and keep just making explosive runs, it's awesome.”

Unfortunately for Hansen, it was also a tale of two halves against Minnesota. Hansen’s entire 126-yard performance came in the first 29 minutes of the game, as he limped off the field with a minute left in the second quarter and didn’t return after the half.

“I do think he'll be all right,” Campbell said. “I don’t think it’s a significant injury, but we’ll certainly know more probably earlier this week about what his availability will be next week.”

Regardless, Hansen’s production had been steadily growing throughout Big Ten play. He now has back-to-back 100-yard performances against Washington and Minnesota and 341 yards across his last 10 quarters.

But it hasn’t necessarily been a matter of Hansen doing anything different, as Campbell said “this guy is the same guy all the time.”

“I obviously think it was more of the people around him than it was Carson early in the season, and just consistently getting the running game to where we needed it to get to,” Campbell said. “I think trying to put together the five offensive linemen, finding the consistency, what do they do best, and trying to work through that, that's been a work in progress, but we got there.”

A big reason for Hansen’s newfound success is the offensive line’s growth in run blocking. It opened many holes for Hansen to pick up chunk yardage against the Golden Gophers.

The front five created gaps early for Hansen, who had a 34-yard rush on Penn State’s first drive of the game. On that possession, he was handed the ball four straight times before Becht finished the drive with a passing touchdown.

Hansen had rushes of 47 yards and 22 yards as well. He now has eight rushes over 10 yards in the last three games after having zero in the first four conference matchups of the year.

“The o-line blocked their a— off, and that kind of just opens up everything,” tight end Benjamin Brahmer said.

Part of the reason Hansen’s been able to stay the course this season is his humble demeanor. He’s been “the same person every day,” according to multiple of his teammates, and that’s led to a late-season breakout.

“His confidence has stayed the same,” Becht said. “The person who comes into the facility every single day is the same. The conviction that he has, the trust that he has in everyone, he's stayed the same. He's super humble, and I think it's just for him, everything's just clicking now. He's able to go out there, just play free, have fun, and be a gamer, and that's what Carson is.”

title: 3 takeaways from Penn State's domination of Minnesota
author: Andrew Deal | Wrestling Editor
description:
Penn State and Minnesota met for the Governor’s Victory Bell on a cold and rainy night inside Beaver Stadium.

The Nittany Lions took down the Golden Gophers behind two touchdown receptions from tight end Benjamin Brahmer in a 42-14 victory to clinch bowl eligibility.

Here’s three takeaways from Penn State’s victory.

Brahmer is good at scoring touchdowns

Entering the game, Brahmer had three touchdown receptions on the season, but hadn’t scored one since Week 2 against Temple. That’s a low number given the matchup nightmare the 6-foot-7 tight end is.

Brahmer was targeted three times, all in the end zone, as he came down with two of the passes for touchdowns. While he didn’t make much of an impact outside of the red zone, he contributed two touchdowns to Penn State’s offensive outburst.

“Ben's an elite worker; he doesn't say a word,” Matt Campbell said postgame. “He's a guy that comes out. He's the same guy every single day in practice, and he only continues to showcase his God-given talent every time he gets the opportunity to do it, and we're really proud of him.”

Additionally, Brahmer almost had a third touchdown reception. Similar to his first touchdown catch where he utilized his size to go up and grab it, he reached up to try to snag Rocco Becht’s high pass with one hand. The refs ruled Brahmer didn’t have possession as he went out of bounds.

The tight end’s presence when the Nittany Lions have entered the red zone hasn’t been there prior to Saturday’s game, which could be why Penn State struggled in the red zone during its losing streak, as Becht didn’t utilize his biggest target.

On both of Brahmer’s touchdown receptions, he was a receiver Becht resorted to late in his progression. The connection the two had prior to his season allowed Becht to comfortably feed him the ball in tight windows.

Penn State has found its red zone target, one it should’ve been looking to earlier in the season. But it’s better late than never, as he nearly doubled his touchdown total on the season.

Penn State is a first half team

For the second straight week, Penn State took a big lead into halftime. It also once again played a much different game in the second half.

The Nittany Lions led 28-0 at halftime and had full control of the game, closing it out with a touchdown with under a minute to go. Both sides of the ball were playing at a high level, which changed as the second half began.

Penn State scored a touchdown on its first drive, but it came to a halt after that, as the defense began to allow Minnesota to gain some rhythm on offense.

“We're able to be more detailed in our plays in the first half, and then in the third quarter, we had a little bit of a lull today,” Becht said. “But I felt like we were able to get out of it faster than normal.”

Two long completions from quarterback Drake Lindsey to running back Darius Taylor set up both of the Golden Gophers’ touchdowns. It was two of the longest plays of the game for Minnesota, which was crawling back into the contest.

A 28-point lead turned into a 21-point game at one point in the fourth quarter, with Minnesota driving, and although it won, it still played its best football in the first half.

The Nittany Lions’ final two games are against two of the worst teams in the Big Ten. However, if they don’t start off as hot as they have in the past two weeks, they could end up in a dogfight with either Rutgers or Maryland.

Run game has found consistency

After Penn State had three straight games where it rushed for under 100 yards as a team, it put together two straight strong rushing games out of the bye week.

That continued Saturday night as the duo of Carson Hansen and Cam Wallace showcased its ability to be a strong one-two punch.

Hansen only played the first half, as he left the game limping right before the Nittany Lions’ fourth touchdown. He ran for 126 yards and a touchdown on 12 carries, breaking multiple big runs, with a season-high 10.5 yards per carry.

Wallace was the main running back in the second half, and he tallied 82 yards with a length of 23 yards. He showcased his ability to complement Hansen well, and without Hansen as a counterpart in the second half, the rushing numbers dropped.

“I think trying to put together the five offensive linemen, finding the consistency, what do they do best, and trying to work through that, that's been a work in progress, but we got there,” Campbell said.

The Nittany Lions have quickly found a way to play complementary offense, something it struggled to do early in the season. Because of it, the team has been able to put together a win streak.

Given the weather conditions, having a run game was going to be something either team needed. Penn State ran better and was the team to come out with the victory.

title: Penn State releases availability report, captains ahead of Saturday matchup against Minnesota
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State released its final availability report and captains for Saturday's game against Minnesota.

Cornerback Jahmir Joseph and defensive end Caleb Bacon are out against the Golden Gophers, while offensive lineman Malachi Goodman and safety Jeremiah Cooper are game-time decisions.

Joseph and Bacon were listed as questionable on Thursday and Friday's availability report. Redshirt sophomore Ibn McDaniels will likely see a bigger role in the secondary as a result of Joseph's absence.

Cooper was also listed as questionable leading up to game day, but was upgraded to a game-time decision. This is his second straight week as a game-time decision.

Goodman first missed time against Purdue on Oct. 31. He was probable leading up to last week's game against Washington, but only played the first half. Redshirt sophomore Garrett Sexton took his place.

The Nittany Lions have four of the same captains from the last two weeks, with Rocco Becht, offensive lineman Anthony Donkoh, linebacker Kooper Ebel and cornerback Audavion Collins representing the team.

This is the fourth time the four have been captains this year, as they took the field together in Week 4 against Wisconsin, Week 9 against Purdue and Week 10 against Washington.

Wide receiver Chase Sowell was added for the first time as a fifth captain, marking the first time there have been five captains.

Penn State kicks off against Minnesota at 7 p.m. in Beaver Stadium.
